cards.front: During N2 sleep, a K-complex is followed by a brief burst of EMG activity and a shift to faster EEG frequencies lasting 2 seconds. How should this be scored?
cards.back: Normal N2 variability
cards.rationale: A scored arousal requires an EEG frequency shift lasting at least 3 seconds, so a 2-second shift does not meet arousal criteria.
cards.keyPoint: A scored arousal requires an EEG frequency shift lasting at least 3 seconds, so a 2-second shift does not meet arousal criteria.

cards.front: Which respiratory signal is most sensitive for detecting flow limitation?
cards.back: Nasal pressure transducer
cards.rationale: The nasal pressure signal is the most sensitive routine PSG signal for inspiratory flow limitation and waveform flattening.
cards.keyPoint: The nasal pressure signal is the most sensitive routine PSG signal for inspiratory flow limitation and waveform flattening.

cards.front: A patient shows irregular breathing with waxing and waning tidal volume but no central apneas. What pattern is this?
cards.back: Periodic breathing
cards.rationale: Periodic breathing is a broader waxing-and-waning breathing pattern and may occur without the central-apnea pattern required for Cheyne-Stokes respiration.
cards.keyPoint: Periodic breathing is a broader waxing-and-waning breathing pattern and may occur without the central-apnea pattern required for Cheyne-Stokes respiration.

cards.front: A patient's airflow signal shows flattening but no desaturation or arousal. What event is this most consistent with?
cards.back: Flow limitation without event
cards.rationale: Inspiratory flattening alone suggests flow limitation, but without an arousal or qualifying consequence it is not scored as a hypopnea or RERA.
cards.keyPoint: Inspiratory flattening alone suggests flow limitation, but without an arousal or qualifying consequence it is not scored as a hypopnea or RERA.

cards.front: Which PAP response is appropriate when hypopneas persist but snoring has resolved?
cards.back: Increase pressure
cards.rationale: Persistent obstructive hypopneas during PAP titration generally call for upward pressure adjustment rather than lowering pressure or adding oxygen first.
cards.keyPoint: Persistent obstructive hypopneas during PAP titration generally call for upward pressure adjustment rather than lowering pressure or adding oxygen first.

cards.front: Which of the following is the most likely cause of high-frequency artifact across all EEG channels?
cards.back: Muscle tension
cards.rationale: Diffuse high-frequency artifact across EEG channels is most consistent with muscle activity, not sweat drift or cardiac artifact.
cards.keyPoint: Diffuse high-frequency artifact across EEG channels is most consistent with muscle activity, not sweat drift or cardiac artifact.

cards.front: A patient's thoracic belt shows effort but the abdominal belt does not. What does this suggest?
cards.back: Loose abdominal belt
cards.rationale: When one effort channel drops out while the rest of the respiratory picture remains active, a loose or poorly functioning belt should be considered first.
cards.keyPoint: When one effort channel drops out while the rest of the respiratory picture remains active, a loose or poorly functioning belt should be considered first.

cards.front: Which of the following is required to score N3 sleep?
cards.back: Delta waves >=20% of the epoch
cards.rationale: N3 requires slow-wave activity in at least 20% of the epoch.
cards.keyPoint: N3 requires slow-wave activity in at least 20% of the epoch.

cards.front: A patient shows repeated arousals associated with increasing respiratory effort but no desaturation. What event should be scored?
cards.back: RERA
cards.rationale: Increasing respiratory effort leading to an arousal without meeting apnea or hypopnea criteria is most consistent with a RERA.
cards.keyPoint: Increasing respiratory effort leading to an arousal without meeting apnea or hypopnea criteria is most consistent with a RERA.

cards.front: Which artifact is most likely when EEG amplitude increases dramatically during sweating?
cards.back: Low-frequency drift
cards.rationale: Sweat artifact typically appears as a slow rolling baseline sway or low-frequency drift rather than fast interference.
cards.keyPoint: Sweat artifact typically appears as a slow rolling baseline sway or low-frequency drift rather than fast interference.

cards.front: Which of the following is the best indicator of wake during a respiratory event?
cards.back: Alpha rhythm
cards.rationale: Posterior alpha rhythm remains the strongest classic wake indicator among these options.
cards.keyPoint: Posterior alpha rhythm remains the strongest classic wake indicator among these options.

cards.front: Which EEG frequency range defines theta activity?
cards.back: 4-7 Hz
cards.rationale: Theta activity is defined by a frequency range of 4-7 Hz.
cards.keyPoint: Theta activity is defined by a frequency range of 4-7 Hz.

cards.front: A patient shows airflow reduction of 35% with a 3% desaturation. What should be scored?
cards.back: Hypopnea
cards.rationale: A >=30% airflow reduction lasting at least 10 seconds with a >=3% desaturation meets adult hypopnea criteria.
cards.keyPoint: A >=30% airflow reduction lasting at least 10 seconds with a >=3% desaturation meets adult hypopnea criteria.

cards.front: Which signal is required to identify respiratory effort?
cards.back: Thoracoabdominal belts
cards.rationale: Thoracoabdominal effort belts are the standard signals used to identify respiratory effort.
cards.keyPoint: Thoracoabdominal effort belts are the standard signals used to identify respiratory effort.

cards.front: During N2, a spindle appears immediately after a K-complex. What stage should be scored?
cards.back: N2
cards.rationale: A spindle and K-complex are classic N2 markers, so the epoch is scored as N2 when the rest of the epoch is compatible.
cards.keyPoint: A spindle and K-complex are classic N2 markers, so the epoch is scored as N2 when the rest of the epoch is compatible.

cards.front: A patient on CPAP develops central apneas after pressure increases. What is the most likely cause?
cards.back: CO2 overshoot
cards.rationale: Treatment-emergent central events can follow pressure-related lowering of CO2 below the apnea threshold.
cards.keyPoint: Treatment-emergent central events can follow pressure-related lowering of CO2 below the apnea threshold.

cards.front: Which artifact produces slow, rolling baseline drift?
cards.back: Sweat artifact
cards.rationale: Sweat artifact typically appears as a slow, rolling baseline drift.
cards.keyPoint: Sweat artifact typically appears as a slow, rolling baseline drift.

cards.front: Arousals in NREM require which EEG change?
cards.back: Alpha or faster activity >=3 seconds
cards.rationale: NREM arousals require an abrupt EEG frequency shift including alpha, theta, or frequencies greater than 16 Hz lasting at least 3 seconds.
cards.keyPoint: NREM arousals require an abrupt EEG frequency shift including alpha, theta, or frequencies greater than 16 Hz lasting at least 3 seconds.

cards.front: Which PAP adjustment is appropriate when obstructive apneas persist?
cards.back: Increase EPAP
cards.rationale: With bilevel therapy, persistent obstructive apneas point toward increasing EPAP because EPAP addresses upper-airway splinting.
cards.keyPoint: With bilevel therapy, persistent obstructive apneas point toward increasing EPAP because EPAP addresses upper-airway splinting.

cards.front: Which EEG feature is most consistent with N3 sleep?
cards.back: Delta >=20%
cards.rationale: Stage N3 requires slow-wave activity occupying at least 20% of the epoch.
cards.keyPoint: Stage N3 requires slow-wave activity occupying at least 20% of the epoch.

cards.front: A patient shows rhythmic EEG deflections synchronized with the ECG R-wave. What is this?
cards.back: Cardiac artifact
cards.rationale: EEG activity time-locked to the ECG R-wave is most consistent with cardiac artifact.
cards.keyPoint: EEG activity time-locked to the ECG R-wave is most consistent with cardiac artifact.

cards.front: Which respiratory pattern is most consistent with Cheyne-Stokes respiration?
cards.back: Crescendo-decrescendo pattern with central apneas
cards.rationale: Cheyne-Stokes respiration features a crescendo-decrescendo breathing pattern linked with central apneas or hypopneas.
cards.keyPoint: Cheyne-Stokes respiration features a crescendo-decrescendo breathing pattern linked with central apneas or hypopneas.

cards.front: Which signal is most sensitive for detecting flow limitation?
cards.back: Nasal pressure
cards.rationale: Nasal pressure is the most sensitive commonly used PSG signal for inspiratory flow limitation.
cards.keyPoint: Nasal pressure is the most sensitive commonly used PSG signal for inspiratory flow limitation.

cards.front: A patient shows delta waves occupying 18% of the epoch with a spindle present. How should the epoch be scored?
cards.back: N2
cards.rationale: Because slow-wave activity does not reach the 20% threshold for N3 and an N2 marker is present, the epoch is scored as N2.
cards.keyPoint: Because slow-wave activity does not reach the 20% threshold for N3 and an N2 marker is present, the epoch is scored as N2.

cards.front: According to AASM guidelines, what is the required maximum impedance level for EEG and EOG electrodes?
cards.back: 5 kOhm
cards.rationale: EEG and EOG electrodes should be maintained at 5 kOhm or less to support quality signal acquisition.
cards.keyPoint: EEG and EOG electrodes should be maintained at 5 kOhm or less to support quality signal acquisition.

cards.front: Which of the following defines the frequency of posterior dominant rhythm (also known as alpha rhythm) in a healthy adult?
cards.rationale: Posterior dominant rhythm (also known as alpha rhythm) is typically defined by the 8-13 Hz frequency range in adults.
cards.keyPoint: Posterior dominant rhythm (also known as alpha rhythm) is typically defined by the 8-13 Hz frequency range in adults.

cards.front: In the International 10-20 system, what is the distance from Fp1 to O1 if the total measurement from Nasion to Inion is 36 cm?
cards.back: This cannot be calculated from the Nasion to Inion measurement alone.
cards.rationale: A single nasion-to-inion measurement does not provide enough information to calculate the diagonal distance from Fp1 to O1.
cards.keyPoint: A single nasion-to-inion measurement does not provide enough information to calculate the diagonal distance from Fp1 to O1.

cards.front: According to AASM scoring rules, a pediatric obstructive apnea is scored when the event lasts for at least:
cards.back: 2 missed breaths
cards.rationale: Pediatric obstructive apnea is scored using a duration of at least two missed breaths.
cards.keyPoint: Pediatric obstructive apnea is scored using a duration of at least two missed breaths.

cards.front: What are the standard Low Frequency Filter (LFF) and High Frequency Filter (HFF) settings for an EMG channel?
cards.back: LFF 10 Hz, HFF 100 Hz
cards.rationale: The standard EMG filter settings are a 10 Hz low frequency filter and a 100 Hz high frequency filter.
cards.keyPoint: The standard EMG filter settings are a 10 Hz low frequency filter and a 100 Hz high frequency filter.

cards.front: Which of the following is a primary characteristic of Stage N1 sleep?
cards.back: Slow rolling eye movements (SEMs)
cards.rationale: Slow rolling eye movements are a classic N1 feature, whereas K-complexes and spindles indicate N2.
cards.keyPoint: Slow rolling eye movements are a classic N1 feature, whereas K-complexes and spindles indicate N2.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: During a Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT), a Sleep Onset REM Period (SOREMP) is recorded when REM sleep occurs within how many minutes of sleep onset?
cards.back: 15 minutes
cards.rationale: A SOREMP is scored when REM occurs within 15 minutes of sleep onset, and Version 3 adds a dedicated reporting section for MSLT and MWT.
cards.keyPoint: A SOREMP is scored when REM occurs within 15 minutes of sleep onset, and Version 3 adds a dedicated reporting section for MSLT and MWT.

cards.front: When performing a CPAP titration, the guidelines state that CPAP pressure should be increased for an adult patient after observing:
cards.back: 3 hypopneas
cards.rationale: Adult CPAP titration guidelines allow pressure increases after three hypopneas, among other event thresholds.
cards.keyPoint: Adult CPAP titration guidelines allow pressure increases after three hypopneas, among other event thresholds.

cards.front: What is the minimum duration required to score a Periodic Limb Movement (PLM)?
cards.back: 0.5 seconds
cards.rationale: A limb movement must last at least 0.5 seconds to be counted for PLM scoring.
cards.keyPoint: A limb movement must last at least 0.5 seconds to be counted for PLM scoring.

cards.front: To score a sequence of limb movements as PLMs, what is the minimum number of consecutive limb movements that must occur?
cards.rationale: PLMS require a sequence of at least four qualifying limb movements.
cards.keyPoint: PLMS require a sequence of at least four qualifying limb movements.

cards.front: The appearance of 60 Hz artifact in an EEG channel is most commonly caused by:
cards.back: High electrode impedance
cards.rationale: High impedance and poor grounding increase susceptibility to 60 Hz electrical interference.
cards.keyPoint: High impedance and poor grounding increase susceptibility to 60 Hz electrical interference.

cards.front: In a normal adult sleep architecture, Stage N3 (slow-wave sleep) typically accounts for approximately what percentage of total sleep time?
cards.rationale: A healthy adult commonly spends about 15-25% of total sleep time in Stage N3.
cards.keyPoint: A healthy adult commonly spends about 15-25% of total sleep time in Stage N3.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: What does End-Tidal CO2 (ETCO2) monitoring primarily measure?
cards.back: Carbon dioxide concentration at the end of an exhaled breath
cards.rationale: ETCO2 monitoring measures carbon dioxide at end exhalation, reflecting ventilatory status.
cards.keyPoint: ETCO2 monitoring measures carbon dioxide at end exhalation, reflecting ventilatory status.

cards.front: Which medication class is known to significantly reduce or suppress REM sleep?
cards.back: Antidepressants (SSRIs)
cards.rationale: SSRIs are well known for suppressing or reducing REM sleep.
cards.keyPoint: SSRIs are well known for suppressing or reducing REM sleep.

cards.front: The natural pacemaker of the heart is the:
cards.back: SA node
cards.rationale: The sinoatrial node is the heart's natural pacemaker.
cards.keyPoint: The sinoatrial node is the heart's natural pacemaker.

cards.front: When scoring an arousal during NREM sleep, the EEG frequency shift must last for at least:
cards.back: 3 seconds
cards.rationale: NREM arousals require an abrupt EEG frequency shift lasting at least 3 seconds.
cards.keyPoint: NREM arousals require an abrupt EEG frequency shift lasting at least 3 seconds.

cards.front: For scoring an arousal in Stage R (REM) sleep, the AASM rules require an EEG frequency shift of at least 3 seconds AND:
cards.back: A concurrent increase in submental EMG tone lasting at least 1 second
cards.rationale: REM arousals require the 3-second EEG shift plus at least 1 second of concurrent submental EMG increase.
cards.keyPoint: REM arousals require the 3-second EEG shift plus at least 1 second of concurrent submental EMG increase.

cards.front: A Cheyne-Stokes respiration pattern is defined by episodes of central apneas/hypopneas accompanied by:
cards.back: A crescendo-decrescendo pattern of breathing volume
cards.rationale: Cheyne-Stokes respiration features a crescendo-decrescendo breathing pattern linked to central events.
cards.keyPoint: Cheyne-Stokes respiration features a crescendo-decrescendo breathing pattern linked to central events.

cards.front: Which sensor is recommended by the AASM for detecting respiratory effort?
cards.back: Respiratory inductance plethysmography (RIP) belts
cards.rationale: Thoracoabdominal RIP belts are the recommended standard for respiratory effort monitoring.
cards.keyPoint: Thoracoabdominal RIP belts are the recommended standard for respiratory effort monitoring.

cards.front: Sweat artifact in an EEG recording typically appears as:
cards.back: Slow, rolling baseline sway
cards.rationale: Sweat artifact appears as a slow, wandering baseline drift rather than fast interference.
cards.keyPoint: Sweat artifact appears as a slow, wandering baseline drift rather than fast interference.

cards.front: If a patient's heart rate drops below 40 beats per minute during sleep, this is classified as:
cards.back: Bradycardia
cards.rationale: A heart rate below 40 bpm is classified as bradycardia.
cards.keyPoint: A heart rate below 40 bpm is classified as bradycardia.

cards.front: According to AASM rules, a major body movement (MBM) artifact that obscures the EEG for more than 15 seconds of an epoch should be scored as:
cards.back: Both A and B are correct depending on the presence of posterior dominant rhythm
cards.rationale: MBM epochs are scored Wake if posterior dominant rhythm is present; otherwise they may inherit the previous stage under AASM rules.
cards.keyPoint: MBM epochs are scored Wake if posterior dominant rhythm is present; otherwise they may inherit the previous stage under AASM rules.

cards.front: Which of the following is the recommended sensor for scoring apneas?
cards.back: Oronasal thermal airflow sensor (thermistor/thermocouple)
cards.rationale: Oronasal thermal airflow sensors are the recommended apnea-detection sensor for scoring apneas.
cards.keyPoint: Oronasal thermal airflow sensors are the recommended apnea-detection sensor for scoring apneas.

cards.front: The presence of paradoxical breathing (chest moving inward while abdomen moves outward during inspiration) is typically an indicator of:
cards.back: Upper airway resistance/obstruction
cards.rationale: Paradoxical breathing suggests upper-airway obstruction rather than normal breathing or central apnea.
cards.keyPoint: Paradoxical breathing suggests upper-airway obstruction rather than normal breathing or central apnea.

cards.front: Which stage of sleep is most commonly characterized by the presence of vertex sharp waves?
cards.back: Stage N1
cards.rationale: Vertex sharp waves are most commonly associated with Stage N1 sleep.
cards.keyPoint: Vertex sharp waves are most commonly associated with Stage N1 sleep.

cards.front: According to AASM pediatric scoring rules, a respiratory event is scored as a hypopnea if the amplitude drops by at least 30% and is associated with an arousal, an awakening, or a drop in SpO2 of at least:
cards.rationale: Pediatric hypopnea criteria use a >=30% amplitude reduction plus an arousal, awakening, or >=3% desaturation.
cards.keyPoint: Pediatric hypopnea criteria use a >=30% amplitude reduction plus an arousal, awakening, or >=3% desaturation.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: During an MSLT, the patient's mean sleep latency is 6 minutes, and they exhibit 2 Sleep Onset REM Periods (SOREMPs). These findings are most indicative of:
cards.back: Narcolepsy
cards.rationale: A short mean sleep latency with two SOREMPs is strongly suggestive of narcolepsy.
cards.keyPoint: A short mean sleep latency with two SOREMPs is strongly suggestive of narcolepsy.

cards.front: AASM recommends which of the following for monitoring hypoventilation during pediatric sleep studies?
cards.back: End-tidal or transcutaneous PCO2
cards.rationale: Pediatric hypoventilation is monitored using end-tidal or transcutaneous CO2 rather than oximetry alone.
cards.keyPoint: Pediatric hypoventilation is monitored using end-tidal or transcutaneous CO2 rather than oximetry alone.

cards.front: In a healthy adult, a typical sleep cycle (progressing from NREM through REM) lasts approximately:
cards.back: 90-120 minutes
cards.rationale: A typical adult sleep cycle is approximately 90 to 120 minutes in length.
cards.keyPoint: A typical adult sleep cycle is approximately 90 to 120 minutes in length.

cards.front: During biocalibrations, the patient is instructed to "look left" and then "look right." Assuming standard electrode placement, the Left and Right EOG channels should show:
cards.back: Out-of-phase deflections
cards.rationale: Conjugate eye movements produce opposite-polarity EOG deflections on the standard left and right EOG channels.
cards.keyPoint: Conjugate eye movements produce opposite-polarity EOG deflections on the standard left and right EOG channels.

cards.front: To accurately measure head circumference in the 10-20 system, the tape measure should pass through which specific landmarks?
cards.back: Fpz, T3, Oz, T4, Fpz
cards.rationale: Head circumference in the 10-20 system is measured around the head through Fpz, T3, Oz, T4, and back to Fpz.
cards.keyPoint: Head circumference in the 10-20 system is measured around the head through Fpz, T3, Oz, T4, and back to Fpz.

cards.front: Which common class of medications is known to increase Stage N2 sleep while decreasing both Stage N3 and REM sleep?
cards.back: Benzodiazepines
cards.rationale: Benzodiazepines typically increase Stage N2 while reducing deeper sleep and REM.
cards.keyPoint: Benzodiazepines typically increase Stage N2 while reducing deeper sleep and REM.

cards.front: According to AASM guidelines, the recommended maximum averaging time for an oximeter used during PSG is:
cards.back: 3 seconds
cards.rationale: Oximeters used during PSG should have an averaging time of no more than 3 seconds.
cards.keyPoint: Oximeters used during PSG should have an averaging time of no more than 3 seconds.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: During an MSLT, if a patient falls asleep, the nap trial must be terminated:
cards.back: 15 minutes from the first epoch of scored sleep
cards.rationale: When sleep occurs in an MSLT nap, the trial continues for 15 minutes from the first epoch of scored sleep; Version 3 also adds dedicated reporting guidance for MSLT and MWT.
cards.keyPoint: When sleep occurs in an MSLT nap, the trial continues for 15 minutes from the first epoch of scored sleep; Version 3 also adds dedicated reporting guidance for MSLT and MWT.

cards.front: A patient slept for 360 minutes and had a total of 120 respiratory events (apneas + hypopneas). What is their Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI)?
cards.rationale: AHI = 120 events / 6 hours of sleep = 20 events per hour.
cards.keyPoint: AHI = 120 events / 6 hours of sleep = 20 events per hour.

cards.front: When scoring a hypopnea in an adult according to the AASM "Acceptable" rule (often used for Medicare compliance), the flow must drop by at least 30% for 10 seconds and be associated with:
cards.back: A >=4% oxygen desaturation
cards.rationale: The adult acceptable hypopnea rule uses a >=4% oxygen desaturation.
cards.keyPoint: The adult acceptable hypopnea rule uses a >=4% oxygen desaturation.

cards.front: Which of the following defines a Premature Ventricular Contraction (PVC) on an EKG?
cards.back: A wide, bizarre QRS complex not preceded by a P wave
cards.rationale: PVCs are premature wide QRS complexes that are not preceded by a normal P wave.
cards.keyPoint: PVCs are premature wide QRS complexes that are not preceded by a normal P wave.

cards.front: According to AASM guidelines for PAP titration, "optimal" pressure is reached when the RDI is reduced to less than:
cards.back: 5 per hour (for at least a 15-minute period, including supine REM)
cards.rationale: An optimal titration reduces RDI to less than 5 per hour for at least 15 minutes and includes supine REM sleep.
cards.keyPoint: An optimal titration reduces RDI to less than 5 per hour for at least 15 minutes and includes supine REM sleep.

cards.front: In adults, sleep hypoventilation is scored when the arterial PCO2 (or surrogate) exceeds 55 mmHg for at least:
cards.back: 10 minutes
cards.rationale: Adult sleep hypoventilation is scored when PCO2 exceeds 55 mmHg for at least 10 minutes.
cards.keyPoint: Adult sleep hypoventilation is scored when PCO2 exceeds 55 mmHg for at least 10 minutes.

cards.front: The physical facial characteristic known as "Micrognathia," which is a risk factor for sleep apnea, refers to a:
cards.back: Small, recessed lower jaw
cards.rationale: Micrognathia refers to a small, recessed lower jaw, which can increase upper-airway obstruction risk.
cards.keyPoint: Micrognathia refers to a small, recessed lower jaw, which can increase upper-airway obstruction risk.

cards.front: When titrating supplemental oxygen during a PAP study, oxygen is introduced and titrated upward by 1 L/min when the SpO2 remains below 88% for:
cards.back: 5 minutes
cards.rationale: Supplemental oxygen is typically introduced when SpO2 remains below 88% for 5 minutes during PAP titration.
cards.keyPoint: Supplemental oxygen is typically introduced when SpO2 remains below 88% for 5 minutes during PAP titration.

cards.front: According to the AASM, what is the desired sampling rate for the EKG channel?
cards.back: 500 Hz
cards.rationale: The desired ECG sampling rate is 500 Hz even though lower minimums may also exist, and Version 3 updates the ECG high-frequency filter setting to 100 Hz.
cards.keyPoint: The desired ECG sampling rate is 500 Hz even though lower minimums may also exist, and Version 3 updates the ECG high-frequency filter setting to 100 Hz.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: During a Maintenance of Wakefulness Test (MWT), the trial is terminated if the patient achieves unequivocal sleep, which is defined as:
cards.back: 3 consecutive epochs of N1, or 1 epoch of any other sleep stage
cards.rationale: Unequivocal sleep during MWT is defined as three consecutive epochs of N1 or one epoch of another sleep stage, and Version 3 adds dedicated reporting guidance for MWT.
cards.keyPoint: Unequivocal sleep during MWT is defined as three consecutive epochs of N1 or one epoch of another sleep stage, and Version 3 adds dedicated reporting guidance for MWT.

cards.front: According to AASM scoring rules, a leg movement is scored as part of a PLM sequence if the interval between the onsets of consecutive movements is between:
cards.back: 5 to 90 seconds
cards.rationale: PLMS require intervals of 5 to 90 seconds between movement onsets.
cards.keyPoint: PLMS require intervals of 5 to 90 seconds between movement onsets.

cards.front: Which frequency band characterizes the Theta rhythm?
cards.rationale: Theta rhythm is characterized by frequencies from about 4 to 7.9 Hz.
cards.keyPoint: Theta rhythm is characterized by frequencies from about 4 to 7.9 Hz.

cards.front: In a differential amplifier, what does the Common Mode Rejection Ratio (CMRR) do?
cards.back: Eliminates identical electrical signals picked up by both the exploring and reference electrodes
cards.rationale: CMRR suppresses signals common to both inputs, improving rejection of shared electrical noise.
cards.keyPoint: CMRR suppresses signals common to both inputs, improving rejection of shared electrical noise.

cards.front: During standard pre-study biocalibrations, instructing the patient to "clench your teeth" is primarily used to verify the proper function of which channel?
cards.back: Chin EMG
cards.rationale: Teeth clenching primarily verifies chin EMG responsiveness during biocalibrations.
cards.keyPoint: Teeth clenching primarily verifies chin EMG responsiveness during biocalibrations.

cards.front: A patient in the sleep clinic reports a sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotions such as laughter or surprise. This specific symptom is known as:
cards.back: Cataplexy
cards.rationale: Emotion-triggered sudden loss of muscle tone is classic cataplexy.
cards.keyPoint: Emotion-triggered sudden loss of muscle tone is classic cataplexy.

cards.front: The primary purpose of a "notch filter" (usually set at 50 or 60 Hz) is to:
cards.back: Block environmental electrical interference from power lines and equipment
cards.rationale: A notch filter is used to suppress environmental line-frequency interference.
cards.keyPoint: A notch filter is used to suppress environmental line-frequency interference.

cards.front: In polysomnographic instrumentation, the time constant is directly related to the:
cards.back: Low Frequency Filter (LFF)
cards.rationale: Time constant is directly tied to the low-frequency filter behavior of the recording system.
cards.keyPoint: Time constant is directly tied to the low-frequency filter behavior of the recording system.

cards.front: An EKG rhythm characterized by a PR interval greater than 0.20 seconds, with a QRS complex following every P wave, is classified as:
cards.back: First-degree AV block
cards.rationale: A prolonged PR interval with 1:1 conduction is first-degree AV block.
cards.keyPoint: A prolonged PR interval with 1:1 conduction is first-degree AV block.

cards.front: According to AASM scoring rules, a patient must be continuously asleep for a minimum of how many seconds prior to an event to score an arousal?
cards.back: 10 seconds
cards.rationale: Arousal scoring requires at least 10 seconds of stable sleep preceding the event.
cards.keyPoint: Arousal scoring requires at least 10 seconds of stable sleep preceding the event.

cards.front: Which of the following best describes the criteria for scoring an epoch as stage N1 from stage W in an adult?
cards.back: Alpha rhythm is attenuated and replaced by low-amplitude, mixed-frequency activity for more than 50% of the epoch
cards.rationale: N1 from wake is identified when alpha attenuates and low-amplitude mixed-frequency activity dominates more than half the epoch.
cards.keyPoint: N1 from wake is identified when alpha attenuates and low-amplitude mixed-frequency activity dominates more than half the epoch.

cards.front: According to AASM rules, what is the maximum duration of a respiratory event (apnea or hypopnea) that can be scored in an adult?
cards.back: There is no maximum duration limit
cards.rationale: AASM scoring defines minimum duration criteria for respiratory events but no maximum duration limit.
cards.keyPoint: AASM scoring defines minimum duration criteria for respiratory events but no maximum duration limit.

cards.front: Which sleep disorder is characterized by an uncontrollable urge to move the legs, often accompanied by uncomfortable sensations that worsen in the evening or at rest, but are relieved by movement?
cards.back: Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS)
cards.rationale: Restless Legs Syndrome is defined by an urge to move the legs that worsens at rest and improves with movement.
cards.keyPoint: Restless Legs Syndrome is defined by an urge to move the legs that worsens at rest and improves with movement.

cards.front: If the measurement from the left preauricular point to the right preauricular point over the vertex (Cz) is 36 cm, what is the proper distance from the left preauricular point to the T3 electrode?
cards.back: 3.6 cm
cards.rationale: T3 is located 10% of the preauricular-to-preauricular distance from the left preauricular point.
cards.keyPoint: T3 is located 10% of the preauricular-to-preauricular distance from the left preauricular point.

cards.front: In electrophysiology recording, "Sensitivity" is mathematically defined as:
cards.back: Voltage divided by pen deflection (V/mm)
cards.rationale: Sensitivity is classically expressed as voltage per unit of vertical deflection.
cards.keyPoint: Sensitivity is classically expressed as voltage per unit of vertical deflection.

cards.front: The appearance of slow-wave sleep (Stage N3) is typically most prominent during which portion of the night in a healthy adult?
cards.back: The first third of the night
cards.rationale: Stage N3 is most prominent during the first third of the night in healthy adults.
cards.keyPoint: Stage N3 is most prominent during the first third of the night in healthy adults.

cards.front: Bilevel Positive Airway Pressure (BPAP) in Spontaneous/Timed (S/T) mode incorporates a backup respiratory rate. This mode is most beneficial for patients with:
cards.back: Central Sleep Apnea
cards.rationale: A backup rate is most useful in central apnea and related ventilatory-control disorders.
cards.keyPoint: A backup rate is most useful in central apnea and related ventilatory-control disorders.

cards.front: To score a hypopnea in an adult, the required drop in airflow amplitude must last for at least:
cards.back: 10 seconds
cards.rationale: Adult hypopneas must last at least 10 seconds.
cards.keyPoint: Adult hypopneas must last at least 10 seconds.

cards.front: Standard PSG thermal sensors (thermocouples and thermistors) detect airflow by measuring:
cards.back: Temperature differences between inhaled and exhaled air
cards.rationale: Thermal sensors detect airflow from the temperature difference between inhaled and exhaled air.
cards.keyPoint: Thermal sensors detect airflow from the temperature difference between inhaled and exhaled air.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: The normal range for End-Tidal CO2 (EtCO2) in a healthy, awake adult is approximately:
cards.back: 35-45 mmHg
cards.rationale: Normal awake end-tidal CO2 values are approximately 35 to 45 mmHg.
cards.keyPoint: Normal awake end-tidal CO2 values are approximately 35 to 45 mmHg.

cards.front: A completely flat EKG baseline with no discernable electrical activity for an extended period is known as:
cards.back: Asystole
cards.rationale: A flatline EKG with no discernible electrical activity is asystole.
cards.keyPoint: A flatline EKG with no discernible electrical activity is asystole.

cards.front: Snoring artifact seen clearly in the EEG channels is typically considered what type of artifact?
cards.back: Mechanical/Vibration artifact
cards.rationale: Snoring can transmit mechanical vibration into EEG leads, producing vibration artifact.
cards.keyPoint: Snoring can transmit mechanical vibration into EEG leads, producing vibration artifact.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: In the event of a fire breaking out in the sleep lab, the technologist's FIRST priority, according to the standard RACE protocol, should be to:
cards.back: Rescue or remove patients in immediate danger
cards.rationale: RACE begins with Rescue, making immediate patient rescue the first priority.
cards.keyPoint: RACE begins with Rescue, making immediate patient rescue the first priority.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: During an MSLT, the patient's "sleep latency" is defined as the time from "lights out" to the:
cards.back: First epoch of any stage of sleep
cards.rationale: Sleep latency in MSLT is measured from lights out to the first epoch of any sleep stage.
cards.keyPoint: Sleep latency in MSLT is measured from lights out to the first epoch of any sleep stage.

cards.front: The structure in the brain known as the "biological clock," responsible for regulating circadian rhythms, is the:
cards.back: Suprachiasmatic Nucleus (SCN)
cards.rationale: The suprachiasmatic nucleus is the body's primary circadian pacemaker.
cards.keyPoint: The suprachiasmatic nucleus is the body's primary circadian pacemaker.

cards.front: According to AASM PAP titration guidelines, supplemental oxygen is added if the patient's SpO2 remains below 88% for 5 minutes. The initial starting flow rate for supplemental O2 in adults is usually:
cards.back: 1 L/min
cards.rationale: When supplemental oxygen is added during PAP titration, the usual adult starting flow is 1 L/min.
cards.keyPoint: When supplemental oxygen is added during PAP titration, the usual adult starting flow is 1 L/min.

cards.front: According to the AASM scoring rules, an epoch of Stage N2 sleep ends when:
cards.back: All of the above
cards.rationale: N2 may end with transition to another stage, arousal leading to new stage criteria, or MBM rules followed by qualifying EEG/EOG changes.
cards.keyPoint: N2 may end with transition to another stage, arousal leading to new stage criteria, or MBM rules followed by qualifying EEG/EOG changes.

cards.front: Which sleep state is most associated with the most irregular breathing pattern?
cards.back: REM
cards.rationale: Breathing becomes more variable and irregular in REM sleep.
cards.keyPoint: Breathing becomes more variable and irregular in REM sleep.

cards.front: End-tidal CO2 monitoring primarily reflects:
cards.back: Carbon dioxide at the end of exhalation
cards.rationale: ETCO2 tracks exhaled CO2 near the end of a breath.
cards.keyPoint: ETCO2 tracks exhaled CO2 near the end of a breath.

cards.front: Which method is most useful when monitoring for sleep-related hypoventilation in the lab?
cards.back: Transcutaneous or end-tidal CO2 monitoring
cards.rationale: Hypoventilation is best recognized with CO2 monitoring, not airflow alone.
cards.keyPoint: Hypoventilation is best recognized with CO2 monitoring, not airflow alone.

cards.front: Which statement best matches normal upper-airway physiology during sleep?
cards.back: Upper-airway muscle tone decreases during sleep
cards.rationale: Reduced upper-airway muscle tone makes the airway more collapsible during sleep.
cards.keyPoint: Reduced upper-airway muscle tone makes the airway more collapsible during sleep.

cards.front: A study shows 120 apneas and hypopneas over 6 hours of total sleep time. What is the AHI?
cards.rationale: AHI = total apneas + hypopneas divided by total sleep time in hours. 120 / 6 = 20.
cards.keyPoint: AHI = total apneas + hypopneas divided by total sleep time in hours. 120 / 6 = 20.

cards.front: A patient had 360 minutes of total bedtime and 288 minutes of total sleep time. What is the sleep efficiency?
cards.rationale: Sleep efficiency = TST / total bedtime x 100. 288 / 360 x 100 = 80%.
cards.keyPoint: Sleep efficiency = TST / total bedtime x 100. 288 / 360 x 100 = 80%.

cards.front: If total sleep time is 390 minutes and WASO is 30 minutes, what is the sleep period time (SPT)?
cards.back: 420 minutes
cards.rationale: SPT = TST + WASO.
cards.keyPoint: SPT = TST + WASO.

cards.front: A report shows mild overall AHI, but the study had almost no REM sleep and very little supine sleep. What is the best interpretation watch point to avoid?
cards.back: Assuming the study may have underestimated severity
cards.rationale: OSA can worsen in REM and supine sleep, so limited time in those conditions can make severity look lower than usual.
cards.keyPoint: OSA can worsen in REM and supine sleep, so limited time in those conditions can make severity look lower than usual.

cards.front: Which report value is most helpful for separating REM-predominant OSA from more uniform OSA across the night?
cards.back: REM AHI compared with NREM AHI
cards.rationale: Comparing REM and NREM event burden helps show whether obstruction is more prominent in REM sleep.
cards.keyPoint: Comparing REM and NREM event burden helps show whether obstruction is more prominent in REM sleep.

cards.front: Which value is calculated using only apneas and hypopneas, not RERAs?
cards.back: AHI
cards.rationale: AHI uses apneas and hypopneas; RDI includes a broader respiratory-event picture depending on the definition being used.
cards.keyPoint: AHI uses apneas and hypopneas; RDI includes a broader respiratory-event picture depending on the definition being used.

cards.front: To score an arousal in NREM sleep, the EEG frequency shift must last at least:
cards.back: 3 seconds
cards.rationale: NREM arousals require an abrupt EEG frequency shift lasting at least 3 seconds.
cards.keyPoint: NREM arousals require an abrupt EEG frequency shift lasting at least 3 seconds.

cards.front: Before an arousal can be scored, there must be at least how much stable sleep immediately before it?
cards.back: 10 seconds
cards.rationale: You need at least 10 seconds of continuous sleep before the arousal.
cards.keyPoint: You need at least 10 seconds of continuous sleep before the arousal.

cards.front: In REM sleep, an arousal requires the EEG shift plus:
cards.back: An increase in chin EMG lasting at least 1 second
cards.rationale: REM arousals need the EEG change and a concurrent chin EMG increase.
cards.keyPoint: REM arousals need the EEG change and a concurrent chin EMG increase.

cards.front: Which leg movement duration fits a scoreable limb movement?
cards.back: 0.5 to 10 seconds
cards.rationale: A scoreable leg movement falls within that duration range.
cards.keyPoint: A scoreable leg movement falls within that duration range.

cards.front: How many consecutive limb movements are needed for a PLM series?
cards.rationale: A PLM series requires at least 4 qualifying movements.
cards.keyPoint: A PLM series requires at least 4 qualifying movements.

cards.front: To be part of the same PLM sequence, the interval between movement onsets must be:
cards.back: 5 to 90 seconds
cards.rationale: That onset-to-onset interval defines a PLM sequence.
cards.keyPoint: That onset-to-onset interval defines a PLM sequence.

cards.front: A patient has repeated leg movements, but each movement occurs 2 seconds after the previous one. How should these be treated?
cards.back: As movements that do not meet PLM interval criteria
cards.rationale: The interval is too short for a standard PLM sequence.
cards.keyPoint: The interval is too short for a standard PLM sequence.

cards.front: A K-complex appears in an epoch, but it is immediately followed by low-amplitude mixed-frequency activity without a spindle. If no other stage-defining feature appears, the epoch is still most likely:
cards.back: N2
cards.rationale: A K-complex is a defining N2 feature.
cards.keyPoint: A K-complex is a defining N2 feature.

cards.front: An epoch contains 18% slow-wave activity and also a clear sleep spindle. How should it be scored?
cards.back: N2
cards.rationale: Slow-wave activity does not reach N3 threshold, and the spindle supports N2.
cards.keyPoint: Slow-wave activity does not reach N3 threshold, and the spindle supports N2.

cards.front: A major body movement obscures much of the epoch, but posterior dominant rhythm (alpha rhythm) is clearly seen in part of it. The best score is:
cards.back: Wake
cards.rationale: If wake features such as posterior dominant rhythm are clearly present, score wake rather than leaving it as obscured movement.
cards.keyPoint: If wake features such as posterior dominant rhythm are clearly present, score wake rather than leaving it as obscured movement.

cards.front: Which report value is most helpful when deciding whether leg movements are clinically disrupting sleep continuity?
cards.back: PLM arousal index
cards.rationale: The PLM arousal index better reflects sleep disruption than raw movement count alone.
cards.keyPoint: The PLM arousal index better reflects sleep disruption than raw movement count alone.

cards.front: A study has many respiratory events and many leg movements. What is the main scoring watch point to avoid?
cards.back: Assuming every leg movement is an independent PLM
cards.rationale: Leg movements can occur secondary to respiratory events, so they should not automatically be treated as separate PLMs.
cards.keyPoint: Leg movements can occur secondary to respiratory events, so they should not automatically be treated as separate PLMs.

cards.front: Which finding most strongly supports wake rather than N1 when posterior dominant rhythm is absent?
cards.back: Frequent blinking and movement artifact
cards.rationale: Blinks and waking movement patterns support wakefulness more than N1.
cards.keyPoint: Blinks and waking movement patterns support wakefulness more than N1.

cards.front: A patient has an arousal immediately after a respiratory event and then a leg movement. Which event should usually be considered first in sequence interpretation?
cards.back: Respiratory-related arousal with a subsequent movement
cards.rationale: Respiratory events often trigger arousal and movement, so sequence matters.
cards.keyPoint: Respiratory events often trigger arousal and movement, so sequence matters.

cards.front: Which staging/report mistake is most likely to inflate sleep fragmentation artificially?
cards.back: Scoring brief nonspecific shifts that do not meet arousal criteria
cards.rationale: Overcalling arousals makes sleep look more fragmented than it really was.
cards.keyPoint: Overcalling arousals makes sleep look more fragmented than it really was.

cards.front: Which structure is the normal pacemaker of the heart?
cards.back: SA node
cards.rationale: The sinoatrial node normally initiates the heartbeat.
cards.keyPoint: The sinoatrial node normally initiates the heartbeat.

cards.front: A rhythm strip shows a slow but regular rhythm with a visible P wave before each QRS. What is the best description?
cards.back: Sinus bradycardia
cards.rationale: A slow, regular sinus rhythm with P waves before each QRS fits sinus bradycardia.
cards.keyPoint: A slow, regular sinus rhythm with P waves before each QRS fits sinus bradycardia.

cards.front: Which EKG feature is most consistent with atrial fibrillation?
cards.back: Irregularly irregular rhythm without clear organized P waves
cards.rationale: Atrial fibrillation is identified by an irregularly irregular rhythm and absence of consistent P waves.
cards.keyPoint: Atrial fibrillation is identified by an irregularly irregular rhythm and absence of consistent P waves.

cards.front: A wide premature beat appears early and is not preceded by a normal P wave. What is this most likely?
cards.back: PVC
cards.rationale: A premature ventricular contraction is classically wide and premature without a normal preceding P wave.
cards.keyPoint: A premature ventricular contraction is classically wide and premature without a normal preceding P wave.

cards.front: Which rhythm is a flat line without organized electrical activity?
cards.back: Asystole
cards.rationale: Asystole is essentially absence of detectable organized cardiac electrical activity.
cards.keyPoint: Asystole is essentially absence of detectable organized cardiac electrical activity.

cards.front: A PR interval is consistently longer than 0.20 seconds, but every P wave is followed by a QRS. What is this?
cards.back: First-degree AV block
cards.rationale: Prolonged PR with one-to-one conduction fits first-degree AV block.
cards.keyPoint: Prolonged PR with one-to-one conduction fits first-degree AV block.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: During a study, the patient reports chest pain and appears distressed. What should the technologist do first?
cards.back: Assess the patient and follow emergency protocol immediately
cards.rationale: Patient safety comes first; possible emergency symptoms require immediate response.
cards.keyPoint: Patient safety comes first; possible emergency symptoms require immediate response.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: In the RACE fire response model, what does the 'R' stand for?
cards.back: Rescue
cards.rationale: RACE begins with rescuing or removing anyone in immediate danger.
cards.keyPoint: RACE begins with rescuing or removing anyone in immediate danger.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: Which action is most appropriate after exposure to blood or body fluids in the lab?
cards.back: Follow exposure and cleanup protocol immediately
cards.rationale: Blood or body fluid exposure should be addressed promptly according to lab safety policy.
cards.keyPoint: Blood or body fluid exposure should be addressed promptly according to lab safety policy.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: Which infection-control practice is most appropriate during hookup?
cards.back: Use standard precautions with every patient
cards.rationale: Standard precautions apply to all patients, not just known infectious cases.
cards.keyPoint: Standard precautions apply to all patients, not just known infectious cases.

cards.front: A patient asks whether someone will be watching them overnight. What is the best response?
cards.back: Yes, the study is monitored and you can communicate with staff if needed.
cards.rationale: Clear patient education helps reduce anxiety and improves cooperation.
cards.keyPoint: Clear patient education helps reduce anxiety and improves cooperation.

cards.front: Which pre-study step best supports good patient interaction and study quality?
cards.back: Explain the study process and how to contact the technologist during the night
cards.rationale: Proper explanation updates trust and improves the study experience.
cards.keyPoint: Proper explanation updates trust and improves the study experience.

cards.front: A patient becomes anxious during hookup and says they are unsure they can complete the test. What is the best first approach?
cards.back: Provide calm reassurance and explain the process step by step
cards.rationale: Calm education and reassurance are often the best first response to anxiety.
cards.keyPoint: Calm education and reassurance are often the best first response to anxiety.

cards.front: Which action is the best example of protecting patient confidentiality in the sleep lab?
cards.back: Limiting discussion of patient information to appropriate clinical purposes
cards.rationale: Patient information should be handled discreetly and only for proper clinical use.
cards.keyPoint: Patient information should be handled discreetly and only for proper clinical use.

cards.front: Which patient-interaction mistake is most likely to reduce study quality?
cards.back: Giving incomplete or confusing instructions about the night's process
cards.rationale: Poor communication can increase anxiety, reduce cooperation, and hurt data quality.
cards.keyPoint: Poor communication can increase anxiety, reduce cooperation, and hurt data quality.

cards.front: A patient falls asleep very late and wakes late when allowed their preferred schedule, yet sleeps normally on that delayed schedule. Which pattern fits best?
cards.back: Delayed sleep-wake phase disorder
cards.rationale: A stable but delayed schedule with otherwise normal sleep fits delayed phase rather than insomnia alone.
cards.keyPoint: A stable but delayed schedule with otherwise normal sleep fits delayed phase rather than insomnia alone.

cards.front: A patient becomes sleepy unusually early in the evening and wakes very early in the morning despite attempts to stay up later. Which pattern fits best?
cards.back: Advanced sleep-wake phase disorder
cards.rationale: An early and stubborn schedule pattern fits advanced phase.
cards.keyPoint: An early and stubborn schedule pattern fits advanced phase.

cards.front: A toddler repeatedly calls the parent back for one more hug, one more story, and refuses to stay in bed. Which pediatric insomnia pattern fits best?
cards.back: Limit-setting behavioral insomnia
cards.rationale: Curtain-call behavior and refusal to stay in bed are typical of limit-setting issues.
cards.keyPoint: Curtain-call behavior and refusal to stay in bed are typical of limit-setting issues.

cards.front: In the BEARS pediatric screening tool, the letter B stands for:
cards.back: Bedtime problems
cards.rationale: BEARS begins with bedtime problems before daytime sleepiness, awakenings, regularity, and snoring/breathing concerns.
cards.keyPoint: BEARS begins with bedtime problems before daytime sleepiness, awakenings, regularity, and snoring/breathing concerns.

cards.front: Regular daytime napping in an adolescent should make the technologist think first about:
cards.back: Insufficient sleep or another sleep disorder
cards.rationale: Frequent napping in adolescents can reflect sleep debt or an underlying sleep problem and should not be dismissed automatically.
cards.keyPoint: Frequent napping in adolescents can reflect sleep debt or an underlying sleep problem and should not be dismissed automatically.

cards.front: Which pre-study action most improves both patient cooperation and study quality?
cards.back: Explain the procedure and how to communicate overnight
cards.rationale: Clear explanation lowers anxiety and improves cooperation during the study.
cards.keyPoint: Clear explanation lowers anxiety and improves cooperation during the study.

cards.front: A patient becomes anxious during hookup and says they may not tolerate the study. What is the best first response?
cards.back: Calmly explain the process and reassure the patient
cards.rationale: Reassurance and clear step-by-step explanation are the best first response to anxiety.
cards.keyPoint: Reassurance and clear step-by-step explanation are the best first response to anxiety.

cards.front: A patient taking benzodiazepines shows unusually prominent spindle activity on PSG. What should be considered first?
cards.back: Medication effect
cards.rationale: Benzodiazepines can increase spindle activity and alter architecture.
cards.keyPoint: Benzodiazepines can increase spindle activity and alter architecture.

cards.front: Which medication group is most associated with REM suppression?
cards.back: SSRIs and similar antidepressants
cards.rationale: Several antidepressants suppress REM sleep and can alter REM timing and expression.
cards.keyPoint: Several antidepressants suppress REM sleep and can alter REM timing and expression.

cards.front: A patient reports recent provider-directed discontinuation of a REM-suppressing medication just before testing. What interpretation issue should be considered?
cards.back: REM rebound may affect the results
cards.rationale: Abrupt withdrawal can increase REM expression and complicate interpretation of testing.
cards.keyPoint: Abrupt withdrawal can increase REM expression and complicate interpretation of testing.

cards.front: Which setup mistake is most likely to make rapid eye movements appear blunted or less sharp than expected?
cards.back: Low EOG sampling or poor EOG placement
cards.rationale: EOG detail depends on proper lead placement and adequate signal capture.
cards.keyPoint: EOG detail depends on proper lead placement and adequate signal capture.

cards.front: If the low-frequency filter is set too high on EEG, what problem can happen?
cards.back: Delta and eye movement signals can be attenuated
cards.rationale: A high low-frequency filter reduces slow-wave content and can distort slow physiologic signals.
cards.keyPoint: A high low-frequency filter reduces slow-wave content and can distort slow physiologic signals.

cards.front: Which channel typically uses the highest low-frequency filter setting among these PSG signals?
cards.back: Chin EMG
cards.rationale: EMG channels generally use a much higher low-frequency filter than EEG or EOG.
cards.keyPoint: EMG channels generally use a much higher low-frequency filter than EEG or EOG.

cards.front: Which statement about sampling is most accurate?
cards.back: Slowly varying thoracic motion can be sampled lower than EEG or EMG
cards.rationale: Slow signals can be sampled lower, while rapidly changing signals such as EEG and EMG need higher rates.
cards.keyPoint: Slow signals can be sampled lower, while rapidly changing signals such as EEG and EMG need higher rates.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: Which biocalibration instruction is best for checking alpha attenuation and return?
cards.back: Open your eyes, then close them
cards.rationale: Open and closed eyes help verify attenuation and reappearance of posterior alpha activity.
cards.keyPoint: Open and closed eyes help verify attenuation and reappearance of posterior alpha activity.

cards.front: Which statement best fits routine EOG placement for sleep staging?
cards.back: One electrode is placed slightly above and lateral to one outer canthus and the other slightly below and lateral to the opposite outer canthus
cards.rationale: This arrangement helps produce the expected out-of-phase eye movement deflections.
cards.keyPoint: This arrangement helps produce the expected out-of-phase eye movement deflections.

cards.front: The distance from the left preauricular point to the right preauricular point over the vertex is 36 cm. How far above each preauricular point is the 10% mark?
cards.back: 3.6 cm
cards.rationale: Ten percent of 36 cm is 3.6 cm.
cards.keyPoint: Ten percent of 36 cm is 3.6 cm.

cards.front: Which chin EMG setup best reflects standard three-electrode placement?
cards.back: One electrode above the mandible and two below it
cards.rationale: Standard chin EMG uses one superior and two inferior electrodes around the mandibular region.
cards.keyPoint: Standard chin EMG uses one superior and two inferior electrodes around the mandibular region.

cards.front: A single EEG electrode becomes unstable and creates sharp transient artifact. Which pattern is most likely?
cards.back: Artifact appearing in channels sharing that electrode
cards.rationale: Any derivation using that unstable electrode can become contaminated.
cards.keyPoint: Any derivation using that unstable electrode can become contaminated.

cards.front: A flat signal appears in one EEG channel, while the rest of the montage looks normal. What is the most likely cause?
cards.back: Isolated lead disconnection or failure
cards.rationale: If only one lead is affected, the problem is usually local to that channel or electrode.
cards.keyPoint: If only one lead is affected, the problem is usually local to that channel or electrode.

cards.front: A thoracic effort channel gradually flattens even though the patient is still breathing and the other signals suggest continued effort. What is the best explanation?
cards.back: Loose belt artifact
cards.rationale: A loose or displaced belt can flatten the effort tracing without true loss of respiratory effort.
cards.keyPoint: A loose or displaced belt can flatten the effort tracing without true loss of respiratory effort.

cards.front: An abdominal effort belt loses signal every time the patient rolls. What is the best next step?
cards.back: Reposition or refit the belt
cards.rationale: Position-related signal loss usually reflects a mechanical belt problem.
cards.keyPoint: Position-related signal loss usually reflects a mechanical belt problem.

cards.front: During PAP, the thermal airflow sensor shifts out of position and no longer tracks inhalation and exhalation well. What problem is this?
cards.back: Misplaced thermocouple artifact
cards.rationale: A displaced thermal sensor may not detect airflow-related temperature change accurately.
cards.keyPoint: A displaced thermal sensor may not detect airflow-related temperature change accurately.

cards.front: Why is it helpful when a technologist documents when the patient coughed, moved, or changed position?
cards.back: It helps correlate behavior and artifact with the tracing
cards.rationale: Good documentation improves later interpretation of confusing segments.
cards.keyPoint: Good documentation improves later interpretation of confusing segments.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: A patient reports chest pain and looks distressed during the study. What should the technologist do first?
cards.back: Assess the patient and follow emergency protocol immediately
cards.rationale: Possible emergency symptoms require immediate patient assessment and protocol-based response.
cards.keyPoint: Possible emergency symptoms require immediate patient assessment and protocol-based response.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: In the RACE fire-response model, what does the letter R stand for?
cards.back: Rescue
cards.rationale: RACE begins with rescue of anyone in immediate danger.
cards.keyPoint: RACE begins with rescue of anyone in immediate danger.

cards.front: A K-complex is followed by 2 seconds of faster EEG activity during NREM sleep. What is the best interpretation?
cards.back: Do not score an arousal
cards.rationale: A scored arousal requires at least 3 seconds of qualifying EEG shift.
cards.keyPoint: A scored arousal requires at least 3 seconds of qualifying EEG shift.

cards.front: A K-complex appears in an epoch and is followed by low-amplitude mixed-frequency activity without a spindle. If no other stage-defining feature appears, how should the epoch be scored?
cards.back: N2
cards.rationale: A K-complex is a stage-defining marker for N2 sleep.
cards.keyPoint: A K-complex is a stage-defining marker for N2 sleep.

cards.front: An epoch contains 18% slow-wave activity and a clear sleep spindle. How should it be scored?
cards.back: N2
cards.rationale: Slow-wave activity does not meet N3 threshold, while the spindle supports N2.
cards.keyPoint: Slow-wave activity does not meet N3 threshold, while the spindle supports N2.

cards.front: To score an arousal, how much continuous sleep must occur immediately before it?
cards.back: 10 seconds
cards.rationale: Arousal scoring requires at least 10 seconds of stable sleep before the EEG shift.
cards.keyPoint: Arousal scoring requires at least 10 seconds of stable sleep before the EEG shift.

cards.front: Which mistake most likely inflates sleep-fragmentation indices artificially?
cards.back: Scoring brief nonspecific shifts that do not meet arousal criteria
cards.rationale: Overcalling arousals makes sleep appear more fragmented than it truly was.
cards.keyPoint: Overcalling arousals makes sleep appear more fragmented than it truly was.

cards.front: A patient has repeated leg movements, but each movement begins about 2 seconds after the previous one. How should these be treated?
cards.back: As movements that do not meet PLM interval criteria
cards.rationale: The onset-to-onset interval is too short to qualify as a standard PLM sequence.
cards.keyPoint: The onset-to-onset interval is too short to qualify as a standard PLM sequence.

cards.front: A patient has 120 apneas and hypopneas over 6 hours of total sleep time. What is the AHI?
cards.rationale: AHI equals total apneas plus hypopneas divided by total sleep time in hours: 120 / 6 = 20.
cards.keyPoint: AHI equals total apneas plus hypopneas divided by total sleep time in hours: 120 / 6 = 20.

cards.front: A patient slept 288 minutes out of 360 minutes in bed. What is the sleep efficiency?
cards.rationale: Sleep efficiency equals total sleep time divided by time in bed times 100.
cards.keyPoint: Sleep efficiency equals total sleep time divided by time in bed times 100.

cards.front: If total sleep time is 390 minutes and wake after sleep onset is 30 minutes, what is the sleep period time?
cards.back: 420 minutes
cards.rationale: Sleep period time equals total sleep time plus wake after sleep onset.
cards.keyPoint: Sleep period time equals total sleep time plus wake after sleep onset.

cards.front: A study shows mild overall AHI, but the patient had almost no REM sleep and very little supine sleep. What interpretation caution is most appropriate?
cards.back: Severity may have been underestimated
cards.rationale: Limited REM and supine time can hide worse disease expression.
cards.keyPoint: Limited REM and supine time can hide worse disease expression.

cards.front: Which report value is most useful for separating REM-predominant OSA from more uniform OSA across the night?
cards.back: REM AHI compared with NREM AHI
cards.rationale: Comparing REM and NREM event burden shows whether obstruction is particularly worse in REM sleep.
cards.keyPoint: Comparing REM and NREM event burden shows whether obstruction is particularly worse in REM sleep.

cards.front: On an MSLT, sleep latency is measured from lights out to:
cards.back: The first epoch scored as sleep
cards.rationale: MSLT sleep latency runs from lights out to the first epoch scored as sleep.
cards.keyPoint: MSLT sleep latency runs from lights out to the first epoch scored as sleep.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: Which result pattern most strongly supports narcolepsy on a properly prepared MSLT?
cards.back: Mean sleep latency under 5 minutes with 2 or more SOREMPs
cards.rationale: Marked physiologic sleepiness with multiple SOREMPs strongly supports narcolepsy when the study is properly prepared.
cards.keyPoint: Marked physiologic sleepiness with multiple SOREMPs strongly supports narcolepsy when the study is properly prepared.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: If untreated sleep apnea is present on the PSG before an MSLT, what is the best next step?
cards.back: Treat the sleep apnea first and reassess testing if needed
cards.rationale: Untreated OSA can confound daytime sleepiness testing and should be addressed before using MSLT findings to support narcolepsy.
cards.keyPoint: Untreated OSA can confound daytime sleepiness testing and should be addressed before using MSLT findings to support narcolepsy.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: Which test is designed to measure the ability to remain awake under soporific conditions?
cards.back: MWT
cards.rationale: The Maintenance of Wakefulness Test evaluates the ability to stay awake.
cards.keyPoint: The Maintenance of Wakefulness Test evaluates the ability to stay awake.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: In standard MWT protocol language, a 40-minute trial is ended early when:
cards.back: Three consecutive epochs of N1 or one epoch of any other sleep stage occurs
cards.rationale: Unequivocal sleep on the MWT ends the trial early under standard protocol logic.
cards.keyPoint: Unequivocal sleep on the MWT ends the trial early under standard protocol logic.

cards.front: On bilevel PAP, obstructive apneas are controlled but hypopneas and snoring persist. What is the best next adjustment?
cards.back: Raise IPAP while holding EPAP steady
cards.rationale: Once apneas are controlled with adequate EPAP, IPAP is increased to treat residual hypopneas and snoring.
cards.keyPoint: Once apneas are controlled with adequate EPAP, IPAP is increased to treat residual hypopneas and snoring.

cards.front: An OSA patient on bilevel still has obstructive apneas. Which pressure is the main target to raise first?
cards.back: EPAP
cards.rationale: EPAP is the primary target for eliminating obstructive apneas on bilevel PAP.
cards.keyPoint: EPAP is the primary target for eliminating obstructive apneas on bilevel PAP.

cards.front: Which patient problem can limit unattended APAP use even when the device algorithm is functioning correctly?
cards.back: Significant mask or mouth leak
cards.rationale: Large leak can limit APAP performance and reduce the reliability of residual event assessment.
cards.keyPoint: Large leak can limit APAP performance and reduce the reliability of residual event assessment.

cards.front: Which statement about APAP is most accurate?
cards.back: APAP devices may use different algorithms targeting snoring, airflow limitation, apnea-hypopneas, or impedance
cards.rationale: Different APAP devices do not use identical event-detection strategies or adjustment logic.
cards.keyPoint: Different APAP devices do not use identical event-detection strategies or adjustment logic.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: A patient's oxygen saturation stays fairly stable, but CO2 rises steadily during sleep. What problem does this most strongly suggest?
cards.back: Hypoventilation
cards.rationale: A steady rise in CO2 points toward inadequate ventilation rather than isolated oxygenation failure.
cards.keyPoint: A steady rise in CO2 points toward inadequate ventilation rather than isolated oxygenation failure.

cards.front: A patient has repeated abrupt nocturnal events that are very brief, highly stereotyped, and nearly identical each time. What should be strongly considered?
cards.back: Nocturnal seizure
cards.rationale: Highly stereotyped repetitive spells raise concern for nocturnal seizures rather than routine parasomnia.
cards.keyPoint: Highly stereotyped repetitive spells raise concern for nocturnal seizures rather than routine parasomnia.

cards.front: Which feature best supports REM behavior disorder rather than a typical NREM parasomnia?
cards.back: Complex behavior associated with dream enactment later in the night
cards.rationale: RBD is linked to REM sleep and often appears later in the night with dream enactment.
cards.keyPoint: RBD is linked to REM sleep and often appears later in the night with dream enactment.

cards.front: A patient awakens frightened in the second half of the night and recalls a vivid dream in detail. What is this most consistent with?
cards.back: Nightmare
cards.rationale: Nightmares usually arise from REM sleep later in the night and are remembered in detail.
cards.keyPoint: Nightmares usually arise from REM sleep later in the night and are remembered in detail.

cards.front: A child sits up screaming in the first third of the night, is hard to console, and has no clear recall the next morning. What is this most consistent with?
cards.back: Sleep terror
cards.rationale: Sleep terrors usually arise out of deep NREM sleep early in the night and leave little recall.
cards.keyPoint: Sleep terrors usually arise out of deep NREM sleep early in the night and leave little recall.

cards.front: Sleep bruxism is most likely to appear as:
cards.back: Repeated rhythmic jaw-muscle activity
cards.rationale: Sleep bruxism is associated with rhythmic masticatory muscle activity rather than generalized body behavior.
cards.keyPoint: Sleep bruxism is associated with rhythmic masticatory muscle activity rather than generalized body behavior.

cards.front: A tracing shows posterior alpha when the eyes are closed, and that alpha attenuates when the eyes open. Which state does this most strongly support?
cards.back: Wakefulness
cards.rationale: Posterior alpha that attenuates with eye opening is a classic wake finding.
cards.keyPoint: Posterior alpha that attenuates with eye opening is a classic wake finding.

cards.front: An epoch contains low-amplitude mixed-frequency EEG and no alpha, but eye blinks and waking movement artifact are present. What is the best stage?
cards.back: Wake
cards.rationale: When alpha is absent, waking blinks and movement artifact can still support wake rather than N1.
cards.keyPoint: When alpha is absent, waking blinks and movement artifact can still support wake rather than N1.

cards.front: Which sleep state most reduces upper-airway dilator muscle activity and can therefore worsen airway collapse?
cards.back: REM
cards.rationale: REM sleep produces the greatest drop in skeletal muscle tone, including upper-airway dilators.
cards.keyPoint: REM sleep produces the greatest drop in skeletal muscle tone, including upper-airway dilators.

cards.front: Compared with wakefulness, the ventilatory response to carbon dioxide during sleep is generally:
cards.back: Reduced
cards.rationale: Ventilatory responsiveness decreases during sleep, especially in REM.
cards.keyPoint: Ventilatory responsiveness decreases during sleep, especially in REM.

cards.front: A patient is being evaluated for chronic insomnia. Which additional tool is most useful for clarifying schedule pattern before the study?
cards.back: Sleep diary
cards.rationale: A sleep diary helps identify schedule pattern, variability, and mismatch between complaint and timing.
cards.keyPoint: A sleep diary helps identify schedule pattern, variability, and mismatch between complaint and timing.

cards.front: In pediatric screening, the BEARS element most directly addressing snoring is:
cards.back: Sleep-disordered breathing
cards.rationale: The S in BEARS focuses on snoring and related breathing concerns during sleep.
cards.keyPoint: The S in BEARS focuses on snoring and related breathing concerns during sleep.

cards.front: A patient arrives for MSLT after drinking several large coffees that morning. What is the best action?
cards.back: Document it and consider whether testing validity is affected
cards.rationale: Stimulants such as caffeine can affect latency testing and should be documented when interpreting or rescheduling.
cards.keyPoint: Stimulants such as caffeine can affect latency testing and should be documented when interpreting or rescheduling.

cards.front: A patient asks whether they can call the technologist during the study night. What is the best response?
cards.back: Yes, explain how they can communicate during the study
cards.rationale: Clear instructions about overnight communication improve comfort and study quality.
cards.keyPoint: Clear instructions about overnight communication improve comfort and study quality.

cards.front: Which intervention is most strongly timing-dependent in circadian treatment?
cards.back: Melatonin and light exposure
cards.rationale: The direction of circadian phase shifting depends heavily on the timing of light and melatonin.
cards.keyPoint: The direction of circadian phase shifting depends heavily on the timing of light and melatonin.

cards.front: After sleep deprivation, what rebound feature is most expected early in recovery sleep?
cards.back: Increased slow-wave sleep pressure
cards.rationale: Homeostatic pressure after deprivation increases slow-wave sleep intensity and amount.
cards.keyPoint: Homeostatic pressure after deprivation increases slow-wave sleep intensity and amount.

cards.front: A patient reports recent provider-directed discontinuation of a REM-suppressing antidepressant shortly before testing. Which finding could become more likely and complicate interpretation?
cards.back: REM rebound
cards.rationale: Recent provider-directed discontinuation of REM-suppressing agents may increase REM expression and alter interpretation.
cards.keyPoint: Recent provider-directed discontinuation of REM-suppressing agents may increase REM expression and alter interpretation.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: A patient appears pale, diaphoretic, and says they may faint before hookup is complete. What is the best first action?
cards.back: Assess the patient and follow safety protocol immediately
cards.rationale: Potential acute instability takes priority over study completion.
cards.keyPoint: Potential acute instability takes priority over study completion.

cards.front: Why are EOG electrodes intentionally placed above one outer canthus and below the other?
cards.back: To make eye movements appear out of phase and easier to recognize
cards.rationale: The asymmetric placement creates opposite-polarity eye movement deflections that aid recognition.
cards.keyPoint: The asymmetric placement creates opposite-polarity eye movement deflections that aid recognition.

cards.front: A saturation channel appears erratic, but the pleth waveform remains strong and stable. What is the best first thought?
cards.back: Likely transient calculation or averaging issue rather than sensor loss
cards.rationale: A stable pleth with odd saturation values suggests checking signal processing or artifact before assuming true desaturation.
cards.keyPoint: A stable pleth with odd saturation values suggests checking signal processing or artifact before assuming true desaturation.

cards.front: A sudden sharp transient appears at the same time in every derivation that uses one shared reference electrode. What is the most likely source?
cards.back: Single bad shared electrode
cards.rationale: A problem in a shared electrode contaminates all derivations that include it.
cards.keyPoint: A problem in a shared electrode contaminates all derivations that include it.

cards.front: Lowering sampling rate too far most directly risks which problem?
cards.back: Waveform distortion and loss of fidelity
cards.rationale: Undersampling can make physiologic signals appear blunted, jagged, or misleading.
cards.keyPoint: Undersampling can make physiologic signals appear blunted, jagged, or misleading.

cards.front: Which setting most directly controls how much very slow signal is allowed through a channel?
cards.back: Low-frequency filter
cards.rationale: The low-frequency filter determines preservation or attenuation of very slow components.
cards.keyPoint: The low-frequency filter determines preservation or attenuation of very slow components.

cards.front: If the high-frequency filter is set too low on EMG, what is the most likely effect?
cards.back: Fast EMG detail may be shaved off
cards.rationale: A low high-frequency cutoff attenuates fast activity, including EMG detail.
cards.keyPoint: A low high-frequency cutoff attenuates fast activity, including EMG detail.

cards.front: A thoracic belt signal remains present, but the abdominal belt intermittently inverts only when the patient twists. What is the best first response?
cards.back: Check belt placement and tension
cards.rationale: Mechanical belt issues should be excluded before interpreting abnormal effort patterns as physiologic.
cards.keyPoint: Mechanical belt issues should be excluded before interpreting abnormal effort patterns as physiologic.

cards.front: A rhythm strip shows no organized P waves and an irregularly irregular ventricular response. Which rhythm is most likely?
cards.back: Atrial fibrillation
cards.rationale: An irregularly irregular rhythm without organized P waves is classic atrial fibrillation.
cards.keyPoint: An irregularly irregular rhythm without organized P waves is classic atrial fibrillation.

cards.front: A flat baseline appears briefly on the ECG channel, but the patient is moving and all other channels show large artifact. What is the best interpretation first?
cards.back: Likely signal artifact until verified
cards.rationale: Serious rhythm calls should not be made from a channel clearly contaminated by movement without verification.
cards.keyPoint: Serious rhythm calls should not be made from a channel clearly contaminated by movement without verification.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: Which pre-study maneuver most directly checks the left-right EOG response?
cards.back: Look left then right
cards.rationale: Horizontal gaze biocalibrations confirm expected EOG polarity and function.
cards.keyPoint: Horizontal gaze biocalibrations confirm expected EOG polarity and function.

cards.front: Which sensor is preferred for scoring apnea because it best detects near-complete airflow cessation?
cards.back: Oronasal thermal sensor
cards.rationale: Thermal airflow sensors are commonly preferred for apnea detection because they indicate cessation of airflow well.
cards.keyPoint: Thermal airflow sensors are commonly preferred for apnea detection because they indicate cessation of airflow well.

cards.front: The head measurement from left to right preauricular point over the vertex is 34 cm. Approximately how far is the initial 10% mark from each preauricular point?
cards.back: 3.4 cm
cards.rationale: Ten percent of 34 cm is 3.4 cm.
cards.keyPoint: Ten percent of 34 cm is 3.4 cm.

cards.front: During nasal PAP, which pattern most strongly suggests probable mouth leak?
cards.back: High unintentional leak with unstable airflow despite proper mask position
cards.rationale: High leak values despite seemingly stable mask fit should raise suspicion for mouth leak.
cards.keyPoint: High leak values despite seemingly stable mask fit should raise suspicion for mouth leak.
