cards.front: A sleep spindle appears at the start of the epoch and the remainder of the epoch shows low-amplitude mixed-frequency sleep without arousal. What is the best score?
cards.back: N2
cards.rationale: A recognized spindle establishes N2 when the remainder of the epoch otherwise fits sleep.
cards.keyPoint: A recognized spindle establishes N2 when the remainder of the epoch otherwise fits sleep.

cards.front: A major body movement obscures most of an epoch, but the epoch is between two clear wake epochs. How should it usually be scored?
cards.back: Wake
cards.rationale: An obscured epoch between two wake epochs is generally scored as wake rather than as an indeterminate sleep stage.
cards.keyPoint: An obscured epoch between two wake epochs is generally scored as wake rather than as an indeterminate sleep stage.

cards.front: An abrupt EEG shift lasts 4 seconds during N2, but only 6 seconds of sleep occurred immediately before it. How should it be handled?
cards.back: Do not score an arousal
cards.rationale: Arousals require at least 10 seconds of continuous sleep before the event.
cards.keyPoint: Arousals require at least 10 seconds of continuous sleep before the event.

cards.front: Rapid eye movements are seen, but chin tone remains relatively high and the EEG is not convincingly REM-like. What is the safest conclusion?
cards.back: REM remains unconfirmed
cards.rationale: Eye movements alone are not enough to call REM without the overall REM pattern.
cards.keyPoint: Eye movements alone are not enough to call REM without the overall REM pattern.

cards.front: A respiratory event shows a qualifying reduction in airflow for at least 10 seconds and ends in an arousal without desaturation. In adult scoring, what is the best classification?
cards.back: Hypopnea
cards.rationale: An adult hypopnea may be scored when the qualifying airflow reduction is associated with an arousal.
cards.keyPoint: An adult hypopnea may be scored when the qualifying airflow reduction is associated with an arousal.

cards.front: A sequence shows increasing respiratory effort and inspiratory flattening, then an arousal, but it does not meet apnea or hypopnea criteria. What is the best score?
cards.back: RERA
cards.rationale: Increasing effort or flow limitation terminating in arousal without meeting apnea/hypopnea criteria supports RERA.
cards.keyPoint: Increasing effort or flow limitation terminating in arousal without meeting apnea/hypopnea criteria supports RERA.

cards.front: An event begins with no effort and later shows clear inspiratory effort before airflow returns. Which event type best fits?
cards.back: Mixed apnea
cards.rationale: Mixed apnea begins with central characteristics and ends with obstructive effort before recovery.
cards.keyPoint: Mixed apnea begins with central characteristics and ends with obstructive effort before recovery.

cards.front: Five qualifying leg movements occur 25 seconds apart. Which statement is best?
cards.back: They meet criteria for a PLM series
cards.rationale: At least four qualifying movements with onset intervals between 5 and 90 seconds meet PLM series criteria.
cards.keyPoint: At least four qualifying movements with onset intervals between 5 and 90 seconds meet PLM series criteria.

cards.front: A leg movement occurs immediately after a respiratory arousal. What is the main scoring caution?
cards.back: Consider whether it is related to the respiratory event
cards.rationale: Leg movements tied to respiratory events are not automatically scored as independent PLMs.
cards.keyPoint: Leg movements tied to respiratory events are not automatically scored as independent PLMs.

cards.front: A patient has 330 minutes of total sleep time and 30 minutes of wake after sleep onset. What is the sleep period time?
cards.back: 360 minutes
cards.rationale: Sleep period time equals total sleep time plus wake after sleep onset.
cards.keyPoint: Sleep period time equals total sleep time plus wake after sleep onset.

cards.front: A study recorded 48 apneas, 24 hypopneas, and 12 RERAs over 6 hours of sleep. Which value is the AHI?
cards.rationale: AHI uses apneas plus hypopneas only: 72 events divided by 6 hours equals 12.
cards.keyPoint: AHI uses apneas plus hypopneas only: 72 events divided by 6 hours equals 12.

cards.front: An overall AHI is borderline, but the study had almost no supine sleep and very little REM. What is the best report caution?
cards.back: Severity may be underestimated
cards.rationale: Limited REM or supine exposure can make obstructive disease appear milder than usual.
cards.keyPoint: Limited REM or supine exposure can make obstructive disease appear milder than usual.

cards.front: In pediatric respiratory scoring, which concept differs importantly from adult scoring?
cards.back: Events are breath-based and not always fixed to 10-second duration
cards.rationale: Pediatric respiratory scoring uses breath-based rules and differs from adult fixed-duration conventions.
cards.keyPoint: Pediatric respiratory scoring uses breath-based rules and differs from adult fixed-duration conventions.

cards.front: A pediatric event has absent airflow and absent effort, lasts less than 20 seconds, and is associated with arousal and desaturation. What is the best interpretation?
cards.back: It may still meet pediatric central apnea criteria
cards.rationale: Pediatric central-apnea scoring may allow shorter events when accompanied by associated consequences such as desaturation or arousal.
cards.keyPoint: Pediatric central-apnea scoring may allow shorter events when accompanied by associated consequences such as desaturation or arousal.

cards.front: Which test is best suited for objective measurement of physiologic tendency to fall asleep?
cards.back: MSLT
cards.rationale: The MSLT is designed to measure tendency to fall asleep, whereas the MWT measures ability to stay awake.
cards.keyPoint: The MSLT is designed to measure tendency to fall asleep, whereas the MWT measures ability to stay awake.

cards.front: During adult CPAP titration, loud persistent snoring remains after obstructive apneas are gone. What is the best next action?
cards.back: Increase pressure per titration protocol
cards.rationale: Residual loud snoring may justify further pressure increases during titration protocols.
cards.keyPoint: Residual loud snoring may justify further pressure increases during titration protocols.

cards.front: Which situation most strongly raises concern for treatment-emergent central events during PAP titration?
cards.back: Central apneas appear after obstructive events improve with pressure
cards.rationale: Central events that emerge as obstruction resolves with PAP raise concern for treatment-emergent central apnea.
cards.keyPoint: Central events that emerge as obstruction resolves with PAP raise concern for treatment-emergent central apnea.

cards.front: When oxygen is added during PAP because saturation remains low, what important principle still applies?
cards.back: Underlying obstructive events still need appropriate PAP management
cards.rationale: Supplemental oxygen does not replace proper treatment of obstructive respiratory events.
cards.keyPoint: Supplemental oxygen does not replace proper treatment of obstructive respiratory events.

cards.front: A patient reports severe nasal dryness during PAP and the leak is otherwise acceptable. Which adjustment may help comfort without directly changing event scoring?
cards.back: Humidification or interface comfort adjustment
cards.rationale: Comfort adjustments such as humidification can improve tolerance without being the primary event-management step.
cards.keyPoint: Comfort adjustments such as humidification can improve tolerance without being the primary event-management step.

cards.front: Which statement best fits oral appliance therapy in sleep medicine?
cards.back: It may be an alternative treatment option for selected obstructive cases
cards.rationale: Oral appliance therapy can be an alternative option in selected obstructive sleep apnea patients.
cards.keyPoint: Oral appliance therapy can be an alternative option in selected obstructive sleep apnea patients.

cards.front: Which issue most threatens reliable PAP event detection during unattended auto-adjusting PAP use?
cards.back: Large unintentional leak
cards.rationale: Large leak can interfere with the device's ability to detect and respond accurately to events.
cards.keyPoint: Large leak can interfere with the device's ability to detect and respond accurately to events.

cards.front: Why might a backup rate be useful in a timed bilevel mode?
cards.back: It helps provide breaths when spontaneous effort falls away
cards.rationale: Timed or spontaneous/timed bilevel modes include a backup rate to support ventilation when spontaneous breathing is insufficient.
cards.keyPoint: Timed or spontaneous/timed bilevel modes include a backup rate to support ventilation when spontaneous breathing is insufficient.

cards.front: Which instruction is most useful when sending a PAP user home after a successful titration?
cards.back: Basic explanation of mask use, leak issues, and when to seek help
cards.rationale: Simple practical education improves adherence and helps patients troubleshoot early issues.
cards.keyPoint: Simple practical education improves adherence and helps patients troubleshoot early issues.

cards.front: A patient has severe sleep fragmentation but a relatively low AHI. Which additional report value may better explain symptoms?
cards.back: Arousal index
cards.rationale: Arousal burden may help explain symptoms when respiratory index alone seems low.
cards.keyPoint: Arousal burden may help explain symptoms when respiratory index alone seems low.

cards.front: Why are technologist notes and video especially helpful during artifact-heavy behavioral events?
cards.back: They can help correlate behavior with distorted signals
cards.rationale: When movement obscures physiologic data, video and contemporaneous notes improve interpretation.
cards.keyPoint: When movement obscures physiologic data, video and contemporaneous notes improve interpretation.

cards.front: Which impedance pattern is most likely to increase the chance of prominent 60-Hz interference during recording?
cards.back: Markedly unequal impedances between paired electrodes
cards.rationale: Large impedance mismatch between paired electrodes makes environmental electrical interference more likely to appear in the tracing.
cards.keyPoint: Large impedance mismatch between paired electrodes makes environmental electrical interference more likely to appear in the tracing.

cards.front: Why is a higher sampling rate required for EEG than for a slowly changing effort signal?
cards.back: EEG contains faster signal changes that can be distorted if undersampled
cards.rationale: Rapidly changing signals such as EEG need higher sampling rates so their morphology is not blunted or misrepresented.
cards.keyPoint: Rapidly changing signals such as EEG need higher sampling rates so their morphology is not blunted or misrepresented.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: A thermal airflow sensor keeps drifting away from the patient's mouth during setup. What is the best next step?
cards.back: Reposition and secure the sensor before lights out
cards.rationale: A displaced thermal sensor can weaken airflow detection, so it should be repositioned and secured before recording begins.
cards.keyPoint: A displaced thermal sensor can weaken airflow detection, so it should be repositioned and secured before recording begins.

cards.front: Why are machine and signal calibrations performed before the study begins?
cards.back: To confirm the system is recording expected polarity and amplitude
cards.rationale: Calibration verifies that the recording system is behaving correctly before patient interpretation depends on the data.
cards.keyPoint: Calibration verifies that the recording system is behaving correctly before patient interpretation depends on the data.

cards.front: Which technologist action best improves later interpretation when unusual movements occur during the night?
cards.back: Document the time, behavior, and any intervention in real time
cards.rationale: Real-time notes help correlate patient behavior with physiologic changes and improve review of unusual events.
cards.keyPoint: Real-time notes help correlate patient behavior with physiologic changes and improve review of unusual events.

cards.front: An EEG channel suddenly develops intermittent sharp nonphysiologic jumps while nearby leads remain usable. What is the best first troubleshooting step?
cards.back: Inspect and resecure the involved electrode
cards.rationale: A localized sharp artifact pattern often points to an unstable electrode connection that should be checked first.
cards.keyPoint: A localized sharp artifact pattern often points to an unstable electrode connection that should be checked first.

cards.front: Which airflow signal is generally more useful for recognizing complete airflow cessation than for measuring partial flow reduction?
cards.back: Thermal airflow sensor
cards.rationale: Thermal airflow sensing is especially useful for detecting absent airflow, whereas nasal pressure is better for proportional airflow reduction.
cards.keyPoint: Thermal airflow sensing is especially useful for detecting absent airflow, whereas nasal pressure is better for proportional airflow reduction.

cards.front: A patient's end-tidal CO2 waveform shows no stable plateau and values vary sharply breath to breath after the sampling line kinks. What is the best interpretation?
cards.back: The tracing may be unreliable because of sampling-line obstruction
cards.rationale: A kinked or obstructed sampling line can distort the end-tidal waveform and make the displayed values unreliable.
cards.keyPoint: A kinked or obstructed sampling line can distort the end-tidal waveform and make the displayed values unreliable.

cards.front: What does a transcutaneous CO2 monitor primarily help the technologist assess during sleep testing?
cards.back: Ventilation trend
cards.rationale: Transcutaneous CO2 monitoring is used to follow ventilation trends and help identify hypoventilation.
cards.keyPoint: Transcutaneous CO2 monitoring is used to follow ventilation trends and help identify hypoventilation.

cards.front: Which report statement is most appropriate when a study shows prolonged desaturation but airflow and effort data were poor for part of the night?
cards.back: Document the limitation and interpret cautiously
cards.rationale: When signal quality is limited, the report should acknowledge the limitation so interpretation is not overstated.
cards.keyPoint: When signal quality is limited, the report should acknowledge the limitation so interpretation is not overstated.

cards.front: A patient has 150 respiratory events over 7.5 hours of total sleep time. What is the AHI?
cards.rationale: AHI equals total apneas plus hypopneas divided by hours of sleep. 150 divided by 7.5 equals 20.
cards.keyPoint: AHI equals total apneas plus hypopneas divided by hours of sleep. 150 divided by 7.5 equals 20.

cards.front: Which interface consideration becomes especially important when persistent mouth leak is limiting effective nasal PAP therapy?
cards.back: Consider an oronasal or full-face option if appropriate
cards.rationale: Persistent mouth leak may require a different interface approach when nasal PAP alone is not being tolerated effectively.
cards.keyPoint: Persistent mouth leak may require a different interface approach when nasal PAP alone is not being tolerated effectively.

cards.front: A patient becomes anxious as PAP is introduced even though the pressure is low. What is the best first response?
cards.back: Slow down, coach breathing, and provide reassurance
cards.rationale: Early reassurance, pacing, and coaching often improve PAP tolerance better than escalating pressure quickly.
cards.keyPoint: Early reassurance, pacing, and coaching often improve PAP tolerance better than escalating pressure quickly.

cards.front: Why should oxygen therapy during a PAP study be documented carefully rather than treated as a minor add-on?
cards.back: It can change interpretation of oxygenation and treatment response
cards.rationale: Supplemental oxygen can affect saturation patterns and treatment response, so its use must be documented clearly.
cards.keyPoint: Supplemental oxygen can affect saturation patterns and treatment response, so its use must be documented clearly.

cards.front: Which statement best fits positional therapy in obstructive sleep apnea care?
cards.back: It aims to reduce events that worsen in certain body positions
cards.rationale: Positional therapy is directed at patients whose obstruction is significantly worse in specific sleep positions.
cards.keyPoint: Positional therapy is directed at patients whose obstruction is significantly worse in specific sleep positions.

cards.front: Which explanation is most helpful before applying many sensors to a nervous first-time patient?
cards.back: Explain what the sensors monitor and reassure the patient that communication remains available overnight
cards.rationale: Simple explanation and reassurance improve cooperation and reduce anxiety before testing begins.
cards.keyPoint: Simple explanation and reassurance improve cooperation and reduce anxiety before testing begins.

cards.front: A patient says, "I can tolerate PAP here, but I am worried I will stop using it at home." What support response is best?
cards.back: Provide practical troubleshooting and encourage early follow-up if problems occur
cards.rationale: Practical support and early troubleshooting guidance improve the chances of successful PAP use after the study.
cards.keyPoint: Practical support and early troubleshooting guidance improve the chances of successful PAP use after the study.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: Which statement best reflects standard precautions in the sleep center?
cards.back: Use them with every patient encounter
cards.rationale: Standard precautions are applied consistently because not all infectious risks are known in advance.
cards.keyPoint: Standard precautions are applied consistently because not all infectious risks are known in advance.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: A patient becomes acutely short of breath and chest pain is reported during the study. What is the best immediate response?
cards.back: Assess the patient and activate emergency response per protocol
cards.rationale: Possible acute cardiopulmonary events require immediate patient assessment and emergency action according to protocol.
cards.keyPoint: Possible acute cardiopulmonary events require immediate patient assessment and emergency action according to protocol.

cards.front: Artifact Lab: The tracing shows regular high-frequency contamination that looks electrically noisy across the channel rather than physiologic.
cards.back: Electrical interference / 60 Hz artifact
cards.rationale: Regular fast interference suggests line noise or grounding-related contamination more than patient physiology. Best first step: Check grounding and nearby electrical interference sources before trusting the channel.
cards.keyPoint: Regular fast interference suggests line noise or grounding-related contamination more than patient physiology. Best first step: Check grounding and nearby electrical interference sources before trusting the channel.

cards.front: Artifact Lab: There is slow wandering baseline drift that does not behave like organized sleep physiology.
cards.back: Sweat artifact / drifting baseline
cards.rationale: A drifting slow baseline is more typical of sweat artifact than true cerebral rhythm change. Best first step: Improve electrode site condition and reassess impedance and environmental comfort.
cards.keyPoint: A drifting slow baseline is more typical of sweat artifact than true cerebral rhythm change. Best first step: Improve electrode site condition and reassess impedance and environmental comfort.

cards.front: Artifact Lab: The airflow signal becomes unreliable while other related channels suggest the patient is still breathing.
cards.back: Displaced cannula / airflow sensor problem
cards.rationale: If effort continues and the airflow tracing suddenly fails, the sensor or placement should be questioned first. Best first step: Check cannula position, connection, and signal quality before scoring an event.
cards.keyPoint: If effort continues and the airflow tracing suddenly fails, the sensor or placement should be questioned first. Best first step: Check cannula position, connection, and signal quality before scoring an event.

cards.front: Artifact Lab: One effort channel appears flat or unreliable while the rest of the respiratory picture still has activity.
cards.back: Loose or poorly functioning effort belt
cards.rationale: A flat or inconsistent belt signal with preserved related physiology points to signal acquisition trouble first. Best first step: Reposition or secure the belt and verify the channel response.
cards.keyPoint: A flat or inconsistent belt signal with preserved related physiology points to signal acquisition trouble first. Best first step: Reposition or secure the belt and verify the channel response.

cards.front: Artifact Lab: The oximetry signal drops out or becomes erratic during movement and does not match the rest of the respiratory picture.
cards.back: Motion artifact / poor pulse oximeter signal
cards.rationale: SpO2 motion artifact often produces abrupt unreliable changes that do not fit the rest of the record. Best first step: Check probe placement, perfusion, and motion before using the saturation trend clinically.
cards.keyPoint: SpO2 motion artifact often produces abrupt unreliable changes that do not fit the rest of the record. Best first step: Check probe placement, perfusion, and motion before using the saturation trend clinically.

cards.front: Artifact Lab: Therapy looks unstable and leak information suggests poor interface seal rather than a simple pressure problem.
cards.back: Mask leak
cards.rationale: Large leak can distort therapy delivery and make the tracing look worse than the patient's actual control of breathing. Best first step: Reassess mask seal, fit, and interface comfort before escalating settings.
cards.keyPoint: Large leak can distort therapy delivery and make the tracing look worse than the patient's actual control of breathing. Best first step: Reassess mask seal, fit, and interface comfort before escalating settings.

cards.front: EKG Lab: The rhythm is regular and slow with a rate below typical wake values, but the complexes remain organized.
cards.back: Sinus bradycardia
cards.rationale: A slow but organized rhythm during sleep can represent sinus bradycardia rather than chaotic pathology. Best first step: Confirm signal quality, assess the patient context, and document according to protocol.
cards.keyPoint: A slow but organized rhythm during sleep can represent sinus bradycardia rather than chaotic pathology. Best first step: Confirm signal quality, assess the patient context, and document according to protocol.

cards.front: EKG Lab: The rhythm is irregularly irregular and does not show a steady repeating pattern of atrial activity.
cards.back: Atrial fibrillation
cards.rationale: An irregularly irregular rhythm is a classic clue for atrial fibrillation rather than a simple sinus variation. Best first step: Verify the signal, note the abnormal rhythm, and follow lab protocol for review or escalation.
cards.keyPoint: An irregularly irregular rhythm is a classic clue for atrial fibrillation rather than a simple sinus variation. Best first step: Verify the signal, note the abnormal rhythm, and follow lab protocol for review or escalation.

cards.front: EKG Lab: An early wide abnormal beat interrupts the underlying rhythm and is followed by a compensatory pause.
cards.back: PVCs
cards.rationale: A premature wide beat with a pause afterward is a classic description of a PVC pattern. Best first step: Confirm the lead signal, identify the ectopy pattern, and document frequency and context.
cards.keyPoint: A premature wide beat with a pause afterward is a classic description of a PVC pattern. Best first step: Confirm the lead signal, identify the ectopy pattern, and document frequency and context.

cards.front: EKG Lab: There is a rapid rhythm with broad complexes that does not resemble the normal baseline pattern.
cards.back: Wide-complex tachycardia concern
cards.rationale: A fast rhythm with broad complexes deserves immediate attention and should not be brushed off as ordinary variation. Best first step: Check lead integrity quickly, assess the patient, and escalate according to lab emergency protocol.
cards.keyPoint: A fast rhythm with broad complexes deserves immediate attention and should not be brushed off as ordinary variation. Best first step: Check lead integrity quickly, assess the patient, and escalate according to lab emergency protocol.

cards.front: EKG Lab: There is a notable gap in expected cardiac activity that raises concern for a significant pause.
cards.back: Possible significant pause / asystole concern
cards.rationale: A prolonged pause on ECG may represent serious rhythm disturbance and must be distinguished from signal loss quickly. Best first step: Differentiate true pause from lead problem immediately, assess the patient, and follow emergency protocol if confirmed.
cards.keyPoint: A prolonged pause on ECG may represent serious rhythm disturbance and must be distinguished from signal loss quickly. Best first step: Differentiate true pause from lead problem immediately, assess the patient, and follow emergency protocol if confirmed.

cards.front: A study shows N1 = 22 min, N2 = 188 min, N3 = 46 min, and REM = 74 min. What is the TST?
cards.back: 330 min
cards.rationale: Add all sleep stages together: 22 + 188 + 46 + 74 = 330 minutes.
cards.keyPoint: Add all sleep stages together: 22 + 188 + 46 + 74 = 330 minutes.

cards.front: If TST is 330 minutes and TRT is 420 minutes, what is the sleep efficiency?
cards.rationale: Sleep efficiency = (330 / 420) x 100 = 78.57%, which rounds to 78.6%.
cards.keyPoint: Sleep efficiency = (330 / 420) x 100 = 78.57%, which rounds to 78.6%.

cards.front: Lights out is at 10:00 PM and the first epoch of sleep starts at 10:23 PM. What is the sleep latency?
cards.back: 23 min
cards.rationale: Sleep latency is the time from lights out to the first epoch scored as sleep, so 23 minutes.
cards.keyPoint: Sleep latency is the time from lights out to the first epoch scored as sleep, so 23 minutes.

cards.front: If TRT is 420 min, sleep latency is 23 min, and TST is 330 min, what is WASO?
cards.back: 67 min
cards.rationale: WASO = 420 - 23 - 330 = 67 minutes.
cards.keyPoint: WASO = 420 - 23 - 330 = 67 minutes.

cards.front: A patient has 24 apneas and 36 hypopneas with a TST of 300 minutes. What is the AHI?
cards.rationale: AHI = (24 + 36) x 60 / 300 = 60 x 60 / 300 = 12 events per hour.
cards.keyPoint: AHI = (24 + 36) x 60 / 300 = 60 x 60 / 300 = 12 events per hour.

cards.front: Sleep onset occurs at 10:23 PM and the first REM epoch begins at 11:52 PM. What is the REM latency?
cards.back: 89 min
cards.rationale: From 10:23 PM to 11:52 PM is 1 hour 29 minutes, or 89 minutes.
cards.keyPoint: From 10:23 PM to 11:52 PM is 1 hour 29 minutes, or 89 minutes.

cards.front: Report Lab: The technologist is looking at the night's sleep architecture summary and needs to interpret stage progression rather than just stare at individual epochs.
cards.back: Use the hypnogram to understand sleep architecture and stage flow across the night
cards.rationale: A hypnogram is a visual summary of the night and helps connect staging decisions to the overall architecture pattern. Best verification step: Review the stage progression across the night and confirm that the summarized architecture matches the scored record.
cards.keyPoint: A hypnogram is a visual summary of the night and helps connect staging decisions to the overall architecture pattern. Best verification step: Review the stage progression across the night and confirm that the summarized architecture matches the scored record.

cards.front: Report Lab: A PAP titration summary table lists pressure levels and associated results, and the technologist must interpret the table rather than just copy numbers forward.
cards.back: Use the titration table to connect pressure changes with response and summary documentation
cards.rationale: Titration tables help summarize how pressure adjustments related to events, sleep, and treatment response during the night. Best verification step: Review the pressure progression and verify that the summary reflects the response shown in the titration table.
cards.keyPoint: Titration tables help summarize how pressure adjustments related to events, sleep, and treatment response during the night. Best verification step: Review the pressure progression and verify that the summary reflects the response shown in the titration table.

cards.front: Report Lab: The study is scored, but the written technologist summary still needs to reflect the night accurately and support the final report.
cards.back: Make sure the written technologist summary aligns with the scored data and key events of the night
cards.rationale: The technologist summary should support the record clearly and not conflict with the scored findings or important night events. Best verification step: Compare the summary language to the scored data, important observations, and overall night progression before finalizing it.
cards.keyPoint: The technologist summary should support the record clearly and not conflict with the scored findings or important night events. Best verification step: Compare the summary language to the scored data, important observations, and overall night progression before finalizing it.

cards.front: Report Lab: The report contains calculated values and visual summaries, and the technologist must think about whether the pieces fit together logically.
cards.back: Cross-check calculations, graphic summaries, and narrative interpretation for consistency
cards.rationale: A clean report should make sense across numbers, graphs, and written interpretation rather than presenting disconnected pieces. Best verification step: Review whether the graphic summaries, calculations, and narrative all support the same overall interpretation.
cards.keyPoint: A clean report should make sense across numbers, graphs, and written interpretation rather than presenting disconnected pieces. Best verification step: Review whether the graphic summaries, calculations, and narrative all support the same overall interpretation.

cards.front: Report Lab: The technologist has both architecture and event information available and needs to think about how the visual summary supports the overall impression of the night.
cards.back: Use report graphics to support a coherent summary of sleep architecture and event burden
cards.rationale: Report graphics are not decoration. They help explain what kind of night the patient had and whether the summary makes sense. Best verification step: Interpret the graphics in context and confirm the report summary reflects both architecture and event patterns accurately.
cards.keyPoint: Report graphics are not decoration. They help explain what kind of night the patient had and whether the summary makes sense. Best verification step: Interpret the graphics in context and confirm the report summary reflects both architecture and event patterns accurately.

cards.front: PAP Simulator: Airflow still shows recurrent reduction with continuing effort despite CPAP being in place.
cards.back: Residual obstructive events remain and the pressure response should be reconsidered
cards.rationale: This simulated strip is meant to teach that CPAP on the patient does not automatically mean the obstruction is fully controlled.
cards.keyPoint: This simulated strip is meant to teach that CPAP on the patient does not automatically mean the obstruction is fully controlled.

cards.front: PAP Simulator: The leak signal is persistently elevated and the airflow pattern looks unstable in a way that suggests poor mask seal.
cards.back: Large mask leak is likely distorting the therapy picture
cards.rationale: This teaches the technologist to question the interface and leak first rather than automatically increasing pressure.
cards.keyPoint: This teaches the technologist to question the interface and leak first rather than automatically increasing pressure.

cards.front: PAP Simulator: Airflow appears smoother, leak is modest, and the overall treatment pattern looks more stable.
cards.back: The strip suggests more stable breathing with fewer obvious residual disturbances
cards.rationale: This teaches the technologist to recognize a more controlled PAP response without assuming perfection in every case.
cards.keyPoint: This teaches the technologist to recognize a more controlled PAP response without assuming perfection in every case.

cards.front: PAP Simulator: Ventilation still looks shallow and limited despite therapy, and the technologist needs to think beyond a one-pressure mindset.
cards.back: The strip suggests a situation where bilevel-style support thinking may be more relevant than fixed CPAP alone
cards.rationale: This is meant to teach that some treatment questions are really about support and ventilation assistance, not only upper-airway splinting.
cards.keyPoint: This is meant to teach that some treatment questions are really about support and ventilation assistance, not only upper-airway splinting.

cards.front: PAP Simulator: The technologist should recognize that therapy questions may involve changing pressure needs rather than one fixed pressure story all night.
cards.back: The teaching point is to think about automatic pressure response to changing obstruction burden across the night
cards.rationale: This simulator case reinforces the idea that some therapy concepts involve variable pressure response rather than a static one-setting approach.
cards.keyPoint: This simulator case reinforces the idea that some therapy concepts involve variable pressure response rather than a static one-setting approach.

cards.front: PAP Simulator: This case pushes the learner to think about central-event patterns and the idea that some advanced therapy questions are about more than obstruction.
cards.back: The learning point is to recognize a central-event treatment frame rather than only obstructive-event thinking
cards.rationale: This case is for exam-focused mode recognition only and helps separate obstructive therapy thinking from central-event treatment framing.
cards.keyPoint: This case is for exam-focused mode recognition only and helps separate obstructive therapy thinking from central-event treatment framing.

cards.front: PAP Simulator: The technologist should think about pediatric therapy support and the fact that mask tolerance and age-aware reasoning matter.
cards.back: The key teaching point is age-aware PAP support, comfort, and fit rather than automatic adult-mode assumptions
cards.rationale: This case reinforces that pediatric PAP questions are not solved well by ignoring age, comfort, and support needs.
cards.keyPoint: This case reinforces that pediatric PAP questions are not solved well by ignoring age, comfort, and support needs.

cards.front: Epoch Lab: Posterior alpha dominates and the epoch has not transitioned into sleep.
cards.back: Wake
cards.rationale: Sustained alpha without clear sleep features supports wake.
cards.keyPoint: Sustained alpha without clear sleep features supports wake.

cards.front: Epoch Lab: Low-amplitude mixed-frequency EEG appears with slow rolling eye movements.
cards.back: N1
cards.rationale: Slow rolling eyes with fading alpha support N1.
cards.keyPoint: Slow rolling eyes with fading alpha support N1.

cards.front: Epoch Lab: A spindle appears in an otherwise compatible sleep epoch.
cards.back: N2
cards.rationale: A spindle strongly supports N2 when the epoch is otherwise compatible.
cards.keyPoint: A spindle strongly supports N2 when the epoch is otherwise compatible.

cards.front: Epoch Lab: High-amplitude slow-wave activity dominates the epoch.
cards.back: N3
cards.rationale: Dominant high-amplitude slow-wave activity supports N3.
cards.keyPoint: Dominant high-amplitude slow-wave activity supports N3.

cards.front: Epoch Lab: Rapid eye movements appear with low chin tone.
cards.back: REM
cards.rationale: Rapid eye movements with low chin tone support REM.
cards.keyPoint: Rapid eye movements with low chin tone support REM.

cards.front: Epoch Lab: Airflow drops out while respiratory effort continues.
cards.back: Obstructive Apnea
cards.rationale: Absent airflow with continued effort supports obstructive apnea.
cards.keyPoint: Absent airflow with continued effort supports obstructive apnea.

cards.front: Epoch Lab: Airflow and effort both drop away during the event.
cards.back: Central Apnea
cards.rationale: Absent airflow with absent or markedly reduced effort supports central apnea.
cards.keyPoint: Absent airflow with absent or markedly reduced effort supports central apnea.

cards.front: Epoch Lab: Airflow is reduced but not absent and the pattern still represents a respiratory event.
cards.back: Hypopnea
cards.rationale: A partial reduction in airflow is more consistent with hypopnea than apnea.
cards.keyPoint: A partial reduction in airflow is more consistent with hypopnea than apnea.

cards.front: Epoch Lab: A brief EEG shift appears with a momentary increase in chin activity.
cards.back: Arousal
cards.rationale: A brief shift with supportive EMG change fits arousal thinking.
cards.keyPoint: A brief shift with supportive EMG change fits arousal thinking.

cards.front: Epoch Lab: Multiple channels jump together in a way that looks nonphysiologic and motion-related.
cards.back: Artifact
cards.rationale: Broad channel disruption across signals supports artifact rather than a physiologic event.
cards.keyPoint: Broad channel disruption across signals supports artifact rather than a physiologic event.

cards.front: Epoch Lab: Recurrent limb EMG bursts appear while the respiratory picture remains stable.
cards.back: Periodic Limb Movement
cards.rationale: Repetitive limb EMG bursts support movement-event scoring awareness.
cards.keyPoint: Repetitive limb EMG bursts support movement-event scoring awareness.

cards.front: Epoch Lab: The epoch contains a classic N2 support feature and otherwise compatible sleep.
cards.back: N2
cards.rationale: A spindle within a compatible epoch supports N2.
cards.keyPoint: A spindle within a compatible epoch supports N2.

cards.front: Epoch Lab: This epoch still looks more like eyes-closed wake than true sleep onset.
cards.back: Wake
cards.rationale: Persistent alpha and lack of definitive sleep features support wake.
cards.keyPoint: Persistent alpha and lack of definitive sleep features support wake.

cards.front: Epoch Lab: Sleep onset features are present but the epoch has not yet matured into N2.
cards.back: N1
cards.rationale: This is more consistent with early sleep onset than N2 or REM.
cards.keyPoint: This is more consistent with early sleep onset than N2 or REM.

cards.front: Epoch Lab: Low chin tone and eye activity fit a classic stage pattern.
cards.back: REM
cards.rationale: Low chin tone with eye movements supports REM.
cards.keyPoint: Low chin tone with eye movements supports REM.

cards.front: Epoch Lab: The event pattern suggests continued effort against reduced airflow.
cards.back: Obstructive Apnea
cards.rationale: Ongoing effort against absent airflow supports an obstructive event.
cards.keyPoint: Ongoing effort against absent airflow supports an obstructive event.

cards.front: Epoch Lab: The event lacks the continuing effort expected in an obstructive event.
cards.back: Central Apnea
cards.rationale: Reduced or absent effort during the event supports central apnea.
cards.keyPoint: Reduced or absent effort during the event supports central apnea.

cards.front: Epoch Lab: The tracing becomes unstable across channels in a way that fails the physiology cross-check.
cards.back: Artifact
cards.rationale: When multiple channels jump together nonphysiologically, artifact should be considered early.
cards.keyPoint: When multiple channels jump together nonphysiologically, artifact should be considered early.

cards.front: Epoch Lab: This epoch shows deep-sleep slow-wave dominance.
cards.back: N3
cards.rationale: Slow-wave dominance supports N3.
cards.keyPoint: Slow-wave dominance supports N3.

cards.front: Epoch Lab: An N2 support feature is present and the epoch fits that stage overall.
cards.back: N2
cards.rationale: This strip is most consistent with N2.
cards.keyPoint: This strip is most consistent with N2.

cards.back: Interface fit and patient tolerance
cards.rationale: Fit, comfort, and support are core PAP administration considerations.
cards.keyPoint: Fit, comfort, and support are core PAP administration considerations.

cards.front: Which statement best fits pediatric PAP reasoning?
cards.back: Age-aware reasoning matters and adult assumptions should not be copied blindly
cards.rationale: The blueprint includes pediatric PAP guideline awareness.
cards.keyPoint: The blueprint includes pediatric PAP guideline awareness.

cards.front: Which idea best fits oxygen questions on the exam?
cards.back: Think about indications, contraindications, and titration guidance
cards.rationale: Oxygen therapy questions are guideline-based, not automatic add-on decisions.
cards.keyPoint: Oxygen therapy questions are guideline-based, not automatic add-on decisions.

cards.front: Which option best belongs with alternative therapy awareness rather than PAP administration?
cards.back: Oral appliance, positional, or surgical pathway thinking
cards.rationale: Alternative therapies are a distinct blueprint task.
cards.keyPoint: Alternative therapies are a distinct blueprint task.

cards.front: What is the key first step when a treatment question is not really about PAP?
cards.back: Identify which non-PAP therapy category the question points toward
cards.rationale: Alternative therapy questions should be recognized and handled in their own lane.
cards.keyPoint: Alternative therapy questions should be recognized and handled in their own lane.

cards.front: Why is it useful to review the purpose of the study before hookup begins?
cards.back: It helps place the technical work in clinical context
cards.rationale: The purpose of the study helps the technologist understand the patient story and the reason for testing.
cards.keyPoint: The purpose of the study helps the technologist understand the patient story and the reason for testing.

cards.front: Which item best belongs with history and physical awareness for the technologist?
cards.back: Relevant symptoms and clinical background that may affect the study
cards.rationale: Clinical background provides context for the study and supports better interpretation and support.
cards.keyPoint: Clinical background provides context for the study and supports better interpretation and support.

cards.front: Which educational topic best supports cooperation during the study?
cards.back: Explaining what sensors do and what the patient may experience
cards.rationale: Simple explanation of the study process can reduce confusion and improve cooperation.
cards.keyPoint: Simple explanation of the study process can reduce confusion and improve cooperation.

cards.front: Why is caregiver education relevant in some sleep-lab situations?
cards.back: Because caregiver understanding can support patient cooperation and follow-through
cards.rationale: Caregiver understanding may matter, especially when support or follow-through is important.
cards.keyPoint: Caregiver understanding may matter, especially when support or follow-through is important.

cards.front: Which action best fits PAP desensitization support?
cards.back: Helping the patient gradually tolerate the interface and therapy
cards.rationale: PAP desensitization is part of therapy support and patient tolerance building.
cards.keyPoint: PAP desensitization is part of therapy support and patient tolerance building.

cards.front: Which thought best fits download-report awareness in therapy support questions?
cards.back: Therapy data may help frame support and compliance conversations
cards.rationale: The blueprint includes assessment of the download report as part of therapy support awareness.
cards.keyPoint: The blueprint includes assessment of the download report as part of therapy support awareness.

cards.front: Why does electrode application quality matter before the study gets underway?
cards.back: Poor application can compromise signal quality and interpretation
cards.rationale: Electrode application quality directly affects the integrity of the recording.
cards.keyPoint: Electrode application quality directly affects the integrity of the recording.

cards.front: Which item best fits equipment-and-supplies readiness?
cards.back: Having the correct supplies available and prepared for the ordered study
cards.rationale: Technical preparation includes ensuring the right equipment and supplies are ready.
cards.keyPoint: Technical preparation includes ensuring the right equipment and supplies are ready.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: What distinguishes MSLT from routine overnight PSG thinking?
cards.back: It uses scheduled daytime nap opportunities and protocol timing
cards.rationale: MSLT involves structured daytime nap opportunities and a specific protocol.
cards.keyPoint: MSLT involves structured daytime nap opportunities and a specific protocol.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: What distinguishes HSAT from attended in-lab PSG workflow?
cards.back: Portable home workflow and patient instruction become central
cards.rationale: HSAT depends on patient instruction and home equipment workflow rather than attended in-lab setup.
cards.keyPoint: HSAT depends on patient instruction and home equipment workflow rather than attended in-lab setup.

cards.front: Which concept best fits calibration awareness?
cards.back: Calibration helps verify system behavior before trusting the record
cards.rationale: Calibration supports confidence that the system is behaving as expected.
cards.keyPoint: Calibration supports confidence that the system is behaving as expected.

cards.front: Why are biocals educationally useful for new technologists?
cards.back: They teach what patient-generated signal changes should look like
cards.rationale: Biocals help new s connect instructed actions to expected channel responses.
cards.keyPoint: Biocals help new s connect instructed actions to expected channel responses.

cards.front: Which stage is strongly supported by high-amplitude slow-wave activity?
cards.back: N3
cards.rationale: High-amplitude slow-wave activity is a defining feature of N3 sleep.
cards.keyPoint: High-amplitude slow-wave activity is a defining feature of N3 sleep.

cards.front: Which pattern most strongly supports REM sleep?
cards.back: Rapid eye movements with low chin tone
cards.rationale: REM is strongly associated with rapid eye movements and low chin tone.
cards.keyPoint: REM is strongly associated with rapid eye movements and low chin tone.

cards.front: Why do arousals matter in scoring awareness?
cards.back: They are part of event interpretation and sleep-fragmentation thinking
cards.rationale: Arousals are part of PSG scoring and interpretation of disturbed sleep.
cards.keyPoint: Arousals are part of PSG scoring and interpretation of disturbed sleep.

cards.front: What is a safe first mindset when approaching infant scoring?
cards.back: Recognize infant studies require their own age-specific framework
cards.rationale: Infant scoring requires age-specific interpretation rather than adult default logic.
cards.keyPoint: Infant scoring requires age-specific interpretation rather than adult default logic.

cards.front: Why should the technologist summary be reviewed against the record?
cards.back: Because the written summary should align with scored findings and key night events
cards.rationale: The technologist summary should accurately reflect the record and the night's key features.
cards.keyPoint: The technologist summary should accurately reflect the record and the night's key features.

cards.front: Which item belongs with graphic-summary awareness?
cards.back: Using visuals to support architecture and treatment interpretation
cards.rationale: Graphics help communicate the overall pattern of the night and should be interpreted thoughtfully.
cards.keyPoint: Graphics help communicate the overall pattern of the night and should be interpreted thoughtfully.

cards.front: Why is PAP mode recognition important on the exam?
cards.back: Because therapy questions may point to different mode families
cards.rationale: PAP mode recognition matters because not all therapy questions are simple CPAP questions.
cards.keyPoint: PAP mode recognition matters because not all therapy questions are simple CPAP questions.

cards.front: Which issue should be considered early when therapy looks unstable but leak is elevated?
cards.back: Mask seal and interface problem
cards.rationale: Elevated leak often points back to interface seal and fit.
cards.keyPoint: Elevated leak often points back to interface seal and fit.

cards.front: What is one core idea in pediatric PAP questions?
cards.back: Age-aware therapy reasoning matters
cards.rationale: Pediatric PAP questions require age-aware therapy thinking.
cards.keyPoint: Pediatric PAP questions require age-aware therapy thinking.

cards.front: Which statement best fits oxygen-therapy reasoning?
cards.back: The should think about why oxygen is being used and under what guidance
cards.rationale: Oxygen questions center on indications, contraindications, and guidance-based use.
cards.keyPoint: Oxygen questions center on indications, contraindications, and guidance-based use.

cards.front: Which question best fits alternative-therapy thinking?
cards.back: Is this question pointing toward oral appliance, positional, or surgical therapy?
cards.rationale: Alternative-therapy questions should be recognized as their own category rather than forced into PAP-only thinking.
cards.keyPoint: Alternative-therapy questions should be recognized as their own category rather than forced into PAP-only thinking.

cards.front: What is a useful first move when the treatment question is clearly non-PAP?
cards.back: Think about the appropriate non-PAP pathway and its indications
cards.rationale: Non-PAP treatment questions should be approached in the appropriate therapy lane.
cards.keyPoint: Non-PAP treatment questions should be approached in the appropriate therapy lane.

cards.front: Why does the technologist care about pain or mobility during assessment?
cards.back: These factors may affect safety, positioning, and tolerance during the study
cards.rationale: Pain and mobility can affect safety, positioning, and how the patient tolerates the study.
cards.keyPoint: Pain and mobility can affect safety, positioning, and how the patient tolerates the study.

cards.front: What is one reason to review age-specific considerations before testing?
cards.back: Age can influence baseline needs and how the study should be approached
cards.rationale: Age-specific care needs are part of the clinical overview and baseline mindset.
cards.keyPoint: Age-specific care needs are part of the clinical overview and baseline mindset.

cards.front: Which statement best fits pre-study education?
cards.back: Clear explanation can reduce anxiety and improve cooperation
cards.rationale: Simple, clear explanation often improves patient comfort and cooperation.
cards.keyPoint: Simple, clear explanation often improves patient comfort and cooperation.

cards.front: What is one reason to discuss therapy mechanics in simple language?
cards.back: It can support patient understanding and tolerance
cards.rationale: Simple explanation of therapy can help support tolerance and engagement.
cards.keyPoint: Simple explanation of therapy can help support tolerance and engagement.

cards.front: Which idea best fits a compliance-support mindset?
cards.back: Helping the patient understand barriers and supporting use
cards.rationale: Compliance support involves practical understanding and coaching, not blame.
cards.keyPoint: Compliance support involves practical understanding and coaching, not blame.

cards.front: Why should the ordered study type influence technical setup?
cards.back: Different studies may require different preparation and workflow
cards.rationale: The ordered study type affects technical preparation and workflow.
cards.keyPoint: The ordered study type affects technical preparation and workflow.

cards.front: What is one benefit of good supply readiness before hookup?
cards.back: It supports smoother workflow and fewer avoidable delays
cards.rationale: Good preparation supports smoother, safer, more efficient workflow.
cards.keyPoint: Good preparation supports smoother, safer, more efficient workflow.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: Why should overnight context be reviewed before next-day MSLT or MWT?
cards.back: The daytime study depends on proper overnight context and protocol compliance
cards.rationale: Daytime studies should be considered in relation to the overnight study and protocol context.
cards.keyPoint: Daytime studies should be considered in relation to the overnight study and protocol context.

cards.front: What is a good first question when a signal looks wrong?
cards.back: Does this fit physiology or could it be technical artifact?
cards.rationale: Artifact and technical problems should be considered early when a signal looks wrong.
cards.keyPoint: Artifact and technical problems should be considered early when a signal looks wrong.

cards.front: Why is documentation part of troubleshooting?
cards.back: Because what happened and how it was addressed may matter later in interpretation
cards.rationale: Documentation helps preserve context about issues and responses during the study.
cards.keyPoint: Documentation helps preserve context about issues and responses during the study.

cards.front: What is one reason respiratory-event scoring cannot rely on airflow alone?
cards.back: Related channels such as effort and consequence matter too
cards.rationale: Respiratory-event interpretation should use the overall pattern, not just one channel.
cards.keyPoint: Respiratory-event interpretation should use the overall pattern, not just one channel.

cards.front: Which item belongs with REM scoring awareness?
cards.back: Eye movements and chin tone help support interpretation
cards.rationale: REM interpretation often relies on eye movements and low chin tone, not a single isolated clue.
cards.keyPoint: REM interpretation often relies on eye movements and low chin tone, not a single isolated clue.

cards.front: Why should pediatric events not be labeled too quickly with adult habits?
cards.back: Because age-specific interpretation matters
cards.rationale: Age-specific interpretation helps avoid adult-style overgeneralization.
cards.keyPoint: Age-specific interpretation helps avoid adult-style overgeneralization.

cards.front: What is one reason to compare narrative interpretation with calculated values?
cards.back: The story of the report should match the numbers
cards.rationale: Narrative, numbers, and graphics should support the same overall interpretation.
cards.keyPoint: Narrative, numbers, and graphics should support the same overall interpretation.

cards.front: Why might a titration table be useful beyond a list of settings?
cards.back: It helps connect pressure changes with response across the night
cards.rationale: A titration table helps summarize how settings changed and what happened in response.
cards.keyPoint: A titration table helps summarize how settings changed and what happened in response.

cards.front: Why is leak recognition important in PAP interpretation?
cards.back: Leak can distort therapy appearance and mislead decision-making
cards.rationale: Leak can make therapy look worse or different than the patient's true response.
cards.keyPoint: Leak can make therapy look worse or different than the patient's true response.

cards.front: What is one reason bilevel thinking may differ from one-pressure CPAP thinking?
cards.back: Some therapy questions involve support/ventilation concepts beyond fixed CPAP
cards.rationale: bilevel questions may involve support and ventilation concepts rather than simple one-pressure thinking.
cards.keyPoint: bilevel questions may involve support and ventilation concepts rather than simple one-pressure thinking.

cards.front: What is one useful thought in APAP-style questions?
cards.back: Pressure needs may vary across the night rather than staying fixed
cards.rationale: APAP thinking involves awareness that obstruction burden and pressure response may vary.
cards.keyPoint: APAP thinking involves awareness that obstruction burden and pressure response may vary.

cards.front: What is the key teaching point in central-event treatment framing?
cards.back: Not all therapy reasoning is purely obstructive-event reasoning
cards.rationale: Some therapy questions push the technologist to think beyond purely obstructive-event framing.
cards.keyPoint: Some therapy questions push the technologist to think beyond purely obstructive-event framing.

cards.front: Why should oxygen use be connected to indications and contraindications?
cards.back: Because therapy decisions should follow guidance rather than automatic habits
cards.rationale: Oxygen questions are about guideline-aware therapy reasoning, not reflexive use.
cards.keyPoint: Oxygen questions are about guideline-aware therapy reasoning, not reflexive use.

cards.front: During BPAP titration, obstructive apneas continue despite therapy. Which pressure is generally adjusted first to address the obstructive apneas?
cards.back: Increase EPAP
cards.rationale: EPAP is the expiratory pressure component used to splint the upper airway and is the pressure generally adjusted first for persistent obstructive apneas on BPAP.
cards.keyPoint: EPAP is the expiratory pressure component used to splint the upper airway and is the pressure generally adjusted first for persistent obstructive apneas on BPAP.

cards.front: According to standard PSG technical recommendations, what is the minimum recommended sampling rate for EEG channels during digital polysomnography?
cards.back: 200 Hz
cards.rationale: A 200 Hz sampling rate is the minimum recommended setting for EEG during digital PSG, while higher rates such as 500 Hz are often desirable.
cards.keyPoint: A 200 Hz sampling rate is the minimum recommended setting for EEG during digital PSG, while higher rates such as 500 Hz are often desirable.

cards.front: Standard submental EMG placement uses one electrode 1 cm above the inferior edge of the mandible. Where are the other two electrodes placed?
cards.back: 2 cm below the inferior edge of the mandible and 2 cm left and right of midline
cards.rationale: The standard chin EMG montage places one electrode above the mandible and two electrodes below the mandible, left and right of midline, to capture submental tone effectively.
cards.keyPoint: The standard chin EMG montage places one electrode above the mandible and two electrodes below the mandible, left and right of midline, to capture submental tone effectively.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: For a large blood or body-fluid spill in the lab, which bleach-to-water ratio is commonly used for the initial cleanup step before terminal disinfection per facility protocol?
cards.rationale: A 1:10 bleach dilution is commonly used for the initial treatment of large blood or body-fluid spills, followed by additional cleaning and disinfection steps according to protocol.
cards.keyPoint: A 1:10 bleach dilution is commonly used for the initial treatment of large blood or body-fluid spills, followed by additional cleaning and disinfection steps according to protocol.

cards.front: During adult CPAP titration, pressure may be increased after observing loud or unambiguous snoring for at least how long?
cards.back: 3 minutes
cards.rationale: Adult CPAP titration guidelines allow pressure increases for loud or unambiguous snoring after at least 3 minutes of observation.
cards.keyPoint: Adult CPAP titration guidelines allow pressure increases for loud or unambiguous snoring after at least 3 minutes of observation.

cards.front: Which pattern best supports scoring a pediatric central apnea rather than an obstructive apnea?
cards.back: Absent airflow with absent or markedly reduced respiratory effort
cards.rationale: Central apneas are identified by loss of airflow along with absent or markedly reduced respiratory effort, while obstructive events preserve effort.
cards.keyPoint: Central apneas are identified by loss of airflow along with absent or markedly reduced respiratory effort, while obstructive events preserve effort.

cards.front: Which combination best supports definite REM sleep onset?
cards.back: Rapid eye movements with low-amplitude mixed-frequency EEG and low chin EMG tone
cards.rationale: Definite REM is supported by the overall REM pattern, including rapid eye movements, low-amplitude mixed-frequency EEG, and low submental EMG tone.
cards.keyPoint: Definite REM is supported by the overall REM pattern, including rapid eye movements, low-amplitude mixed-frequency EEG, and low submental EMG tone.

cards.front: Discussing a patient's sleep study results with a spouse is generally permitted only when which condition is met?
cards.back: The patient agrees, does not object, or the disclosure is otherwise appropriate under professional judgment and privacy rules
cards.rationale: Sleep study information should be shared in accordance with patient permission, lack of objection, or appropriate professional judgment under privacy rules, not automatically.
cards.keyPoint: Sleep study information should be shared in accordance with patient permission, lack of objection, or appropriate professional judgment under privacy rules, not automatically.

cards.front: When posterior dominant rhythm (alpha rhythm) is absent, which EEG feature best helps distinguish Stage N1 from wake?
cards.back: Vertex sharp waves
cards.rationale: Vertex sharp waves provide a more specific clue to N1 than low-amplitude mixed-frequency activity alone when alpha is absent.
cards.keyPoint: Vertex sharp waves provide a more specific clue to N1 than low-amplitude mixed-frequency activity alone when alpha is absent.

cards.front: During REM sleep, repeated increased chin EMG activity without limb involvement is most consistent with which finding?
cards.back: REM without atonia
cards.rationale: Increased chin EMG activity during REM suggests REM without atonia or abnormal REM motor activation rather than PLMS or a classic wake artifact pattern.
cards.keyPoint: Increased chin EMG activity during REM suggests REM without atonia or abnormal REM motor activation rather than PLMS or a classic wake artifact pattern.

cards.front: During nasal-mask PAP titration, which signal is most helpful for recognizing probable mouth leak?
cards.back: Flow generator leak data
cards.rationale: Elevated unintentional leak data from the PAP flow generator is especially helpful for recognizing probable mouth leak during nasal-mask PAP titration.
cards.keyPoint: Elevated unintentional leak data from the PAP flow generator is especially helpful for recognizing probable mouth leak during nasal-mask PAP titration.

cards.front: What impedance goal is recommended at the start of a routine PSG after proper skin preparation?
cards.back: 5,000 ohms or less
cards.rationale: Good skin preparation is used to achieve low electrode impedances, with 5,000 ohms or less being a common recommended start-of-study target.
cards.keyPoint: Good skin preparation is used to achieve low electrode impedances, with 5,000 ohms or less being a common recommended start-of-study target.

cards.front: If a PSG system does not have built-in impedance testing, what should the technologist use?
cards.back: An impedance meter
cards.rationale: When the acquisition system lacks built-in impedance testing, an impedance meter is used to verify that electrode targets have been met.
cards.keyPoint: When the acquisition system lacks built-in impedance testing, an impedance meter is used to verify that electrode targets have been met.

cards.front: Why should the same electrode metal type be used within a recording derivation?
cards.back: Mixing dissimilar metals can generate an electrical potential and add artifact
cards.rationale: Using two different electrode metals within the same derivation can generate a potential and create recording artifact.
cards.keyPoint: Using two different electrode metals within the same derivation can generate a potential and create recording artifact.

cards.front: Which sampling rate pair best matches recommended digital PSG settings for EEG?
cards.back: Desirable 500 Hz, minimum 200 Hz
cards.rationale: A common recommended EEG specification is a desirable sampling rate of 500 Hz with a minimum of 200 Hz.
cards.keyPoint: A common recommended EEG specification is a desirable sampling rate of 500 Hz with a minimum of 200 Hz.

cards.front: What minimum sampling rate is commonly recommended for breathing sensors in digital PSG?
cards.back: 25 Hz
cards.rationale: Breathing sensors are often recorded at a lower minimum sampling rate than EEG, with 25 Hz being a common minimum recommendation.
cards.keyPoint: Breathing sensors are often recorded at a lower minimum sampling rate than EEG, with 25 Hz being a common minimum recommendation.

cards.front: What minimum sampling rate is commonly recommended for oximetry in digital PSG?
cards.back: 10 Hz
cards.rationale: Oximetry is a slower-changing signal than EEG or EMG, and 10 Hz is a common minimum recommendation.
cards.keyPoint: Oximetry is a slower-changing signal than EEG or EMG, and 10 Hz is a common minimum recommendation.

cards.front: Which low-frequency and high-frequency filter pair best matches a typical chin EMG setup?
cards.back: 10 Hz and 100 Hz
cards.rationale: A typical chin EMG setup uses a higher low-frequency filter and higher high-frequency filter than EEG or EOG.
cards.keyPoint: A typical chin EMG setup uses a higher low-frequency filter and higher high-frequency filter than EEG or EOG.

cards.front: Which channel type commonly uses a body-position sampling rate of 1 Hz?
cards.back: Body position sensor
cards.rationale: Body position changes slowly, so position sensors commonly use a very low sampling rate such as 1 Hz.
cards.keyPoint: Body position changes slowly, so position sensors commonly use a very low sampling rate such as 1 Hz.

cards.front: A respiratory channel is blocked because the signal amplitude is too large, but the waveform itself is otherwise intact. What is the best correction?
cards.back: Reduce the gain or sensitivity setting
cards.rationale: If excessive amplitude is causing channel blocking, the technologist corrects the display problem by reducing gain or sensitivity.
cards.keyPoint: If excessive amplitude is causing channel blocking, the technologist corrects the display problem by reducing gain or sensitivity.

cards.front: A central channel shows blocking artifact and no longer provides a usable backup derivation. What is the best response?
cards.back: Repair or replace the electrode as soon as practical
cards.rationale: A lost backup central lead should be corrected promptly so the study retains adequate staging options.
cards.keyPoint: A lost backup central lead should be corrected promptly so the study retains adequate staging options.

cards.front: Why is reviewing the medical record before patient arrival important when strange breathing patterns appear on the tracing?
cards.back: Some unusual patterns may reflect true physiology rather than artifact
cards.rationale: Chart review helps the technologist distinguish unexpected but real physiology from technical problems.
cards.keyPoint: Chart review helps the technologist distinguish unexpected but real physiology from technical problems.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: Why are biocalibrations repeated at the end of the study?
cards.back: To verify that leads and monitoring devices are still functioning properly
cards.rationale: End-of-study biocalibrations help confirm that equipment and lead integrity were maintained through the recording.
cards.keyPoint: End-of-study biocalibrations help confirm that equipment and lead integrity were maintained through the recording.

cards.front: Which item should be documented if the technologist changes amplifier settings during the night?
cards.back: The change and the reason for it
cards.rationale: Amplifier changes and the reason for them belong in the technologist's documentation.
cards.keyPoint: Amplifier changes and the reason for them belong in the technologist's documentation.

cards.front: Which information is part of recommended interval documentation during a PSG?
cards.back: Sleep stage, SpO2 nadir, observed events, and treatment parameters
cards.rationale: Interval documentation often includes the current sleep stage, oxygen nadir, observed events, and treatment information.
cards.keyPoint: Interval documentation often includes the current sleep stage, oxygen nadir, observed events, and treatment information.

cards.front: Why should technologist annotations use accurate, professional language?
cards.back: They become part of the medical record and may undergo legal review
cards.rationale: Technologist notes are medical documentation and should be concise, accurate, and professional.
cards.keyPoint: Technologist notes are medical documentation and should be concise, accurate, and professional.

cards.front: If many M2-referenced channels show the same slow-frequency artifact, what should be suspected first?
cards.back: A reference-related problem affecting M2
cards.rationale: When several channels sharing the same reference are contaminated together, the shared reference should be suspected first.
cards.keyPoint: When several channels sharing the same reference are contaminated together, the shared reference should be suspected first.

cards.front: Electrode popping artifact is most directly caused by what technical change?
cards.back: An abrupt shift in electrode impedance
cards.rationale: Electrode pops come from abrupt impedance shifts caused by unstable electrodes, intermittent shorts, or brief disconnections.
cards.keyPoint: Electrode pops come from abrupt impedance shifts caused by unstable electrodes, intermittent shorts, or brief disconnections.

cards.front: What is the best first correction for an electrode that is popping because it is mechanically unstable?
cards.back: Reaffix or replace the electrode
cards.rationale: Mechanically unstable or intermittently disconnected electrodes should be secured or replaced, not simply filtered away.
cards.keyPoint: Mechanically unstable or intermittently disconnected electrodes should be secured or replaced, not simply filtered away.

cards.front: Which statement best fits the technologist's approach to artifact during recording?
cards.back: Different artifact types require different responses rather than one hard rule
cards.rationale: Artifact management involves trade-offs and depends on the type and source of the problem.
cards.keyPoint: Artifact management involves trade-offs and depends on the type and source of the problem.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: What should be noted in the record when the study begins?
cards.back: The lights-out time
cards.rationale: The start of recording should be documented with the lights-out time and other relevant beginning-of-study information.
cards.keyPoint: The start of recording should be documented with the lights-out time and other relevant beginning-of-study information.

cards.front: Why should the technologist explain the purpose of the sensors before the study begins?
cards.back: It can improve understanding, relaxation, and cooperation
cards.rationale: Clear explanation of the equipment and process can reduce anxiety and help the patient cooperate with testing.
cards.keyPoint: Clear explanation of the equipment and process can reduce anxiety and help the patient cooperate with testing.

cards.front: What is one benefit of prefitting PAP interfaces before lights out when PAP may be needed?
cards.back: It gives the patient time to adapt to the interface
cards.rationale: Early mask exposure can improve adaptation and reduce stress if PAP becomes necessary during the study.
cards.keyPoint: Early mask exposure can improve adaptation and reduce stress if PAP becomes necessary during the study.

cards.front: How should the technologist respond when a patient says, "I do not think I can sleep with all this equipment on"?
cards.back: Provide reassurance and practical explanation
cards.rationale: Patients commonly worry they will not sleep with the equipment, and reassurance is part of good care.
cards.keyPoint: Patients commonly worry they will not sleep with the equipment, and reassurance is part of good care.

cards.front: Why should the technologist allow time for patient and family questions before testing begins?
cards.back: Questions can improve acceptance and engagement with testing or therapy
cards.rationale: Allowing questions helps patients and families understand the process and often improves acceptance.
cards.keyPoint: Allowing questions helps patients and families understand the process and often improves acceptance.

cards.front: Why is the medication list part of the pre-study assessment?
cards.back: Medications can affect sleep architecture and respiratory findings
cards.rationale: Medication history helps the technologist and interpreting clinician understand potential effects on the study.
cards.keyPoint: Medication history helps the technologist and interpreting clinician understand potential effects on the study.

cards.front: How is an obstructive apnea best defined?
cards.back: Complete cessation of airflow in the presence of continued effort
cards.rationale: Obstructive apnea combines loss of airflow with continued respiratory effort.
cards.keyPoint: Obstructive apnea combines loss of airflow with continued respiratory effort.

cards.front: How is a central apnea best defined?
cards.back: Complete cessation of airflow in the absence of effort
cards.rationale: Central apnea is characterized by cessation of airflow without respiratory effort.
cards.keyPoint: Central apnea is characterized by cessation of airflow without respiratory effort.

cards.front: Which statement best compares thermal airflow sensors and nasal pressure transducers?
cards.back: Thermal sensors are especially useful for apneas, while nasal pressure is better for hypopneas and flow limitation
cards.rationale: Thermal sensors help identify complete airflow cessation, while nasal pressure tracks partial airflow reduction and flow limitation more accurately.
cards.keyPoint: Thermal sensors help identify complete airflow cessation, while nasal pressure tracks partial airflow reduction and flow limitation more accurately.

cards.front: What finding is required to score stage N3 in an adult epoch?
cards.back: Slow-wave activity occupying at least 20% of the epoch
cards.rationale: Stage N3 requires sufficient slow-wave activity across the epoch rather than isolated slow waves.
cards.keyPoint: Stage N3 requires sufficient slow-wave activity across the epoch rather than isolated slow waves.

cards.front: Which feature best establishes stage N2?
cards.back: A sleep spindle or K-complex
cards.rationale: A spindle or K-complex is the defining N2 marker when the epoch otherwise fits.
cards.keyPoint: A spindle or K-complex is the defining N2 marker when the epoch otherwise fits.

cards.front: Which finding most strongly supports wakefulness rather than N1?
cards.back: Established alpha activity with blinking
cards.rationale: Posterior alpha and waking eye blinks are classic clues for wakefulness.
cards.keyPoint: Posterior alpha and waking eye blinks are classic clues for wakefulness.

cards.front: Which waveform may appear immediately before rapid eye movements in REM sleep?
cards.back: Sawtooth waves
cards.rationale: Sawtooth waves are not required for REM scoring, but they may appear just before REM bursts.
cards.keyPoint: Sawtooth waves are not required for REM scoring, but they may appear just before REM bursts.

cards.front: A study has a mildly elevated overall AHI, but the REM AHI is much higher and REM time was limited. What is the best interpretation caution?
cards.back: Severity may be underestimated overall
cards.rationale: Limited REM can hide a stronger REM-predominant pattern, so the overall AHI may underrepresent severity.
cards.keyPoint: Limited REM can hide a stronger REM-predominant pattern, so the overall AHI may underrepresent severity.

cards.front: What feature is needed for accurate interpretation of ETCO2 values during PSG?
cards.back: A good alveolar plateau
cards.rationale: ETCO2 values should be interpreted cautiously when the plateau is distorted, because accurate values depend on a good alveolar plateau.
cards.keyPoint: ETCO2 values should be interpreted cautiously when the plateau is distorted, because accurate values depend on a good alveolar plateau.

cards.front: What does partial occlusion of ETCO2 sampling tubing most likely cause?
cards.back: A dampened waveform and inaccurate values
cards.rationale: Partial obstruction of the ETCO2 sampling circuit can dampen the waveform and make the values unreliable.
cards.keyPoint: Partial obstruction of the ETCO2 sampling circuit can dampen the waveform and make the values unreliable.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: Why can ETCO2 be harder to align with the exact breath seen on the PSG tracing?
cards.back: The sampled gas must travel through tubing before being measured
cards.rationale: A transport delay occurs because exhaled gas is aspirated through tubing to the analyzer.
cards.keyPoint: A transport delay occurs because exhaled gas is aspirated through tubing to the analyzer.

cards.front: What is considered the treatment of choice for adult obstructive sleep apnea in routine sleep-lab teaching?
cards.back: CPAP
cards.rationale: CPAP is commonly described as the standard treatment of choice for adult OSA.
cards.keyPoint: CPAP is commonly described as the standard treatment of choice for adult OSA.

cards.front: Which problem is supplemental oxygen most directly used to treat in sleep-lab respiratory thinking?
cards.back: Hypoventilation or hypoxemia
cards.rationale: Oxygen is used for oxygenation problems and may be part of care for hypoventilation or hypoxemia, not as a direct treatment for unrelated disorders.
cards.keyPoint: Oxygen is used for oxygenation problems and may be part of care for hypoventilation or hypoxemia, not as a direct treatment for unrelated disorders.
