cards.back: Temporarily work around the artifact if possible and repair it at a more practical awakening or lighter stage
cards.rationale: Artifact response requires balancing study goals, sleep stage, and repair timing.
cards.keyPoint: Artifact response requires balancing study goals, sleep stage, and repair timing.

cards.front: Which channel is used most directly to record eye movements during a sleep study?
cards.back: Electro-oculogram (EOG)
cards.rationale: Eye movements are recorded with EOG channels.
cards.keyPoint: Eye movements are recorded with EOG channels.

cards.front: What is the best reason to verify electrode impedance after sensor application?

cards.rationale: Impedance verification helps ensure cleaner signal acquisition and fewer technical problems.
cards.keyPoint: Impedance verification helps ensure cleaner signal acquisition and fewer technical problems.

cards.front: When more than half of a 30-second epoch is obscured by artifact in the channels needed for staging, and that epoch is surrounded by wake, how should it be scored?
cards.back: Wake
cards.rationale: An obscured epoch may be movement time, but when surrounded by wake it is scored as wake.
cards.keyPoint: An obscured epoch may be movement time, but when surrounded by wake it is scored as wake.

cards.front: Which questionnaire is commonly used to screen for obstructive sleep apnea risk?
cards.back: STOP-BANG
cards.rationale: STOP-BANG is a common OSA screening questionnaire.
cards.keyPoint: STOP-BANG is a common OSA screening questionnaire.

cards.keyPoint: The handbook's sample item identifies blood oxygenation as the recommended required parameter among the listed options.

cards.front: Which finding is most characteristic of a sleep spindle?
cards.back: 11 to 16 Hz activity lasting at least 0.5 seconds

cards.keyPoint: Sleep spindles are rhythmic bursts in the spindle range and are characteristic of stage N2.

cards.front: What EEG feature is often seen near the transition from stage N1 to stage N2 sleep?

cards.keyPoint: Vertex sharp waves commonly appear near the N1-to-N2 transition.

cards.front: Which waveform pattern is a clue that REM sleep may be present, even though it is not required to score REM?

cards.keyPoint: Sawtooth waves can appear in REM sleep and are a helpful clue.

cards.front: Which definition best matches REM latency?
cards.back: Time from first epoch of sleep to first epoch of REM sleep

cards.keyPoint: REM latency is measured from sleep onset to the first REM epoch.

cards.front: Which formula matches sleep efficiency?

cards.rationale: Sleep efficiency is the percentage of time in bed spent asleep.
cards.keyPoint: Sleep efficiency is the percentage of time in bed spent asleep.

cards.front: Which formula matches the periodic limb movement index shown in the BRPT handbook sample item?

cards.rationale: The sample item in the handbook uses total PLMs multiplied by 60 divided by total sleep time.
cards.keyPoint: The sample item in the handbook uses total PLMs multiplied by 60 divided by total sleep time.

cards.front: Which finding best meets arousal criteria in NREM sleep?

cards.keyPoint: An arousal in NREM is defined by an abrupt shift in EEG frequency of appropriate duration after established sleep.

cards.front: Which PAP interface is generally the best option when a patient has significant nasal obstruction?

cards.keyPoint: EPAP stands for expiratory positive airway pressure.

cards.front: What is sleep debt?

cards.front: In a normal adult sleep period, which pattern is most typical across the night?
cards.back: Slow-wave sleep dominates the first third and REM dominates the last third

cards.front: According to current PAP guidance, what should accompany PAP initiation for adults with OSA?
cards.back: Educational interventions
cards.rationale: Education should be given with initiation of PAP therapy to support successful use and adherence.
cards.keyPoint: Education should be given with initiation of PAP therapy to support successful use and adherence.

cards.front: Which statement best reflects the AASM pediatric CPAP position statement?
cards.back: CPAP can be safe and effective even in younger and smaller pediatric patients when managed by an experienced clinician
cards.rationale: The position statement supports pediatric CPAP even in younger and smaller patients when managed by clinicians with pediatric OSA expertise.
cards.keyPoint: The position statement supports pediatric CPAP even in younger and smaller patients when managed by clinicians with pediatric OSA expertise.

cards.front: A child or adult who would benefit from PAP has marked difficulty tolerating the interface before lights out. What support approach is specifically described for this problem?
cards.back: PAP desensitization
cards.rationale: Desensitization is used when a patient has difficulty acclimating to PAP and may be done in daytime sessions with a technologist.
cards.keyPoint: Desensitization is used when a patient has difficulty acclimating to PAP and may be done in daytime sessions with a technologist.

cards.front: Which quality measure is specifically emphasized for pediatric patients using PAP?
cards.back: Documentation of objective PAP adherence assessment
cards.rationale: Pediatric OSA quality measures include documenting objective PAP adherence assessment as part of quality care.
cards.keyPoint: Pediatric OSA quality measures include documenting objective PAP adherence assessment as part of quality care.

cards.front: Which minimum EEG channel count is listed for a Type 1 adult diagnostic sleep study in the 2024 adult sleep study guideline?
cards.back: 3 channels
cards.rationale: The 2024 adult guideline lists a minimum of three EEG channels for Type 1 diagnostic studies.
cards.keyPoint: The 2024 adult guideline lists a minimum of three EEG channels for Type 1 diagnostic studies.

cards.front: Which of the following is included in the minimum channel set for a Type 1 adult diagnostic sleep study?
cards.back: Body position
cards.rationale: Body position is part of the minimum Type 1 adult study measurement set along with airflow, effort, oximetry, ECG, EEG, EOG, EMG, and related channels.
cards.keyPoint: Body position is part of the minimum Type 1 adult study measurement set along with airflow, effort, oximetry, ECG, EEG, EOG, EMG, and related channels.

cards.front: During PAP acclimation, what CPAP starting pressure is described in the AAST acclimation guideline?
cards.back: 4 cm H2O
cards.rationale: The guideline describes introducing PAP gradually and starting CPAP at 4 cm H2O during acclimation.
cards.keyPoint: The guideline describes introducing PAP gradually and starting CPAP at 4 cm H2O during acclimation.

cards.front: During PAP acclimation, what starting bilevel setting is described in the AAST acclimation guideline?
cards.back: 8/4 cm H2O
cards.rationale: The AAST acclimation guideline describes starting BPAP at 8 IPAP/4 EPAP for acclimation.
cards.keyPoint: The AAST acclimation guideline describes starting BPAP at 8 IPAP/4 EPAP for acclimation.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: Before an MSLT, how much sleep documentation is recommended in the current adult protocols?
cards.back: Two weeks of sleep diary and, when available, actigraphy
cards.rationale: Current MSLT/MWT protocols recommend documenting sleep with two weeks of diary and often actigraphy before testing.
cards.keyPoint: Current MSLT/MWT protocols recommend documenting sleep with two weeks of diary and often actigraphy before testing.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: A patient with OSA is scheduled for MSLT. What should be true before proceeding?
cards.back: OSA treatment should be effective and stable
cards.rationale: Current protocols recommend confirming effective and stable treatment of OSA before MSLT interpretation is used for hypersomnolence evaluation.
cards.keyPoint: Current protocols recommend confirming effective and stable treatment of OSA before MSLT interpretation is used for hypersomnolence evaluation.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: Which follow-up testing statement is most accurate for an asymptomatic patient doing well on PAP?
cards.back: Routine repeat PSG or HSAT is generally not recommended
cards.rationale: Guidance for adults with OSA states that routine repeat PSG or HSAT is not recommended for asymptomatic PAP-treated patients.
cards.keyPoint: Guidance for adults with OSA states that routine repeat PSG or HSAT is not recommended for asymptomatic PAP-treated patients.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: Which situation is a supported reason to consider follow-up PSG or HSAT after OSA diagnosis?
cards.back: Persistent or recurrent symptoms despite good PAP adherence
cards.rationale: Follow-up PSG or HSAT may be used when symptoms persist or recur despite apparently adequate treatment adherence.
cards.keyPoint: Follow-up PSG or HSAT may be used when symptoms persist or recur despite apparently adequate treatment adherence.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: Which of the following is another supported reason to consider repeat sleep testing in a treated OSA patient?
cards.back: Significant weight change
cards.rationale: Follow-up testing may be considered after substantial weight gain or loss because OSA severity and therapy needs can change.
cards.keyPoint: Follow-up testing may be considered after substantial weight gain or loss because OSA severity and therapy needs can change.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: During PAP titration, which CO2 methods are recommended for detecting hypoventilation according to the AAST transcutaneous guideline summary of AASM recommendations?
cards.back: Arterial or transcutaneous PCO2
cards.rationale: For PAP titration, arterial or transcutaneous PCO2 are the recommended methods to detect hypoventilation.
cards.keyPoint: For PAP titration, arterial or transcutaneous PCO2 are the recommended methods to detect hypoventilation.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: Which probe temperature is generally used for PtcCO2 monitoring in pediatric and adult patients?
cards.back: 44  degreesC
cards.rationale: The guideline notes that skin probe temperature is generally 44  degreesC in pediatric and adult patients, with caution for thermal injury.
cards.keyPoint: The guideline notes that skin probe temperature is generally 44  degreesC in pediatric and adult patients, with caution for thermal injury.

cards.front: The transcutaneous CO2 value does not match the clinical picture early in the study. What should the technologist do first?
cards.back: Check sensor application/site contact and re-calibrate if needed
cards.rationale: Questionable TCM values should prompt checking sensor application, site contact, and calibration before using the number for decisions.
cards.keyPoint: Questionable TCM values should prompt checking sensor application, site contact, and calibration before using the number for decisions.

cards.front: Which TcCO2 documentation practice is specifically recommended during recording?
cards.back: Verify that the PSG display matches the transcutaneous monitor values
cards.rationale: The guideline states the technologist should verify that the sleep recording displays the same values as the TCM device and document that verification.
cards.keyPoint: The guideline states the technologist should verify that the sleep recording displays the same values as the TCM device and document that verification.

cards.front: In adults, sleep hypoventilation can be scored when transcutaneous or arterial PCO2 rises above what value for at least 10 minutes?
cards.back: 55 mmHg
cards.rationale: Adult hypoventilation may be scored if PCO2 exceeds 55 mmHg for at least 10 minutes.
cards.keyPoint: Adult hypoventilation may be scored if PCO2 exceeds 55 mmHg for at least 10 minutes.

cards.front: Which alternate adult sleep hypoventilation criterion is correct?
cards.back: A >=10 mmHg rise from awake supine value to a level exceeding 50 mmHg for at least 10 minutes
cards.rationale: Adult hypoventilation can also be scored with a rise of at least 10 mmHg from awake supine value to a level above 50 mmHg for at least 10 minutes.
cards.keyPoint: Adult hypoventilation can also be scored with a rise of at least 10 mmHg from awake supine value to a level above 50 mmHg for at least 10 minutes.

cards.front: In pediatric patients, sleep hypoventilation is scored when more than what proportion of total sleep time shows PCO2 greater than 50 mmHg?
cards.rationale: Pediatric hypoventilation is scored when more than 25% of total sleep time shows a PCO2 value above 50 mmHg.
cards.keyPoint: Pediatric hypoventilation is scored when more than 25% of total sleep time shows a PCO2 value above 50 mmHg.

cards.front: Which statement best matches the pediatric PSG review regarding diagnosis of sleep-related breathing disorders in children?
cards.back: The gold standard is the skillful integration of clinical and polygraphic findings
cards.rationale: The pediatric respiratory review concludes that the gold standard is the knowledgeable integration of clinical and polygraphic findings, not PSG in isolation.
cards.keyPoint: The pediatric respiratory review concludes that the gold standard is the knowledgeable integration of clinical and polygraphic findings, not PSG in isolation.

cards.front: Which of the following is part of the required written interpretation for a Type 1 adult sleep study report?
cards.back: A summary that integrates the raw findings with derived indices
cards.rationale: The 2024 adult guideline emphasizes that the report must integrate the raw physiological findings and derived values into a written interpretation.
cards.keyPoint: The 2024 adult guideline emphasizes that the report must integrate the raw physiological findings and derived values into a written interpretation.

cards.front: Which oxygenation details are specifically required in the adult sleep study report?
cards.back: Baseline before sleep onset, mean stable NREM saturation, and time at or below defined low-saturation thresholds
cards.rationale: The guideline calls for reporting baseline and stable oxygenation plus the duration or percentage of sleep time at or below important saturation thresholds.
cards.keyPoint: The guideline calls for reporting baseline and stable oxygenation plus the duration or percentage of sleep time at or below important saturation thresholds.

cards.front: When transcutaneous CO2 is measured in an adult study, which report element is specifically expected?
cards.back: Baseline before sleep onset plus maximum values in NREM and REM
cards.rationale: The adult guideline indicates that when PtcCO2 is measured, the baseline before sleep onset and the maximum values in NREM and REM should be commented on.
cards.keyPoint: The adult guideline indicates that when PtcCO2 is measured, the baseline before sleep onset and the maximum values in NREM and REM should be commented on.

cards.front: Normative values used to interpret PSG parameters should be:
cards.back: Referenced to a stated source and used with awareness of their limits
cards.rationale: The adult guideline states normative values should be referenced to a source and interpreted with awareness of dataset limitations.
cards.keyPoint: The adult guideline states normative values should be referenced to a source and interpreted with awareness of dataset limitations.

cards.front: Which statement is most consistent with the pediatric respiratory PSG review?
cards.back: Clinical history and examination are often poor predictors of pediatric respiratory PSG findings
cards.rationale: The pediatric evidence review notes that clinical history and physical examination often do not predict respiratory PSG findings well in children.
cards.keyPoint: The pediatric evidence review notes that clinical history and physical examination often do not predict respiratory PSG findings well in children.

cards.front: Which pediatric group has particularly strong evidence supporting the clinical utility of PSG?
cards.back: Children with suspected sleep-related breathing disorders and obesity
cards.rationale: The pediatric review found particularly strong clinical utility of PSG in children with suspected SRBD and obesity, among other high-risk groups.
cards.keyPoint: The pediatric review found particularly strong clinical utility of PSG in children with suspected SRBD and obesity, among other high-risk groups.

cards.front: What is one major value of preoperative PSG before adenotonsillectomy in children with suspected OSA?
cards.back: It helps predict perioperative risk and possible persistence of OSA after surgery
cards.rationale: The pediatric respiratory review notes preoperative PSG helps predict perioperative complications and the likelihood of residual OSA after surgery.
cards.keyPoint: The pediatric respiratory review notes preoperative PSG helps predict perioperative complications and the likelihood of residual OSA after surgery.

cards.front: For routine ongoing adult OSA treatment, which PAP choices are recommended in current guidance?
cards.back: Either CPAP or APAP
cards.rationale: Current AASM guidance recommends either CPAP or APAP for ongoing treatment of adult OSA.
cards.keyPoint: Current AASM guidance recommends either CPAP or APAP for ongoing treatment of adult OSA.

cards.front: For routine adult OSA treatment, what does the guideline suggest using over BPAP?
cards.back: CPAP or APAP
cards.rationale: The guideline suggests CPAP or APAP over BPAP in the routine treatment of adult OSA.
cards.keyPoint: The guideline suggests CPAP or APAP over BPAP in the routine treatment of adult OSA.

cards.front: In adults with OSA and no significant comorbidities, PAP may be initiated using which two strategies?
cards.back: APAP at home or in-laboratory PAP titration
cards.rationale: Current guidance recommends PAP initiation with either home APAP or in-lab PAP titration in appropriate adults without major comorbidities.
cards.keyPoint: Current guidance recommends PAP initiation with either home APAP or in-lab PAP titration in appropriate adults without major comorbidities.

cards.front: Which support measure is suggested during the initial period of PAP therapy besides education?
cards.back: Behavioral and/or troubleshooting interventions
cards.rationale: Behavioral and troubleshooting interventions are suggested during early PAP treatment to improve comfort and adherence.
cards.keyPoint: Behavioral and troubleshooting interventions are suggested during early PAP treatment to improve comfort and adherence.

cards.front: What is another suggested support strategy during the initial PAP period?
cards.back: Telemonitoring-guided interventions
cards.rationale: Telemonitoring-guided interventions are suggested during the initial PAP period in adults with OSA.
cards.keyPoint: Telemonitoring-guided interventions are suggested during the initial PAP period in adults with OSA.

cards.front: According to older APAP practice parameters, APAP titration/treatment was not recommended for which patient type?
cards.back: A patient with congestive heart failure and prominent nocturnal desaturation from another cause
cards.rationale: Older APAP parameters excluded CHF, significant lung disease, daytime hypoxemia/respiratory failure, and prominent non-OSA desaturation from routine APAP use.
cards.keyPoint: Older APAP parameters excluded CHF, significant lung disease, daytime hypoxemia/respiratory failure, and prominent non-OSA desaturation from routine APAP use.

cards.front: Which type of oral appliance is preferred when an oral appliance is prescribed for an adult with OSA?
cards.back: A custom, titratable appliance
cards.rationale: AASM/AADSM guidance recommends a custom, titratable oral appliance when oral appliance therapy is prescribed for adult OSA.
cards.keyPoint: AASM/AADSM guidance recommends a custom, titratable oral appliance when oral appliance therapy is prescribed for adult OSA.

cards.front: When is oral appliance therapy an appropriate discussion point for an adult with OSA?
cards.back: When the patient is intolerant of CPAP or prefers an alternate therapy
cards.rationale: Oral appliance therapy is appropriate for adults with OSA who are intolerant of CPAP or prefer alternate therapy.
cards.keyPoint: Oral appliance therapy is appropriate for adults with OSA who are intolerant of CPAP or prefer alternate therapy.

cards.front: Which adult patient with OSA should have discussion of referral to a sleep surgeon according to current guidance?
cards.back: A PAP-intolerant or PAP-unaccepting patient with BMI less than 40
cards.rationale: Current surgical referral guidance supports discussion of sleep-surgeon referral for PAP-intolerant or PAP-unaccepting adults with BMI under 40.
cards.keyPoint: Current surgical referral guidance supports discussion of sleep-surgeon referral for PAP-intolerant or PAP-unaccepting adults with BMI under 40.

cards.front: Which patient should have discussion of bariatric surgery referral according to the adult OSA surgical consultation guideline?
cards.back: A PAP-intolerant or PAP-unaccepting adult with OSA and BMI 35 or higher
cards.rationale: Current guidance supports discussion of bariatric surgery referral in OSA patients with obesity and BMI 35 or higher who are intolerant or unaccepting of PAP.
cards.keyPoint: Current guidance supports discussion of bariatric surgery referral in OSA patients with obesity and BMI 35 or higher who are intolerant or unaccepting of PAP.

cards.front: Which statement best reflects the older AASM medical therapy review for adult OSA?
cards.back: Weight loss should be routinely recommended to most overweight patients
cards.rationale: The AASM review concluded that weight loss has broad health benefits and should be routinely recommended to most overweight patients with OSA.
cards.keyPoint: The AASM review concluded that weight loss has broad health benefits and should be routinely recommended to most overweight patients with OSA.

cards.front: How did the AASM medical therapy review characterize supplemental oxygen and positional therapy for OSA?
cards.back: They may benefit subsets of patients but do not replace PAP as the most uniformly effective therapy
cards.rationale: The review notes that supplemental oxygen and positional therapy may help selected patients, but PAP remains the most uniformly effective OSA therapy.
cards.keyPoint: The review notes that supplemental oxygen and positional therapy may help selected patients, but PAP remains the most uniformly effective OSA therapy.

cards.front: Which adult OSA rule from ICSD-3 is correct?
cards.back: Adult OSA can be diagnosed with symptoms plus 5 or more predominantly obstructive respiratory events per hour
cards.rationale: ICSD-3 adult OSA can be diagnosed when symptoms or qualifying associated features are present and PSG or OCST shows 5 or more predominantly obstructive respiratory events per hour.
cards.keyPoint: ICSD-3 adult OSA can be diagnosed when symptoms or qualifying associated features are present and PSG or OCST shows 5 or more predominantly obstructive respiratory events per hour.

cards.front: According to ICSD-3 adult OSA criteria, which finding can establish the diagnosis even if classic symptoms are not endorsed?
cards.back: 15 or more predominantly obstructive respiratory events per hour
cards.rationale: ICSD-3 allows adult OSA diagnosis with 15 or more predominantly obstructive respiratory events per hour even without the symptom-based pathway.
cards.keyPoint: ICSD-3 allows adult OSA diagnosis with 15 or more predominantly obstructive respiratory events per hour even without the symptom-based pathway.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: Why does ICSD-3 note that OCST commonly underestimates obstructive respiratory event frequency compared with PSG?
cards.back: OCST uses monitoring time and often lacks EEG-defined sleep time
cards.rationale: ICSD-3 explains that OCST commonly underestimates frequency because actual sleep time is often not recorded, so event rate is based on monitoring time rather than true sleep time.
cards.keyPoint: ICSD-3 explains that OCST commonly underestimates frequency because actual sleep time is often not recorded, so event rate is based on monitoring time rather than true sleep time.

cards.front: Which report term does ICSD-3 say may be used when respiratory event frequency is based on monitoring time rather than total sleep time?
cards.back: REI
cards.rationale: ICSD-3 notes that the term respiratory event index (REI) may be used when event frequency is based on monitoring time rather than total sleep time.
cards.keyPoint: ICSD-3 notes that the term respiratory event index (REI) may be used when event frequency is based on monitoring time rather than total sleep time.

cards.front: How does ICSD-3 classify upper airway resistance syndrome (UARS) in adults?
cards.back: As subsumed under adult obstructive sleep apnea
cards.rationale: ICSD-3 states that UARS is subsumed under the diagnosis of adult obstructive sleep apnea because the pathophysiology does not significantly differ.
cards.keyPoint: ICSD-3 states that UARS is subsumed under the diagnosis of adult obstructive sleep apnea because the pathophysiology does not significantly differ.

cards.front: Which PSG finding meets the ICSD-3 threshold for pediatric OSA by event frequency alone?
cards.back: One or more obstructive apneas, mixed apneas, or hypopneas per hour of sleep
cards.rationale: ICSD-3 pediatric OSA can be established when PSG shows one or more obstructive apneas, mixed apneas, or hypopneas per hour of sleep together with the required clinical features.
cards.keyPoint: ICSD-3 pediatric OSA can be established when PSG shows one or more obstructive apneas, mixed apneas, or hypopneas per hour of sleep together with the required clinical features.

cards.front: Which pattern matches ICSD-3 pediatric obstructive hypoventilation?
cards.back: At least 25% of total sleep time with PaCO2 greater than 50 mm Hg plus obstructive features
cards.rationale: ICSD-3 pediatric OSA includes a pattern of obstructive hypoventilation defined by at least 25% of total sleep time with PaCO2 greater than 50 mm Hg associated with obstructive features such as snoring, inspiratory flattening, or paradoxical motion.
cards.keyPoint: ICSD-3 pediatric OSA includes a pattern of obstructive hypoventilation defined by at least 25% of total sleep time with PaCO2 greater than 50 mm Hg associated with obstructive features such as snoring, inspiratory flattening, or paradoxical motion.

cards.front: A child snores loudly, has paradoxical breathing during sleep, and struggles in school. Which ICSD-3 diagnosis should be high on the technologist's differential?
cards.back: Pediatric obstructive sleep apnea
cards.rationale: ICSD-3 lists snoring, labored or paradoxical breathing during sleep, and sleepiness, hyperactivity, behavioral, or learning problems as clinical features supporting pediatric OSA.
cards.keyPoint: ICSD-3 lists snoring, labored or paradoxical breathing during sleep, and sleepiness, hyperactivity, behavioral, or learning problems as clinical features supporting pediatric OSA.

cards.front: Which set of findings is required for central sleep apnea with Cheyne-Stokes breathing in ICSD-3?
cards.back: Five or more central events per hour, more than half of all apneas/hypopneas central, and a Cheyne-Stokes pattern
cards.rationale: ICSD-3 requires five or more central apneas and/or central hypopneas per hour, greater than 50% of all apneas and hypopneas being central, and a pattern that meets criteria for Cheyne-Stokes breathing.
cards.keyPoint: ICSD-3 requires five or more central apneas and/or central hypopneas per hour, greater than 50% of all apneas and hypopneas being central, and a pattern that meets criteria for Cheyne-Stokes breathing.

cards.front: What must be present for a diagnosis of central sleep apnea due to high-altitude periodic breathing?
cards.back: Symptoms attributable to the breathing disturbance or qualifying PSG findings at altitude
cards.rationale: ICSD-3 treats periodic breathing as a common physiologic response at altitude, so symptoms or qualifying findings are needed to diagnose a disorder.
cards.keyPoint: ICSD-3 treats periodic breathing as a common physiologic response at altitude, so symptoms or qualifying findings are needed to diagnose a disorder.

cards.front: Which statement best fits ICSD-3 sleep-related hypoxemia disorder after the text revision?
cards.back: It is intended for hypoxemia not fully explained by sleep-related hypoventilation, OSA, or another sleep-related breathing disorder
cards.rationale: The ICSD-3-TR clarifies that sleep-related hypoxemia disorder is for hypoxemia not fully explained by sleep-related hypoventilation, obstructive sleep apnea, or another sleep-related breathing disorder.
cards.keyPoint: The ICSD-3-TR clarifies that sleep-related hypoxemia disorder is for hypoxemia not fully explained by sleep-related hypoventilation, obstructive sleep apnea, or another sleep-related breathing disorder.

cards.front: Which sleep-related breathing diagnosis in ICSD-3 requires documentation of awake daytime hypercapnia above 45 mm Hg?
cards.back: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome
cards.rationale: ICSD-3 specifically notes that obesity hypoventilation syndrome requires documentation of awake daytime hypoventilation with PaCO2 greater than 45 mm Hg.
cards.keyPoint: ICSD-3 specifically notes that obesity hypoventilation syndrome requires documentation of awake daytime hypoventilation with PaCO2 greater than 45 mm Hg.

cards.front: What important additional requirement was added in the ICSD-3 Text Revision for treatment-emergent central sleep apnea?
cards.back: Associated signs or symptoms attributable to the central events are required
cards.rationale: The ICSD-3-TR summary states that treatment-emergent central sleep apnea now requires associated signs or symptoms to establish the diagnosis.
cards.keyPoint: The ICSD-3-TR summary states that treatment-emergent central sleep apnea now requires associated signs or symptoms to establish the diagnosis.

cards.front: During CPAP titration, obstructive events resolve but central events now make up more than half of the residual events at a rate of 5 or more per hour. Which diagnosis should the technologist recognize as a possibility?
cards.back: Treatment-emergent central sleep apnea
cards.rationale: ICSD-3 describes treatment-emergent central sleep apnea when obstructive events resolve on PAP without a backup rate and central apneas or hypopneas emerge or persist as the predominant residual abnormality.
cards.keyPoint: ICSD-3 describes treatment-emergent central sleep apnea when obstructive events resolve on PAP without a backup rate and central apneas or hypopneas emerge or persist as the predominant residual abnormality.

cards.front: Which frequency and duration pattern fits ICSD-3 chronic insomnia disorder?
cards.back: At least three times per week for at least three months
cards.rationale: ICSD-3 chronic insomnia disorder requires the sleep disturbance and associated daytime symptoms to occur at least three times per week and be present for at least three months.
cards.keyPoint: ICSD-3 chronic insomnia disorder requires the sleep disturbance and associated daytime symptoms to occur at least three times per week and be present for at least three months.

cards.front: Which statement best fits ICSD-3 short-term insomnia disorder?
cards.back: It is insomnia lasting less than three months with clinically significant concern or impairment
cards.rationale: ICSD-3 short-term insomnia disorder is characterized by sleep/wake difficulties lasting less than three months but still causing clinically significant concern or impairment.
cards.keyPoint: ICSD-3 short-term insomnia disorder is characterized by sleep/wake difficulties lasting less than three months but still causing clinically significant concern or impairment.

cards.front: How did the ICSD-3 Text Revision clarify chronic insomnia disorder criterion F?
cards.back: The sleep disturbance must not be solely due to another current sleep disorder, medical disorder, mental disorder, or medication/substance use
cards.rationale: The ICSD-3-TR changed criterion F to clarify that chronic insomnia disorder can still be diagnosed when symptoms are not solely due to another current sleep disorder, medical disorder, mental disorder, or medication/substance use.
cards.keyPoint: The ICSD-3-TR changed criterion F to clarify that chronic insomnia disorder can still be diagnosed when symptoms are not solely due to another current sleep disorder, medical disorder, mental disorder, or medication/substance use.

cards.front: What narcolepsy type 1 change is highlighted in the ICSD-3 Text Revision summary?
cards.back: Cataplexy plus an overnight SOREMP can satisfy criterion B
cards.rationale: The ICSD-3-TR summary notes that narcolepsy type 1 criterion B can be fulfilled by cataplexy plus an overnight SOREMP based on later evidence.
cards.keyPoint: The ICSD-3-TR summary notes that narcolepsy type 1 criterion B can be fulfilled by cataplexy plus an overnight SOREMP based on later evidence.

cards.front: A patient says they cannot fall asleep until very late but sleep normally when allowed to keep that late schedule. Which diagnosis should be considered before labeling the problem chronic insomnia?
cards.back: Delayed sleep-wake phase disorder
cards.rationale: ICSD-3 notes that delayed sleep-wake phase disorder should be differentiated from chronic insomnia because sleep may be normal when the patient sleeps in phase with the delayed circadian rhythm.
cards.keyPoint: ICSD-3 notes that delayed sleep-wake phase disorder should be differentiated from chronic insomnia because sleep may be normal when the patient sleeps in phase with the delayed circadian rhythm.

cards.front: Which diagnosis should be considered when a patient consistently falls asleep early and wakes earlier than desired but sleeps adequately on that advanced schedule?
cards.back: Advanced sleep-wake phase disorder
cards.rationale: ICSD-3 states that advanced sleep-wake phase disorder should be distinguished from chronic insomnia when sleep is adequate if the patient follows the advanced schedule.
cards.keyPoint: ICSD-3 states that advanced sleep-wake phase disorder should be distinguished from chronic insomnia when sleep is adequate if the patient follows the advanced schedule.

cards.front: Which statement correctly distinguishes restless legs syndrome from periodic limb movement disorder?
cards.back: RLS is defined by a sensory urge to move, whereas PLMD is based on periodic limb movements during sleep with associated clinical significance
cards.rationale: ICSD-3 separates RLS and PLMD: RLS is primarily a clinical sensory-motor complaint, while PLMD depends on periodic limb movements during sleep plus associated consequences and exclusion of better explanations.
cards.keyPoint: ICSD-3 separates RLS and PLMD: RLS is primarily a clinical sensory-motor complaint, while PLMD depends on periodic limb movements during sleep plus associated consequences and exclusion of better explanations.

cards.front: Which ICSD-3 major category includes sleepwalking and sleep terrors?
cards.back: NREM-related parasomnias
cards.rationale: ICSD-3 places sleepwalking and sleep terrors under NREM-related parasomnias as disorders of arousal from NREM sleep.
cards.keyPoint: ICSD-3 places sleepwalking and sleep terrors under NREM-related parasomnias as disorders of arousal from NREM sleep.

cards.front: Which of the following is listed by ICSD-3 as a REM-related parasomnia?
cards.back: REM sleep behavior disorder
cards.rationale: ICSD-3 lists REM sleep behavior disorder, recurrent isolated sleep paralysis, and nightmare disorder as REM-related parasomnias.
cards.keyPoint: ICSD-3 lists REM sleep behavior disorder, recurrent isolated sleep paralysis, and nightmare disorder as REM-related parasomnias.

cards.front: According to ICSD-3, which statement about PSG in chronic insomnia disorder is most accurate?
cards.back: PSG is not indicated routinely, but may be useful to rule out another sleep disorder in selected patients
cards.rationale: ICSD-3 states that polysomnography is not indicated routinely in insomnia but may be useful in selected cases to rule out other sleep disorders.
cards.keyPoint: ICSD-3 states that polysomnography is not indicated routinely in insomnia but may be useful in selected cases to rule out other sleep disorders.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: In ICSD-3 chronic insomnia disorder, when might PSG or MSLT be considered?
cards.back: When another sleep disorder is suspected or when excessive daytime sleepiness raises concern for an alternate diagnosis such as narcolepsy
cards.rationale: ICSD-3 notes that PSG may be used to rule out other sleep disorders and that PSG/MSLT may be warranted when excessive daytime sleepiness suggests an alternate diagnosis such as narcolepsy.
cards.keyPoint: ICSD-3 notes that PSG may be used to rule out other sleep disorders and that PSG/MSLT may be warranted when excessive daytime sleepiness suggests an alternate diagnosis such as narcolepsy.

cards.front: What wording change to adult OSA is highlighted in the ICSD-3 Text Revision summary?
cards.back: The symptom language was broadened to sleepiness, fatigue, insomnia, or other symptoms leading to impaired sleep-related quality of life
cards.rationale: The ICSD-3-TR summary shows the adult OSA symptom wording was broadened to include other symptoms leading to impaired sleep-related quality of life.
cards.keyPoint: The ICSD-3-TR summary shows the adult OSA symptom wording was broadened to include other symptoms leading to impaired sleep-related quality of life.

cards.front: Which additional point is emphasized in the ICSD-3 Text Revision for pediatric OSA?
cards.back: Symptoms are not better explained by another current sleep disorder, medical disorder, medication, or substance use
cards.rationale: The ICSD-3-TR summary clarifies pediatric OSA formatting and adds that the symptoms should not be better explained by another current sleep disorder, medical disorder, medication, or substance use.
cards.keyPoint: The ICSD-3-TR summary clarifies pediatric OSA formatting and adds that the symptoms should not be better explained by another current sleep disorder, medical disorder, medication, or substance use.

cards.front: Which major ICSD-3 sleep-related breathing disorder group contains obesity hypoventilation syndrome and congenital central alveolar hypoventilation syndrome?
cards.back: Sleep-related hypoventilation disorders
cards.rationale: ICSD-3 lists obesity hypoventilation syndrome and congenital central alveolar hypoventilation syndrome within the sleep-related hypoventilation disorders group.
cards.keyPoint: ICSD-3 lists obesity hypoventilation syndrome and congenital central alveolar hypoventilation syndrome within the sleep-related hypoventilation disorders group.

cards.front: What is the main purpose of reviewing the clinician's order before a sleep study?
cards.back: To confirm the ordered test type, indication, and any special instructions
cards.rationale: The order tells the technologist what procedure was requested and what clinical indication or special instruction applies.
cards.keyPoint: The order tells the technologist what procedure was requested and what clinical indication or special instruction applies.

cards.front: Which patient-history item is most directly relevant to planning a safe attended PSG?
cards.back: Comorbid conditions such as heart failure, COPD, seizure history, or mobility limitations
cards.rationale: Comorbidities and functional limits can affect monitoring needs, safety, and procedure planning.
cards.keyPoint: Comorbidities and functional limits can affect monitoring needs, safety, and procedure planning.

cards.front: Which symptom cluster is most suggestive of obstructive sleep apnea risk during screening?
cards.back: Loud snoring, witnessed apneas, and excessive daytime sleepiness
cards.rationale: Snoring, witnessed apneas, and sleepiness are common screening clues for sleep-disordered breathing.
cards.keyPoint: Snoring, witnessed apneas, and sleepiness are common screening clues for sleep-disordered breathing.

cards.front: Why should a technologist review medications before a PSG?
cards.back: Medications can affect sleep architecture, respiratory drive, movement, alertness, or safety
cards.rationale: Medication effects may influence sleep stages, respiratory events, limb movements, and patient safety.
cards.keyPoint: Medication effects may influence sleep stages, respiratory events, limb movements, and patient safety.

cards.front: What should patient orientation to the department include?
cards.back: A clear explanation of the room, equipment, call system, bathroom access, and what to expect
cards.rationale: Orientation reduces anxiety and supports safety by explaining the environment and how to request help.
cards.keyPoint: Orientation reduces anxiety and supports safety by explaining the environment and how to request help.

cards.front: Which item belongs in establishing a clinical baseline before the study?
cards.back: Vital signs, usual sleep schedule, pain level, mobility, and special needs
cards.rationale: Baseline observations help interpret the night and anticipate patient-support needs.
cards.keyPoint: Baseline observations help interpret the night and anticipate patient-support needs.

cards.front: What is the Epworth Sleepiness Scale primarily used to estimate?
cards.back: Subjective daytime sleepiness
cards.rationale: The Epworth Sleepiness Scale asks about chance of dozing in everyday situations.
cards.keyPoint: The Epworth Sleepiness Scale asks about chance of dozing in everyday situations.

cards.front: What does STOP-Bang help screen for?
cards.back: Risk of obstructive sleep apnea
cards.rationale: STOP-Bang is a commonly used OSA risk-screening questionnaire.
cards.keyPoint: STOP-Bang is a commonly used OSA risk-screening questionnaire.

cards.front: A sleep diary or actigraphy history is especially helpful when evaluating which type of problem?
cards.back: Circadian rhythm or sleep-schedule pattern concerns
cards.rationale: Sleep timing patterns over days can support evaluation of circadian or schedule-related complaints.
cards.keyPoint: Sleep timing patterns over days can support evaluation of circadian or schedule-related complaints.

cards.front: Which symptom is a classic clue that should raise concern for narcolepsy type 1?
cards.back: Cataplexy associated with excessive daytime sleepiness
cards.rationale: Cataplexy with excessive daytime sleepiness is a key clinical clue for narcolepsy type 1.
cards.keyPoint: Cataplexy with excessive daytime sleepiness is a key clinical clue for narcolepsy type 1.

cards.front: Which history description best fits restless legs syndrome screening?
cards.back: Urge to move the legs that is worse at rest and relieved by movement
cards.rationale: RLS is associated with uncomfortable leg sensations and urge to move, especially at rest and often in the evening.
cards.keyPoint: RLS is associated with uncomfortable leg sensations and urge to move, especially at rest and often in the evening.

cards.front: Which history item is most relevant when parasomnia or dream-enactment behavior is suspected?
cards.back: Injury risk, timing of behaviors, dream recall, medications, and safety concerns
cards.rationale: Parasomnia histories focus on behaviors during sleep, risk, timing, and safety.
cards.keyPoint: Parasomnia histories focus on behaviors during sleep, risk, timing, and safety.

cards.front: Which patient factor should trigger additional safety planning before hookup?
cards.back: High fall risk or need for assistance with mobility
cards.rationale: Mobility limitations and fall risk affect room setup, call-light use, and monitoring.
cards.keyPoint: Mobility limitations and fall risk affect room setup, call-light use, and monitoring.

cards.front: Which history factor can be associated with central sleep apnea or hypoventilation risk?
cards.back: Opioid use or certain cardiopulmonary/neurologic conditions
cards.rationale: Some medications and medical conditions can alter ventilatory control or breathing stability.
cards.keyPoint: Some medications and medical conditions can alter ventilatory control or breathing stability.

cards.front: What is a key purpose of the pre-study patient interview?
cards.back: To clarify symptoms, usual sleep pattern, safety needs, and procedure-specific concerns
cards.rationale: The interview adds context and identifies concerns that may not be clear from the order alone.
cards.keyPoint: The interview adds context and identifies concerns that may not be clear from the order alone.

cards.front: Which example best represents sleep hygiene education?
cards.back: Encouraging a consistent sleep schedule and limiting sleep-disrupting habits near bedtime
cards.rationale: Sleep hygiene addresses behaviors and environment that support healthier sleep.
cards.keyPoint: Sleep hygiene addresses behaviors and environment that support healthier sleep.

cards.front: What should a technologist emphasize when explaining PSG equipment?
cards.back: Sensors monitor body signals during sleep and should not be painful
cards.rationale: Explaining equipment reduces anxiety and improves cooperation.
cards.keyPoint: Explaining equipment reduces anxiety and improves cooperation.

cards.front: What does PAP compliance education usually focus on?
cards.back: Regular use, comfort troubleshooting, cleaning basics, and follow-up support
cards.rationale: Compliance education helps patients use therapy consistently and seek help when problems arise.
cards.keyPoint: Compliance education helps patients use therapy consistently and seek help when problems arise.

cards.front: Which statement reflects the technologist's appropriate role in patient education?
cards.back: Explain the procedure and general next steps, but do not give a final diagnosis
cards.rationale: Interpretation and diagnosis are physician/provider responsibilities; technologists explain procedures and support care.
cards.keyPoint: Interpretation and diagnosis are physician/provider responsibilities; technologists explain procedures and support care.

cards.front: For a pediatric PSG, why may caregiver education be important?
cards.back: A caregiver may help reduce anxiety and support age-appropriate cooperation
cards.rationale: Pediatric testing often requires family-centered orientation and support.
cards.keyPoint: Pediatric testing often requires family-centered orientation and support.

cards.front: What is a key part of HSAT education?
cards.back: How to apply or verify sensors, start the device, and return equipment as instructed
cards.rationale: HSAT success depends on correct patient instruction and equipment handling.
cards.keyPoint: HSAT success depends on correct patient instruction and equipment handling.

cards.front: Which education approach best supports an anxious PSG patient?
cards.back: Use clear, calm explanations and invite questions about the process
cards.rationale: Clear communication reduces anxiety and improves patient cooperation and safety.
cards.keyPoint: Clear communication reduces anxiety and improves patient cooperation and safety.

cards.front: Which statement is appropriate when introducing PAP therapy during a titration?
cards.back: The device provides pressurized air through a mask to help keep the airway open or support breathing depending on mode
cards.rationale: PAP education should be accurate, reassuring, and mode-appropriate.
cards.keyPoint: PAP education should be accurate, reassuring, and mode-appropriate.

cards.front: What is PAP desensitization intended to do?
cards.back: Help a patient gradually tolerate mask and pressure before or during therapy
cards.rationale: Desensitization can improve tolerance by gradual exposure and coaching.
cards.keyPoint: Desensitization can improve tolerance by gradual exposure and coaching.

cards.front: What is the main reason to assess PAP mask fit carefully?
cards.back: To improve comfort and reduce excessive leak
cards.rationale: Poor mask fit can cause leak, discomfort, arousals, and therapy intolerance.
cards.keyPoint: Poor mask fit can cause leak, discomfort, arousals, and therapy intolerance.

cards.front: Which item is commonly reviewed in a PAP download report?
cards.back: Usage, residual events, leak, and pressure information
cards.rationale: PAP downloads commonly summarize adherence and therapy effectiveness indicators.
cards.keyPoint: PAP downloads commonly summarize adherence and therapy effectiveness indicators.

cards.front: What symptom may improve with heated humidification during PAP therapy?
cards.back: Dry mouth or nasal dryness
cards.rationale: Humidification can improve comfort for dryness related to airflow.
cards.keyPoint: Humidification can improve comfort for dryness related to airflow.

cards.front: Which PAP interface covers both the nose and mouth?
cards.back: Oronasal/full-face mask
cards.rationale: An oronasal or full-face mask covers the nose and mouth.
cards.keyPoint: An oronasal or full-face mask covers the nose and mouth.

cards.front: Which action is within therapy support but not independent diagnosis?
cards.back: Helping a patient troubleshoot comfort issues and encouraging follow-up with the care team
cards.rationale: Technologists support therapy use, education, and troubleshooting while staying within scope and protocol.
cards.keyPoint: Technologists support therapy use, education, and troubleshooting while staying within scope and protocol.

cards.front: Which instruction is generally part of PAP support education?
cards.back: Follow manufacturer and provider instructions for routine cleaning and replacement of supplies
cards.rationale: Cleaning and supply care support safety, comfort, and device function.
cards.keyPoint: Cleaning and supply care support safety, comfort, and device function.

cards.front: Before a PSG begins, why should equipment and supplies be checked?
cards.back: To ensure required sensors, leads, interfaces, and backup supplies are available and functional
cards.rationale: Technical preparation prevents delays and poor data quality.
cards.keyPoint: Technical preparation prevents delays and poor data quality.

cards.front: Which system is commonly used to guide EEG electrode placement in PSG?
cards.back: The international 10-20 system
cards.rationale: PSG EEG placement is based on standardized cranial landmarks from the 10-20 system.
cards.keyPoint: PSG EEG placement is based on standardized cranial landmarks from the 10-20 system.

cards.front: What is the purpose of skin site preparation before electrode application?
cards.back: To lower impedance and improve signal quality
cards.rationale: Proper preparation improves electrode contact and reduces recording problems.
cards.keyPoint: Proper preparation improves electrode contact and reduces recording problems.

cards.front: Why are electrode impedances checked?
cards.back: To verify adequate electrical contact for reliable signal recording
cards.rationale: Impedance checks help identify poor electrode contact before recording.
cards.keyPoint: Impedance checks help identify poor electrode contact before recording.

cards.front: In PSG display settings, what does sensitivity/gain primarily affect?
cards.back: Waveform height or amplitude displayed on the screen
cards.rationale: Sensitivity/gain changes how large signals appear visually.
cards.keyPoint: Sensitivity/gain changes how large signals appear visually.

cards.front: What does the timebase/page speed primarily affect on a digital PSG display?
cards.back: How much time appears across the screen
cards.rationale: Timebase changes the horizontal time window, affecting visual width of events.
cards.keyPoint: Timebase changes the horizontal time window, affecting visual width of events.

cards.front: What is the general purpose of PSG filter settings?
cards.back: To reduce unwanted frequencies while preserving clinically important signals
cards.rationale: Filters shape displayed signals by attenuating selected frequency ranges.
cards.keyPoint: Filters shape displayed signals by attenuating selected frequency ranges.

cards.front: Which channels are typically part of a diagnostic PSG montage?
cards.back: EEG, EOG, chin EMG, ECG, airflow, effort, oximetry, and limb/body position channels
cards.rationale: A PSG montage records neurologic, respiratory, cardiac, movement, and body-position information.
cards.keyPoint: A PSG montage records neurologic, respiratory, cardiac, movement, and body-position information.

cards.front: Which practice is part of sleep-lab infection control?
cards.back: Using appropriate hand hygiene, PPE, and equipment disinfection
cards.rationale: Standard infection-control practices protect patients and staff.
cards.keyPoint: Standard infection-control practices protect patients and staff.

cards.front: What does pulse oximetry estimate during PSG?
cards.back: Peripheral oxygen saturation
cards.rationale: Pulse oximetry estimates oxygen saturation from pulsatile blood flow.
cards.keyPoint: Pulse oximetry estimates oxygen saturation from pulsatile blood flow.

cards.front: Which sensor is commonly used to detect airflow contour and flow limitation?
cards.back: Nasal pressure transducer
cards.rationale: Nasal pressure is commonly used for airflow contour and hypopnea/flow-limitation assessment.
cards.keyPoint: Nasal pressure is commonly used for airflow contour and hypopnea/flow-limitation assessment.

cards.front: Which sensor is commonly used to help detect apnea by temperature change in airflow?
cards.back: Thermal airflow sensor/thermistor
cards.rationale: Thermal airflow sensors detect airflow by temperature changes between inspired and expired air.
cards.keyPoint: Thermal airflow sensors detect airflow by temperature changes between inspired and expired air.

cards.front: What do thoracic and abdominal effort belts help measure?
cards.back: Respiratory effort and breathing movement
cards.rationale: Effort belts help distinguish patterns of respiratory effort during events.
cards.keyPoint: Effort belts help distinguish patterns of respiratory effort during events.

cards.front: Which channel is used when monitoring ventilation through carbon dioxide trends?
cards.back: End-tidal or transcutaneous CO2 monitoring
cards.rationale: CO2 monitoring provides information about ventilation, especially in hypoventilation concerns.
cards.keyPoint: CO2 monitoring provides information about ventilation, especially in hypoventilation concerns.

cards.front: Before PAP titration, which equipment item should be verified?
cards.back: PAP device, tubing, mask/interface options, humidifier setup, and pressure signal
cards.rationale: PAP titration depends on functional equipment and appropriate interface choices.
cards.keyPoint: PAP titration depends on functional equipment and appropriate interface choices.

cards.front: What is the role of reference electrodes in PSG derivations?
cards.back: They provide comparison points for recording differential bioelectric signals
cards.rationale: Many PSG channels are differential recordings comparing active and reference inputs.
cards.keyPoint: Many PSG channels are differential recordings comparing active and reference inputs.

cards.front: Why is video monitoring useful during PSG?
cards.back: It helps correlate physiologic signals with body movement, behaviors, and patient position
cards.rationale: Video can clarify artifact, parasomnia behaviors, movements, and patient activity.
cards.keyPoint: Video can clarify artifact, parasomnia behaviors, movements, and patient activity.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: What is the primary purpose of an attended diagnostic PSG?
cards.back: To record sleep, breathing, movement, cardiac, and related physiologic signals overnight
cards.rationale: Attended PSG collects multiple physiologic signals to support sleep-disorder evaluation.
cards.keyPoint: Attended PSG collects multiple physiologic signals to support sleep-disorder evaluation.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: What is a key difference in pediatric PSG performance?
cards.back: Age-appropriate communication, caregiver involvement, and pediatric-specific scoring/procedure considerations
cards.rationale: Pediatric testing requires age-sensitive setup, comfort, and rule awareness.
cards.keyPoint: Pediatric testing requires age-sensitive setup, comfort, and rule awareness.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: What does the Multiple Sleep Latency Test primarily measure?
cards.back: Tendency to fall asleep during scheduled daytime nap opportunities
cards.rationale: MSLT evaluates objective daytime sleepiness and REM onset patterns in a controlled protocol.
cards.keyPoint: MSLT evaluates objective daytime sleepiness and REM onset patterns in a controlled protocol.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: What does the Maintenance of Wakefulness Test primarily evaluate?
cards.back: Ability to remain awake in a quiet setting
cards.rationale: MWT assesses wakefulness maintenance under standardized conditions.
cards.keyPoint: MWT assesses wakefulness maintenance under standardized conditions.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: Which statement best describes HSAT compared with attended PSG?
cards.back: HSAT usually records a limited set of respiratory and related signals without full attended sleep staging
cards.rationale: HSAT is generally more limited than attended PSG and is used for selected patients.
cards.keyPoint: HSAT is generally more limited than attended PSG and is used for selected patients.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: Why are physiologic calibrations/biocals performed?
cards.back: To verify that patient-generated signals appear correctly before recording sleep
cards.rationale: Biocals confirm that channels respond appropriately to known patient actions.
cards.keyPoint: Biocals confirm that channels respond appropriately to known patient actions.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: What should be documented at lights out?
cards.back: Start time and relevant setup or patient-condition notes
cards.rationale: Accurate time and context documentation supports scoring and reporting.
cards.keyPoint: Accurate time and context documentation supports scoring and reporting.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: During an attended PSG, what is an ongoing technologist responsibility?
cards.back: Monitor signal quality, patient safety, and study integrity
cards.rationale: Attended studies require active monitoring and response.
cards.keyPoint: Attended studies require active monitoring and response.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: Why should lab protocols and practice guidelines be followed during testing?
cards.back: They support consistency, safety, and appropriate technical performance
cards.rationale: Protocols and guidelines standardize technical care and help protect patients and data quality.
cards.keyPoint: Protocols and guidelines standardize technical care and help protect patients and data quality.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: What pre-test factor is commonly controlled or documented for daytime sleepiness tests?
cards.back: Sleep schedule, medication/caffeine considerations, and prior-night sleep adequacy
cards.rationale: Daytime tests can be affected by insufficient sleep, substances, and schedule factors.
cards.keyPoint: Daytime tests can be affected by insufficient sleep, substances, and schedule factors.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: What is a split-night study designed to combine?
cards.back: Diagnostic monitoring and PAP titration in one night when criteria and protocol are met
cards.rationale: Split-night testing includes diagnostic and titration portions when appropriate criteria are satisfied.
cards.keyPoint: Split-night testing includes diagnostic and titration portions when appropriate criteria are satisfied.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: Why is lights-on documentation important?
cards.back: It marks the end of the recording period and supports calculations and report accuracy
cards.rationale: Lights-on time is essential for accurate study timing and reporting.
cards.keyPoint: Lights-on time is essential for accurate study timing and reporting.

cards.front: Which finding commonly suggests movement artifact?
cards.back: Abrupt irregular signal changes across multiple channels during visible movement
cards.rationale: Movement can contaminate several channels and should be correlated with video and context.
cards.keyPoint: Movement can contaminate several channels and should be correlated with video and context.

cards.front: What does electrical interference often look like in PSG signals?
cards.back: Regular high-frequency noise that may affect one or more channels
cards.rationale: Electrical interference can create repetitive high-frequency artifact.
cards.keyPoint: Electrical interference can create repetitive high-frequency artifact.

cards.front: What is the first general response to a lost sensor signal?
cards.back: Check the patient, sensor connection, electrode/site, and equipment pathway
cards.rationale: Signal loss requires troubleshooting the entire pathway from patient to recording system.
cards.keyPoint: Signal loss requires troubleshooting the entire pathway from patient to recording system.

cards.front: Which signals help differentiate obstructive from central apnea?
cards.back: Airflow and respiratory effort channels
cards.rationale: Respiratory effort helps determine whether effort continues or is absent during an apnea.
cards.keyPoint: Respiratory effort helps determine whether effort continues or is absent during an apnea.

cards.front: What is the technologist's role when a concerning rhythm appears?
cards.back: Recognize, document, and follow lab emergency or notification protocol
cards.rationale: Technologists should recognize concerning patterns, document, and escalate according to protocol.
cards.keyPoint: Technologists should recognize concerning patterns, document, and escalate according to protocol.

cards.front: What does a rising CO2 trend most directly suggest?
cards.back: Potential worsening ventilation
cards.rationale: CO2 trends provide information about ventilation and hypoventilation concerns.
cards.keyPoint: CO2 trends provide information about ventilation and hypoventilation concerns.

cards.front: Why should changes to filters, sensitivity, or display settings be documented when relevant?
cards.back: They can affect signal appearance and later review
cards.rationale: Technical setting changes may affect visual interpretation and troubleshooting review.
cards.keyPoint: Technical setting changes may affect visual interpretation and troubleshooting review.

cards.front: What is the purpose of channel calibration?
cards.back: To verify recording system response and signal display accuracy
cards.rationale: Calibration helps verify that channels display expected responses.
cards.keyPoint: Calibration helps verify that channels display expected responses.

cards.front: What should be done when an EEG electrode impedance is unacceptable before lights out?
cards.back: Re-prep or reapply the electrode and recheck impedance
cards.rationale: Poor impedance should be corrected when possible to improve signal quality.
cards.keyPoint: Poor impedance should be corrected when possible to improve signal quality.

cards.front: Which channel type helps identify periodic limb movements?
cards.back: Anterior tibialis EMG
cards.rationale: Leg EMG channels monitor limb muscle activity during sleep.
cards.keyPoint: Leg EMG channels monitor limb muscle activity during sleep.

cards.front: During PAP titration, what does a sudden high leak signal suggest checking first?
cards.back: Mask position, mouth leak, tubing connection, or patient movement
cards.rationale: Leak changes often come from interface fit, mouth leak, tubing, or movement.
cards.keyPoint: Leak changes often come from interface fit, mouth leak, tubing, or movement.

cards.front: Which event should be documented during the night?
cards.back: Significant technical problems, patient complaints, interventions, and unusual physiologic events
cards.rationale: Technologist documentation provides context for scoring and interpretation.
cards.keyPoint: Technologist documentation provides context for scoring and interpretation.

cards.front: In adult sleep scoring, relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed is commonly associated with what rhythm?
cards.back: Posterior dominant alpha rhythm
cards.rationale: Alpha rhythm is a common feature of relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed.
cards.keyPoint: Alpha rhythm is a common feature of relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed.

cards.front: Which feature is commonly associated with N1 sleep?
cards.back: Low-amplitude mixed-frequency EEG with possible slow eye movements
cards.rationale: N1 is a light sleep stage often marked by low-amplitude mixed-frequency activity and slow eye movements.
cards.keyPoint: N1 is a light sleep stage often marked by low-amplitude mixed-frequency activity and slow eye movements.

cards.front: Which graphoelement is strongly associated with N2 sleep?
cards.back: Sleep spindle or K complex
cards.rationale: Sleep spindles and K complexes are key N2 scoring features.
cards.keyPoint: Sleep spindles and K complexes are key N2 scoring features.

cards.front: N3 sleep is primarily identified by which EEG feature?
cards.back: High-amplitude slow-wave activity meeting current scoring criteria
cards.rationale: N3 is scored based on slow-wave activity according to current criteria.
cards.keyPoint: N3 is scored based on slow-wave activity according to current criteria.

cards.front: Which combination supports REM sleep scoring?
cards.back: Low chin EMG tone with rapid eye movements and compatible EEG
cards.rationale: REM sleep typically includes low chin tone, rapid eye movements, and appropriate EEG background.
cards.keyPoint: REM sleep typically includes low chin tone, rapid eye movements, and appropriate EEG background.

cards.front: What is an arousal in sleep scoring?
cards.back: An abrupt shift in EEG frequency meeting scoring-rule duration and context requirements
cards.rationale: Arousals are EEG-defined events scored according to duration and sleep-stage rules.
cards.keyPoint: Arousals are EEG-defined events scored according to duration and sleep-stage rules.

cards.front: What best describes an apnea for scoring purposes?
cards.back: A marked reduction in airflow meeting duration and scoring-rule criteria
cards.rationale: Apneas are airflow events scored using defined reduction and duration criteria.
cards.keyPoint: Apneas are airflow events scored using defined reduction and duration criteria.

cards.front: What distinguishes an obstructive apnea from a central apnea?
cards.back: Respiratory effort persists during the obstructive apnea
cards.rationale: Obstructive apneas show continued or increased effort despite absent/reduced airflow.
cards.keyPoint: Obstructive apneas show continued or increased effort despite absent/reduced airflow.

cards.front: What distinguishes a central apnea from an obstructive apnea?
cards.back: Absent respiratory effort during the event
cards.rationale: Central apneas lack respiratory effort during the airflow reduction.
cards.keyPoint: Central apneas lack respiratory effort during the airflow reduction.

cards.front: What is a mixed apnea?
cards.back: An apnea with both central and obstructive components
cards.rationale: Mixed apneas contain an initial central component and an obstructive component.
cards.keyPoint: Mixed apneas contain an initial central component and an obstructive component.

cards.front: What is scored as a hypopnea?
cards.back: A qualifying partial reduction in airflow with associated scoring-rule criteria
cards.rationale: Hypopneas are partial airflow reductions that meet current scoring requirements.
cards.keyPoint: Hypopneas are partial airflow reductions that meet current scoring requirements.

cards.front: What does RERA stand for?
cards.back: Respiratory effort-related arousal
cards.rationale: RERA is a respiratory event associated with increasing effort or flow limitation ending in arousal but not meeting apnea/hypopnea criteria.
cards.keyPoint: RERA is a respiratory event associated with increasing effort or flow limitation ending in arousal but not meeting apnea/hypopnea criteria.

cards.front: What is an oxygen desaturation?
cards.back: A drop in oxygen saturation from baseline or prior level meeting defined criteria
cards.rationale: Desaturations are scored from oximetry according to defined drop and timing rules.
cards.keyPoint: Desaturations are scored from oximetry according to defined drop and timing rules.

cards.front: Which signal is central to scoring periodic limb movements?
cards.back: Leg EMG activity
cards.rationale: Periodic limb movements are scored from limb EMG patterns using specific criteria.
cards.keyPoint: Periodic limb movements are scored from limb EMG patterns using specific criteria.

cards.front: How should cardiac rhythm observations in PSG be handled?
cards.back: Recognized and documented according to scoring/reporting and lab policy
cards.rationale: ECG is part of PSG monitoring; concerning observations should be documented and escalated as appropriate.
cards.keyPoint: ECG is part of PSG monitoring; concerning observations should be documented and escalated as appropriate.

cards.front: What does AHI represent?
cards.back: Apneas plus hypopneas per hour of sleep
cards.rationale: AHI is an index of apneas and hypopneas divided by sleep time.
cards.keyPoint: AHI is an index of apneas and hypopneas divided by sleep time.

cards.front: What does RDI commonly include beyond apneas and hypopneas?
cards.back: Respiratory effort-related arousals, depending on reporting definition
cards.rationale: RDI is commonly used to include respiratory events such as apneas, hypopneas, and RERAs depending on definitions used.
cards.keyPoint: RDI is commonly used to include respiratory events such as apneas, hypopneas, and RERAs depending on definitions used.

cards.front: Why should artifact be identified before scoring events?
cards.back: Artifact can mimic or obscure physiologic signals
cards.rationale: Scoring requires reliable signals; artifact can cause false interpretation.
cards.keyPoint: Scoring requires reliable signals; artifact can cause false interpretation.

cards.front: Which statement about adult sleep staging is correct?
cards.back: Each epoch is assigned a sleep stage using current scoring rules and available signals
cards.rationale: Staging uses EEG, EOG, EMG, and scoring rules for each epoch.
cards.keyPoint: Staging uses EEG, EOG, EMG, and scoring rules for each epoch.

cards.front: What should a learner use to verify exact scoring cutoffs and definitions?
cards.back: The current AASM scoring manual and current exam/resource expectations
cards.rationale: Scoring rules can be updated; learners should verify exact criteria against current official resources.
cards.keyPoint: Scoring rules can be updated; learners should verify exact criteria against current official resources.

cards.front: Why must pediatric and infant studies be scored with age-appropriate rules?
cards.back: Sleep, breathing, and event criteria can differ by age/development
cards.rationale: Pediatric and infant scoring includes age/development-specific considerations.
cards.keyPoint: Pediatric and infant scoring includes age/development-specific considerations.

cards.front: In pediatric respiratory scoring, what is especially important?
cards.back: Applying pediatric-specific respiratory event definitions and duration criteria
cards.rationale: Children have pediatric-specific respiratory scoring rules.
cards.keyPoint: Children have pediatric-specific respiratory scoring rules.

cards.front: Which concept is associated with infant sleep scoring?
cards.back: Developmental sleep states and age-specific features
cards.rationale: Infant scoring considers developmental sleep-state features and age.
cards.keyPoint: Infant scoring considers developmental sleep-state features and age.

cards.front: Why may CO2 monitoring be especially relevant in pediatric studies?
cards.back: It helps evaluate hypoventilation when ordered or indicated
cards.rationale: CO2 monitoring provides ventilation information, important in hypoventilation evaluation.
cards.keyPoint: CO2 monitoring provides ventilation information, important in hypoventilation evaluation.

cards.front: What should be used when scoring pediatric arousals?
cards.back: Current pediatric scoring rules and appropriate EEG context
cards.rationale: Arousals are scored using defined EEG and context criteria.
cards.keyPoint: Arousals are scored using defined EEG and context criteria.

cards.front: Which signal helps score pediatric limb movements?
cards.back: Leg EMG channels
cards.rationale: Leg EMG supports limb movement scoring in pediatric and adult studies.
cards.keyPoint: Leg EMG supports limb movement scoring in pediatric and adult studies.

cards.front: What is true about pediatric cardiac event review in PSG?
cards.back: Age and clinical context matter when documenting rhythm observations
cards.rationale: Cardiac observations require context, documentation, and protocol-based escalation.
cards.keyPoint: Cardiac observations require context, documentation, and protocol-based escalation.

cards.front: Why should age be clearly available for pediatric scoring/report review?
cards.back: Age affects expected sleep, respiratory, and scoring considerations
cards.rationale: Age is foundational for age-appropriate interpretation and rule application.
cards.keyPoint: Age is foundational for age-appropriate interpretation and rule application.

cards.front: How is sleep efficiency generally calculated?
cards.back: Total sleep time divided by time in bed, multiplied by 100
cards.rationale: Sleep efficiency expresses the percentage of time in bed spent asleep.
cards.keyPoint: Sleep efficiency expresses the percentage of time in bed spent asleep.

cards.front: What does TST stand for?
cards.back: Total sleep time
cards.rationale: TST is the total amount of sleep scored during the recording.
cards.keyPoint: TST is the total amount of sleep scored during the recording.

cards.front: What is sleep latency?
cards.back: Time from lights out to the first epoch of sleep
cards.rationale: Sleep latency measures how long it takes to fall asleep after lights out.
cards.keyPoint: Sleep latency measures how long it takes to fall asleep after lights out.

cards.front: What is REM latency?
cards.back: Time from sleep onset to the first epoch of REM sleep
cards.rationale: REM latency is measured from sleep onset to the first REM epoch.
cards.keyPoint: REM latency is measured from sleep onset to the first REM epoch.

cards.front: What does WASO measure?
cards.back: Wake after sleep onset
cards.rationale: WASO is wake time occurring after sleep has begun.
cards.keyPoint: WASO is wake time occurring after sleep has begun.

cards.front: What should a technologist documentation summary include?
cards.back: Important observations, interventions, patient issues, and technical limitations
cards.rationale: The summary provides objective context for interpretation and quality review.
cards.keyPoint: The summary provides objective context for interpretation and quality review.

cards.front: What does a hypnogram display?
cards.back: Sleep stage progression across the recording period
cards.rationale: A hypnogram is a graphical display of sleep stages across time.
cards.keyPoint: A hypnogram is a graphical display of sleep stages across time.

cards.front: What does a PAP titration table help summarize?
cards.back: Pressure levels, sleep stage/body position, respiratory events, leak, and oxygenation response
cards.rationale: Titration tables summarize response to therapy settings and relevant sleep/respiratory context.
cards.keyPoint: Titration tables summarize response to therapy settings and relevant sleep/respiratory context.

cards.front: What is a key part of verifying a sleep-study report?
cards.back: Checking that scored data, calculations, summaries, and notes are consistent
cards.rationale: Report verification checks accuracy and consistency before final review.
cards.keyPoint: Report verification checks accuracy and consistency before final review.

cards.front: What does REI commonly represent in HSAT reporting?
cards.back: Respiratory event index based on recording/monitoring time, depending on system definition
cards.rationale: HSAT often uses REI because full sleep time may not be measured.
cards.keyPoint: HSAT often uses REI because full sleep time may not be measured.

cards.front: What does CPAP provide?
cards.back: One continuous positive airway pressure level
cards.rationale: CPAP maintains a single set pressure throughout the breathing cycle.
cards.keyPoint: CPAP maintains a single set pressure throughout the breathing cycle.

cards.front: What does bilevel PAP provide?
cards.back: A higher inspiratory pressure and lower expiratory pressure
cards.rationale: Bilevel PAP uses IPAP and EPAP, creating pressure support.
cards.keyPoint: Bilevel PAP uses IPAP and EPAP, creating pressure support.

cards.front: How is pressure support calculated in bilevel PAP?
cards.back: IPAP minus EPAP
cards.rationale: Pressure support is the difference between inspiratory and expiratory pressures.
cards.keyPoint: Pressure support is the difference between inspiratory and expiratory pressures.

cards.front: Which PAP setting is most directly used to splint the upper airway against obstructive events in bilevel therapy?
cards.back: EPAP
cards.rationale: EPAP helps maintain airway patency during exhalation and supports obstruction control.
cards.keyPoint: EPAP helps maintain airway patency during exhalation and supports obstruction control.

cards.front: Which bilevel setting most directly increases inspiratory assistance?
cards.back: IPAP
cards.rationale: IPAP is the inspiratory positive airway pressure.
cards.keyPoint: IPAP is the inspiratory positive airway pressure.

cards.front: What is APAP designed to do?
cards.back: Automatically adjust pressure within a prescribed range in response to detected breathing patterns
cards.rationale: APAP changes pressure within settings based on device algorithms.
cards.keyPoint: APAP changes pressure within settings based on device algorithms.

cards.front: ASV is most associated with treatment of which type of breathing problem?
cards.back: Central breathing instability or certain central/complex sleep apnea patterns when appropriate
