cards.keyPoint: The guideline summary recommends starting at 1 L/min and titrating in 1 L/min increments with intervals no less than 15 minutes until SpO2 is 88%-94% unless facility policy specifies otherwise.

cards.front: An adult diagnostic portion shows AHI 18 after 70 minutes of sleep. Four hours remain in the night. What is the best interpretation for starting PAP under the split-night guideline summary?
cards.back: Criteria are not fully met because at least two hours of sleep in the diagnostic period are recommended
cards.rationale: The split-night summary recommends PAP initiation when moderate-to-severe OSA is observed over at least two hours of sleep time, with sufficient titration time remaining.
cards.keyPoint: The split-night summary recommends PAP initiation when moderate-to-severe OSA is observed over at least two hours of sleep time, with sufficient titration time remaining.

cards.front: A patient meets diagnostic criteria for split-night PAP, but only two hours remain for titration. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
cards.back: A full titration may be preferred because at least three hours are recommended to remain for titration
cards.rationale: The guideline summary recommends at least three hours remain for the titration portion.
cards.keyPoint: The guideline summary recommends at least three hours remain for the titration portion.

cards.front: A 10-year-old meets an adult-style AHI threshold early in the night. Which split-night principle is most important?
cards.back: Split-night studies should not be performed in children younger than 12 under the guideline summary
cards.rationale: The guideline summary states split-night studies should not be performed in children younger than 12.
cards.keyPoint: The guideline summary states split-night studies should not be performed in children younger than 12.

cards.front: After 35 minutes of stable sleep with obstructive events eliminated, the lab protocol allows down-titration. What is the best next action?
cards.back: Reduce EPAP or IPAP by at least 1 cm H2O with no less than a 10-minute interval until obstructive events reappear, then restore control
cards.rationale: Down-titration may be used after at least 30 minutes of sleep time with obstructive events eliminated; reductions are made with longer intervals and then pressure is raised again when events reappear.
cards.keyPoint: Down-titration may be used after at least 30 minutes of sleep time with obstructive events eliminated; reductions are made with longer intervals and then pressure is raised again when events reappear.

cards.front: Obstructive events are controlled but repetitive arousals and flow limitation suggest residual upper airway resistance. Which advanced titration technique may help under protocol?
cards.back: Exploration titration by increasing EPAP or IPAP 2-5 cm H2O above the controlled setting when appropriate
cards.rationale: Exploration titration may be used to eliminate upper airway resistance and repetitive arousals after respiratory events are controlled.
cards.keyPoint: Exploration titration may be used to eliminate upper airway resistance and repetitive arousals after respiratory events are controlled.

cards.front: At CPAP 13, the airflow signal suggests residual hypopneas, but leak suddenly rises above the mask's acceptable range. What should the technologist do first?
cards.back: Address mask or mouth leak and reassess before assuming pressure is inadequate
cards.rationale: Leak can invalidate interpretation and interfere with effective pressure delivery; it should be promptly addressed.
cards.keyPoint: Leak can invalidate interpretation and interfere with effective pressure delivery; it should be promptly addressed.

cards.front: A nasal mask patient has persistent mouth leak with dry mouth and unstable pressure delivery. Which response best fits PAP troubleshooting logic?
cards.back: Refit/adjust and consider chinstrap or an appropriate interface change according to protocol
cards.rationale: Mouth leak may be managed by refit/readjustment, chinstrap, humidification support, or changing interface according to protocol.
cards.keyPoint: Mouth leak may be managed by refit/readjustment, chinstrap, humidification support, or changing interface according to protocol.

cards.front: Which leak finding is most important to distinguish during PAP troubleshooting?
cards.back: Intentional vent leak that prevents rebreathing versus unintentional mask or mouth leak that can reduce effective therapy
cards.rationale: PAP interfaces have intentional leak for CO2 washout; unintentional leak is a therapeutic problem.
cards.keyPoint: PAP interfaces have intentional leak for CO2 washout; unintentional leak is a therapeutic problem.

cards.front: During CPAP titration, obstructive events improve but central apneas emerge in a repetitive pattern after pressure increases. What is the best technologist response?
cards.back: Avoid reflexively increasing CPAP; document the pattern and follow protocol/physician-directed pathway for treatment-emergent central apnea
cards.rationale: Treatment-emergent central apnea can appear during CPAP titration and should not be handled by blindly increasing pressure.
cards.keyPoint: Treatment-emergent central apnea can appear during CPAP titration and should not be handled by blindly increasing pressure.

cards.front: Why is supine REM sleep at the selected pressure especially valuable during PAP titration?
cards.back: Obstructive respiratory events are often most likely in supine REM, so control there strengthens pressure confidence
cards.rationale: Guidance emphasizes confirming therapeutic pressure in NREM and supine REM because obstructive events often worsen in supine REM.
cards.keyPoint: Guidance emphasizes confirming therapeutic pressure in NREM and supine REM because obstructive events often worsen in supine REM.

cards.front: Why should pressure response also be observed in NREM sleep during PAP titration?
cards.back: Treatment-emergent central sleep apnea is more likely to appear in NREM, so NREM observation helps detect instability
cards.rationale: The guideline summary notes obstructive events often worsen in supine REM, while treatment-emergent central sleep apnea is more likely in NREM.
cards.keyPoint: The guideline summary notes obstructive events often worsen in supine REM, while treatment-emergent central sleep apnea is more likely in NREM.

cards.front: During PAP titration, which airflow source is recommended for monitoring airflow under the interface?
cards.back: The airflow signal generated by the PAP device
cards.rationale: The titration guideline summary recommends PAP device-generated airflow during PAP titration and does not recommend an oral-nasal thermal sensor under the PAP interface.
cards.keyPoint: The titration guideline summary recommends PAP device-generated airflow during PAP titration and does not recommend an oral-nasal thermal sensor under the PAP interface.

cards.front: During PAP titration, what oximetry setting principle best supports accurate recognition of oxygen changes?
cards.back: Use a pulse oximeter with a maximum acceptable signal averaging time no greater than 3 seconds at a heart rate of 80 beats per minute
cards.rationale: The guideline summary specifies oximetry averaging expectations; excessive averaging can obscure clinically important changes.
cards.keyPoint: The guideline summary specifies oximetry averaging expectations; excessive averaging can obscure clinically important changes.

cards.front: A patient with suspected hypoventilation is undergoing PAP titration. Which monitoring addition best targets ventilation rather than oxygenation alone?
cards.back: Transcutaneous PCO2 or end-tidal PCO2 monitoring per order/protocol
cards.rationale: CO2 monitoring is used to assess hypoventilation/ventilation; oximetry alone reflects oxygenation and may miss ventilation problems.
cards.keyPoint: CO2 monitoring is used to assess hypoventilation/ventilation; oximetry alone reflects oxygenation and may miss ventilation problems.

cards.front: Which documentation is most important when PAP pressure is changed during titration?
cards.back: Pressure or mode change, rationale, leak, stage/position context, and patient response as required by protocol
cards.rationale: Technical documentation should include pressures, mode changes, reasons, leak, stages/position, patient behavior, and related observations.
cards.keyPoint: Technical documentation should include pressures, mode changes, reasons, leak, stages/position, patient behavior, and related observations.

cards.front: A technologist changes from a nasal mask to an oronasal mask because persistent mouth leak prevents stable pressure delivery. What must be documented?
cards.back: The reason for changing mask/interface and the effect on leak and therapy delivery
cards.rationale: Guidance includes documenting the reason for changing mask or device mode, plus leak and related data.
cards.keyPoint: Guidance includes documenting the reason for changing mask or device mode, plus leak and related data.

cards.front: Before a planned PAP titration, the patient says they have never seen a PAP mask and are worried about suffocating. What is the best pre-titration action?
cards.back: Provide PAP education, hands-on equipment demonstration, careful mask fitting, and acclimation before sleep when possible
cards.rationale: Guidance emphasizes PAP education, demonstration, mask fitting, and acclimation before titration.
cards.keyPoint: Guidance emphasizes PAP education, demonstration, mask fitting, and acclimation before titration.

cards.front: After pressure increases, obstructive events are controlled but the patient repeatedly awakens, complains pressure is too high, and sleep fragments. What is the best response?
cards.back: Reduce to a tolerable effective level or use comfort/BPAP strategies per protocol and document the response
cards.rationale: If the patient awakens and complains pressure is too high, pressure may be reduced to a level that allows return to sleep; comfort strategies or BPAP may be appropriate.
cards.keyPoint: If the patient awakens and complains pressure is too high, pressure may be reduced to a level that allows return to sleep; comfort strategies or BPAP may be appropriate.

cards.front: Which pattern most suggests the technologist should consider possible over-titration or pressure-related instability rather than simply raising pressure?
cards.back: New central apneas and sleep fragmentation appearing after obstruction improves at higher pressures
cards.rationale: Excessive pressure can contribute to sleep fragmentation and treatment-emergent central events; blindly raising pressure may worsen the problem.
cards.keyPoint: Excessive pressure can contribute to sleep fragmentation and treatment-emergent central events; blindly raising pressure may worsen the problem.

cards.front: A patient with OSA cannot tolerate PAP despite repeated mask and pressure-acclimation efforts. Which statement is most appropriate for the technologist's role?
cards.back: Document intolerance and support physician-directed discussion of alternatives such as oral appliance or surgical options; do not independently prescribe alternatives
cards.rationale: The technologist documents and educates within role boundaries; alternative therapy recommendations are physician-directed.
cards.keyPoint: The technologist documents and educates within role boundaries; alternative therapy recommendations are physician-directed.

cards.front: Which patient situation should make a technologist cautious about assuming APAP is appropriate without physician direction?
cards.back: Significant COPD or suspected hypoventilation with need for careful ventilation/oxygenation assessment
cards.rationale: Workbook/titration teaching commonly treats APAP as inappropriate or requiring caution in complex cardiopulmonary/hypoventilation contexts.
cards.keyPoint: Workbook/titration teaching commonly treats APAP as inappropriate or requiring caution in complex cardiopulmonary/hypoventilation contexts.

cards.front: During BPAP titration for hypoventilation risk, SpO2 improves as IPAP is increased and ventilation improves. What should the technologist remember about oxygen?
cards.back: Supplemental oxygen requirements may sometimes decrease as IPAP improves ventilation, but changes must follow order/protocol
cards.rationale: The guideline summary notes oxygen levels can sometimes be reduced in patients on BPAP when IPAP level is increased, but changes follow protocol and physician order.
cards.keyPoint: The guideline summary notes oxygen levels can sometimes be reduced in patients on BPAP when IPAP level is increased, but changes follow protocol and physician order.

cards.front: A BPAP order shows IPAP 18 and EPAP 10. What is the pressure support?
cards.back: 8 cm H2O
cards.rationale: Pressure support is IPAP minus EPAP: 18 - 10 = 8 cm H2O.
cards.keyPoint: Pressure support is IPAP minus EPAP: 18 - 10 = 8 cm H2O.

cards.front: In BPAP titration for OSA, what is EPAP most directly adjusted to control?
cards.back: Obstructive apneas and airway patency during expiration
cards.rationale: EPAP helps maintain airway patency and is increased along with IPAP when obstructive apneas persist.
cards.keyPoint: EPAP helps maintain airway patency and is increased along with IPAP when obstructive apneas persist.

cards.front: In BPAP titration, which problem most directly supports an IPAP increase while EPAP remains adequate?
cards.back: Persistent hypopneas, RERAs, or snoring after obstructive apneas are controlled
cards.rationale: IPAP can be increased for hypopneas, RERAs, and snoring when apnea control is maintained.
cards.keyPoint: IPAP can be increased for hypopneas, RERAs, and snoring when apnea control is maintained.

cards.front: A patient on BPAP has apparent flow limitation, but the mask pressure signal is unstable and the leak graph shows a sudden large leak beginning with a position change. What is the best first action?
cards.back: Check and correct the interface leak, then reassess respiratory events
cards.rationale: Leak and position changes can make signal interpretation unreliable; correct the source before changing therapy.
cards.keyPoint: Leak and position changes can make signal interpretation unreliable; correct the source before changing therapy.

cards.front: Which statement best reflects a high-quality PAP titration mindset?
cards.back: Use protocol-driven pressure changes while balancing event control, leak, oxygenation, sleep continuity, patient tolerance, and documentation
cards.rationale: Titration requires both protocol and judgment: control respiratory events while preserving safety, tolerance, signal quality, and documentation.
cards.keyPoint: Titration requires both protocol and judgment: control respiratory events while preserving safety, tolerance, signal quality, and documentation.

cards.front: A patient with neuromuscular disease and chronic hypoventilation is scheduled in the sleep lab. Which mindset is most appropriate for the technologist?
cards.back: Recognize that standard OSA PAP titration rules may not fully apply and follow physician orders/protocol for ventilatory support and CO2 monitoring
cards.rationale: Complex respiratory disease and hypoventilation require protocolized ventilatory support decisions beyond routine OSA titration.
cards.keyPoint: Complex respiratory disease and hypoventilation require protocolized ventilatory support decisions beyond routine OSA titration.

cards.front: After a difficult titration, the patient asks, 'What pressure will my doctor prescribe?' What is the best response?
cards.back: Explain that the interpreting sleep physician reviews the scored titration and makes the final prescription recommendation
cards.rationale: The technologist can provide general education but the final PAP recommendation comes from physician review.
cards.keyPoint: The technologist can provide general education but the final PAP recommendation comes from physician review.

cards.front: An adult split-night patient has AHI 36 after 2.2 hours of sleep. Three and a half hours remain. After PAP begins, CPAP reaches 15 cm H2O, obstructive hypopneas persist, the patient reports difficulty exhaling, and leak is acceptable. What is the best next step?
cards.back: Consider transition to BPAP per protocol, document the rationale, and continue titration if tolerated
cards.rationale: This combines split-night eligibility, high CPAP, persistent obstructive events, exhalation intolerance, and leak assessment. BPAP consideration is the best next move.
cards.keyPoint: This combines split-night eligibility, high CPAP, persistent obstructive events, exhalation intolerance, and leak assessment. BPAP consideration is the best next move.

cards.front: During physiologic calibrations, the patient performs right leg movement but the right anterior tibialis channel remains flat while the video confirms movement. What is the best first response?
cards.back: Check the electrode/sensor connection and correct the channel before lights out
cards.rationale: Physiologic calibration is the first test of patient-signal integrity; unexpected absent response should be corrected before starting.
cards.keyPoint: Physiologic calibration is the first test of patient-signal integrity; unexpected absent response should be corrected before starting.

cards.front: A physician orders an expanded seizure montage for a parasomnia differential. What should the technologist do during preparation?
cards.back: Set up the ordered montage and verify electrode placements and channel labels before recording
cards.rationale: The montage must match the order/protocol; additional EEG may be needed for seizure/parasomnia questions.
cards.keyPoint: The montage must match the order/protocol; additional EEG may be needed for seizure/parasomnia questions.

cards.front: Two EEG electrodes have very different impedances and the channel shows prominent 60-Hz artifact. Which principle explains why equal electrode quality matters?
cards.back: Common mode rejection works best when input impedances are low and relatively balanced
cards.rationale: Differential amplifiers reject common noise best when electrode impedances are low and balanced.
cards.keyPoint: Differential amplifiers reject common noise best when electrode impedances are low and balanced.

cards.front: An EEG channel has slow electrode artifact. A trainee suggests increasing filters until the tracing looks clean. What is the best response?
cards.back: Excessive filtering can distort/mask data; correct the electrode or source of artifact when possible
cards.rationale: Filters can change signal integrity; artifact should be corrected at the source whenever possible.
cards.keyPoint: Filters can change signal integrity; artifact should be corrected at the source whenever possible.

cards.front: Which filter mainly attenuates slow frequencies while allowing faster activity to pass?
cards.back: Low-frequency filter
cards.rationale: The low-frequency filter attenuates slow activity below its setting; the high-frequency filter attenuates faster activity above its setting.
cards.keyPoint: The low-frequency filter attenuates slow activity below its setting; the high-frequency filter attenuates faster activity above its setting.

cards.front: Chin EMG appears excessively smoothed after a setup change. Which error is most likely?
cards.back: The high-frequency filter may be set too low, attenuating faster muscle activity
cards.rationale: A low HFF can remove high-frequency muscle detail and make EMG appear falsely smoothed.
cards.keyPoint: A low HFF can remove high-frequency muscle detail and make EMG appear falsely smoothed.

cards.front: A 50 microvolt calibration signal displays smaller than expected after sensitivity is changed. What does this most directly affect?
cards.back: Display amplitude calibration/sensitivity, not the patient's actual brain voltage
cards.rationale: Sensitivity/gain affects how voltage is displayed and measured, not the physiologic voltage itself.
cards.keyPoint: Sensitivity/gain affects how voltage is displayed and measured, not the physiologic voltage itself.

cards.front: Modern digital PSG systems commonly store individual electrode data against a system reference. Why is that useful?
cards.back: It allows reformatting/remontaging during review if the recording supports it
cards.rationale: Digital systems often allow derived montages from stored referenced signals, but only if original signals and placements are valid.
cards.keyPoint: Digital systems often allow derived montages from stored referenced signals, but only if original signals and placements are valid.

cards.front: If an EOG electrode is placed incorrectly, what is the most likely consequence?
cards.back: Eye-movement polarity or channel interpretation may be misleading
cards.rationale: EOG electrode placement influences polarity and eye movement interpretation.
cards.keyPoint: EOG electrode placement influences polarity and eye movement interpretation.

cards.front: A leg EMG channel is placed over the wrong muscle group and shows little activity during obvious dorsiflexion. What is the best interpretation?
cards.back: The electrode placement should be checked because leg EMG should target the anterior tibialis region for limb movement detection
cards.rationale: Leg movement monitoring depends on correct anterior tibialis electrode placement.
cards.keyPoint: Leg movement monitoring depends on correct anterior tibialis electrode placement.

cards.front: A nasal pressure channel abruptly becomes flat after the patient turns, but thoracoabdominal effort and video suggest continued breathing. What is the best first action?
cards.back: Check the cannula/sensor position and tubing for displacement or blockage
cards.rationale: Sensor displacement or blockage can mimic absent airflow; troubleshoot before scoring a physiologic event.
cards.keyPoint: Sensor displacement or blockage can mimic absent airflow; troubleshoot before scoring a physiologic event.

cards.front: SpO2 suddenly drops to 72%, but the pleth waveform is poor, pulse rate no longer matches ECG, and the patient is moving. What is the best interpretation?
cards.back: Possible oximetry artifact; check the probe and patient while correlating with other signals
cards.rationale: Oximetry artifact should be evaluated with waveform quality, pulse correlation, motion, and patient assessment.
cards.keyPoint: Oximetry artifact should be evaluated with waveform quality, pulse correlation, motion, and patient assessment.

cards.front: A patient complains of tingling when touching equipment during setup. What is the best response?
cards.back: Stop and assess electrical safety according to facility protocol before continuing
cards.rationale: Electrical-safety complaints must be assessed and escalated per policy; patient safety comes first.
cards.keyPoint: Electrical-safety complaints must be assessed and escalated per policy; patient safety comes first.

cards.front: An EEG electrode remains above acceptable impedance after initial skin prep. What is the best next action?
cards.back: Reassess site preparation/electrode contact and correct it before relying on the channel
cards.rationale: High impedance commonly reflects poor contact and increases artifact risk; fix contact rather than masking artifact.
cards.keyPoint: High impedance commonly reflects poor contact and increases artifact risk; fix contact rather than masking artifact.

cards.front: During signal calibration, an oximeter's expected DC output is not accepted by the PSG software. What should the technologist suspect first?
cards.back: A connection/calibration-file/device-interface problem that needs correction before recording
cards.rationale: Signal calibration checks that ancillary device outputs are correctly processed by the software; failure suggests interface or calibration problems.
cards.keyPoint: Signal calibration checks that ancillary device outputs are correctly processed by the software; failure suggests interface or calibration problems.

cards.front: Sudden artifact appears in only one EEG channel while other channels sharing the patient and room remain clean. What is the most likely starting point?
cards.back: Check the specific electrode/lead involved in that channel
cards.rationale: Artifact limited to one channel often points to a channel-specific electrode or lead issue.
cards.keyPoint: Artifact limited to one channel often points to a channel-specific electrode or lead issue.

cards.front: Which setup best supports distinguishing obstructive from central apnea during PSG?
cards.back: Reliable airflow plus thoracic and abdominal respiratory effort signals
cards.rationale: Obstructive versus central classification depends on airflow and respiratory effort assessment.
cards.keyPoint: Obstructive versus central classification depends on airflow and respiratory effort assessment.

cards.front: A sensor artifact resembles an apnea pattern, but the video shows the cannula has fallen out and the effort belts continue normally. What is the best scoring/response mindset?
cards.back: Correct the sensor and avoid scoring the artifact as a respiratory event
cards.rationale: Video and signal correlation help prevent artifact from being misclassified as physiology.
cards.keyPoint: Video and signal correlation help prevent artifact from being misclassified as physiology.

cards.front: Why does an adequate sampling rate matter for ECG and snore channels?
cards.back: It preserves waveform definition needed for recognition and artifact assessment
cards.rationale: Sampling rate affects waveform definition and the ability to recognize details or artifacts.
cards.keyPoint: Sampling rate affects waveform definition and the ability to recognize details or artifacts.

cards.front: During PSG, the ECG shows a new very slow rhythm and the patient reports dizziness when checked. What is the best technologist response?
cards.back: Stay with/assess the patient and follow facility emergency/escalation protocol while documenting objectively
cards.rationale: New rhythm concern plus symptoms requires patient assessment and escalation per facility protocol.
cards.keyPoint: New rhythm concern plus symptoms requires patient assessment and escalation per facility protocol.

cards.front: A study has 45 obstructive apneas, 5 mixed apneas, 10 central apneas, and 90 hypopneas over 6 hours of sleep. What is the AHI?
cards.back: 25/hr
cards.rationale: AHI equals total apneas plus hypopneas divided by total sleep time: (45+5+10+90)/6 = 25/hr.
cards.keyPoint: AHI equals total apneas plus hypopneas divided by total sleep time: (45+5+10+90)/6 = 25/hr.

cards.front: Total recording time is 420 minutes and total sleep time is 336 minutes. What is sleep efficiency?
cards.rationale: Sleep efficiency = total sleep time divided by total recording time x 100 = 336/420 x 100 = 80%.
cards.keyPoint: Sleep efficiency = total sleep time divided by total recording time x 100 = 336/420 x 100 = 80%.

cards.front: Lights out is 22:30, sleep onset is 22:48, and first epoch of REM is 00:06. What is REM latency using sleep onset as the reference?
cards.back: 78 minutes
cards.rationale: REM latency is measured from sleep onset to first REM: 22:48 to 00:06 = 78 minutes.
cards.keyPoint: REM latency is measured from sleep onset to first REM: 22:48 to 00:06 = 78 minutes.

cards.front: Lights out is 22:17 and the first epoch scored as sleep begins at 22:41. What is sleep onset latency?
cards.back: 24 minutes
cards.rationale: Sleep onset latency is the time from lights out to the first epoch of sleep: 24 minutes.
cards.keyPoint: Sleep onset latency is the time from lights out to the first epoch of sleep: 24 minutes.

cards.front: A patient has 180 periodic limb movements during 6 hours of sleep. What is the PLM index?
cards.back: 30/hr
cards.rationale: PLMI = PLMs divided by hours of sleep = 180/6 = 30/hr.
cards.keyPoint: PLMI = PLMs divided by hours of sleep = 180/6 = 30/hr.

cards.front: TST is 400 minutes. Stage N3 totals 60 minutes. What percentage of TST is N3?
cards.rationale: N3 percentage = 60/400 x 100 = 15%.
cards.keyPoint: N3 percentage = 60/400 x 100 = 15%.

cards.front: A study has AHI 6/hr but frequent RERAs causing arousals. Which metric better captures the added respiratory burden?
cards.back: RDI
cards.rationale: RDI includes apneas, hypopneas, and RERAs; AHI alone may underestimate respiratory disturbance when RERAs are frequent.
cards.keyPoint: RDI includes apneas, hypopneas, and RERAs; AHI alone may underestimate respiratory disturbance when RERAs are frequent.

cards.front: Airflow is absent for a qualifying duration, and respiratory effort continues in both thoracic and abdominal channels. Which event type is most consistent?
cards.back: Obstructive apnea
cards.rationale: Absent airflow with continued effort supports obstructive apnea.
cards.keyPoint: Absent airflow with continued effort supports obstructive apnea.

cards.front: Airflow is absent for a qualifying duration and both thoracic and abdominal effort are absent. Which event type is most consistent?
cards.back: Central apnea
cards.rationale: Absent airflow with absent respiratory effort is consistent with central apnea.
cards.keyPoint: Absent airflow with absent respiratory effort is consistent with central apnea.

cards.front: An apnea begins with absent respiratory effort and later shows resumed effort before airflow returns. Which event type is most consistent?
cards.back: Mixed apnea
cards.rationale: Mixed apnea has central and obstructive components within the same event.
cards.keyPoint: Mixed apnea has central and obstructive components within the same event.

cards.front: Airflow flattens for at least 10 seconds with increasing effort and ends in arousal, but the event does not meet apnea or hypopnea criteria. What is the best classification if criteria are met?
cards.back: RERA
cards.rationale: RERAs involve increased effort/flow limitation ending in arousal without meeting apnea/hypopnea criteria.
cards.keyPoint: RERAs involve increased effort/flow limitation ending in arousal without meeting apnea/hypopnea criteria.

cards.front: Which EEG change best supports scoring an arousal, assuming all current AASM criteria are otherwise met?
cards.back: An abrupt shift in EEG frequency lasting at least 3 seconds after sufficient stable sleep
cards.rationale: Arousals require an abrupt EEG frequency shift lasting the required minimum duration and appropriate preceding sleep.
cards.keyPoint: Arousals require an abrupt EEG frequency shift lasting the required minimum duration and appropriate preceding sleep.

cards.front: After a K complex establishes N2, the next epoch has low-amplitude mixed-frequency EEG without new K complexes or spindles and no transition criteria out of N2. What is the best scoring approach?
cards.back: Continue scoring N2 if no rule-defined end of N2 occurs
cards.rationale: N2 can continue after defining features unless criteria to end N2 are met.
cards.keyPoint: N2 can continue after defining features unless criteria to end N2 are met.

cards.topic: REM with K complex watch point
cards.front: While reviewing a transition into REM, an epoch has low chin EMG and rapid eye movements, but it also contains a clear sleep spindle. What is the safest scoring approach?
cards.back: Do not score REM automatically; apply the current AASM transition and continuation rules because N2-defining activity can alter the stage call
cards.rationale: Low chin EMG and rapid eye movements are REM-supporting features, but a clear N2-defining feature creates a rule-sensitive transition/continuation decision. The scorer should apply current AASM scoring rules rather than using a single-feature shortcut.
cards.keyPoint: Low chin EMG and rapid eye movements are REM-supporting features, but a clear N2-defining feature creates a rule-sensitive transition/continuation decision. The scorer should apply current AASM scoring rules rather than using a single-feature shortcut.

cards.front: An adult epoch contains slow-wave activity meeting amplitude/frequency criteria for 7 seconds in a 30-second epoch. Which stage is most likely if no other rule overrides?
cards.back: Not N3 based on the 20% threshold alone
cards.rationale: N3 requires slow-wave activity occupying at least 20% of the epoch; 7 seconds is below 20% of 30 seconds.
cards.keyPoint: N3 requires slow-wave activity occupying at least 20% of the epoch; 7 seconds is below 20% of 30 seconds.

cards.front: Why should pediatric scoring questions be handled carefully in the app's mock bank?
cards.back: Age-specific scoring and respiratory criteria can differ, so items must identify age and use the current AASM pediatric rules
cards.rationale: Pediatric scoring often has age-specific rules; hard items must give enough age/context and cite current rules.
cards.keyPoint: Pediatric scoring often has age-specific rules; hard items must give enough age/context and cite current rules.

cards.front: An MSLT has sleep latencies of 4, 7, 9, 12, and 18 minutes. What is the mean sleep latency?
cards.back: 10 minutes
cards.rationale: Mean sleep latency = (4+7+9+12+18)/5 = 50/5 = 10 minutes.
cards.keyPoint: Mean sleep latency = (4+7+9+12+18)/5 = 50/5 = 10 minutes.

cards.front: An MSLT shows short sleep latency, but the prior PSG documented insufficient sleep time and frequent untreated respiratory events. What is the best interpretation habit?
cards.back: Treat the MSLT result as potentially confounded and follow protocol/physician interpretation process
cards.rationale: MSLT interpretation depends on prior sleep, medications, untreated disorders, and protocol validity.
cards.keyPoint: MSLT interpretation depends on prior sleep, medications, untreated disorders, and protocol validity.

cards.front: A report lists TST as 300 minutes, apneas as 60, hypopneas as 90, and AHI as 15/hr. What should the scorer recognize?
cards.back: The AHI appears inconsistent and should be checked because 150 events over 5 hours equals 30/hr
cards.rationale: 300 minutes is 5 hours; (60+90)/5 = 30/hr. The report should be corrected before release.
cards.keyPoint: 300 minutes is 5 hours; (60+90)/5 = 30/hr. The report should be corrected before release.

cards.front: Which scoring approach is safest when respiratory signals are unreliable due to artifact during a segment?
cards.back: Use available valid signals, mark/document artifact per protocol, and avoid overcalling events from unreliable channels
cards.rationale: Scoring should use valid signals and document artifact; unreliable channels should not drive unsupported event calls.
cards.keyPoint: Scoring should use valid signals and document artifact; unreliable channels should not drive unsupported event calls.

cards.front: A patient scheduled for PSG/MSLT reports taking an SSRI. What is the best technologist-level concern?
cards.back: Document it because REM-suppressing medications can affect REM/SOREMP interpretation and study context
cards.rationale: Medication/substance review matters because some antidepressants can affect REM expression and daytime testing interpretation.
cards.keyPoint: Medication/substance review matters because some antidepressants can affect REM expression and daytime testing interpretation.

cards.front: A patient on modafinil is scheduled for an MSLT and the medication list was not reviewed until the morning of testing. What is the best technologist action?
cards.back: Notify/follow lab protocol and document the medication because wake-promoting agents can affect sleep latency
cards.rationale: Wake-promoting agents can alter sleep latency; medication information must be documented and handled by protocol.
cards.keyPoint: Wake-promoting agents can alter sleep latency; medication information must be documented and handled by protocol.

cards.front: A patient reports taking an opioid and a sedative before the study. Which is the best technologist-level response?
cards.back: Document the substances, monitor carefully, and follow safety/protocol escalation if respiratory depression or concerning events occur
cards.rationale: Sedating medications and opioids can affect respiration/arousability and must be documented and monitored within protocol.
cards.keyPoint: Sedating medications and opioids can affect respiration/arousability and must be documented and monitored within protocol.

cards.front: A patient complains of excessive daytime sleepiness. Which commonly used questionnaire best quantifies subjective sleepiness for the sleep record?
cards.back: Epworth Sleepiness Scale
cards.rationale: The Epworth Sleepiness Scale is commonly used to assess subjective daytime sleepiness in sleep evaluation.
cards.keyPoint: The Epworth Sleepiness Scale is commonly used to assess subjective daytime sleepiness in sleep evaluation.

cards.front: A night-shift worker reports insomnia when trying to sleep during the day and sleepiness during work hours. What is the best assessment habit?
cards.back: Document work schedule, sleep timing, light exposure, and symptoms as possible circadian/shift-work context
cards.rationale: Sleep schedule and circadian context are key parts of patient assessment, especially for shift workers.
cards.keyPoint: Sleep schedule and circadian context are key parts of patient assessment, especially for shift workers.

cards.front: Before hookup, the technologist notices the order requests PSG with seizure montage, but the schedule label says routine PSG. What is the best action?
cards.back: Clarify the order/protocol before setup so the correct test is performed
cards.rationale: Order review and clarification are essential to performing the correct procedure.
cards.keyPoint: Order review and clarification are essential to performing the correct procedure.

cards.front: A patient becomes tearful during hookup and says they feel feeling confined by the wires. What is the best first response?
cards.back: Pause, reassure, explain each step, offer reasonable comfort adjustments, and continue only as tolerated per protocol
cards.rationale: Patient communication and education improve cooperation and safety; the technologist should stay within role boundaries.
cards.keyPoint: Patient communication and education improve cooperation and safety; the technologist should stay within role boundaries.

cards.front: A patient reports drinking alcohol before the study. Why does that matter for the record?
cards.back: Alcohol can alter sleep architecture, respiratory events, arousal threshold, and interpretation context
cards.rationale: Alcohol can affect sleep and breathing and should be documented for interpretation context.
cards.keyPoint: Alcohol can affect sleep and breathing and should be documented for interpretation context.

cards.front: A patient with morbid obesity, morning headaches, and chronic daytime hypercapnia is ordered for PSG with CO2 monitoring. What should the technologist anticipate?
cards.back: Possible sleep-related hypoventilation/OHS context requiring careful ventilation monitoring per order
cards.rationale: History can indicate hypoventilation risk; CO2 monitoring helps assess ventilation rather than oxygenation alone.
cards.keyPoint: History can indicate hypoventilation risk; CO2 monitoring helps assess ventilation rather than oxygenation alone.

cards.front: After the PSG, the patient asks, 'Do I have sleep apnea and what pressure do I need?' What is the best response?
cards.back: Explain that the physician will interpret the scored study and provide diagnosis/treatment recommendations; avoid giving a diagnosis
cards.rationale: The technologist supports education but should not provide diagnosis or prescription outside scope.
cards.keyPoint: The technologist supports education but should not provide diagnosis or prescription outside scope.

cards.front: Several PSG channels suddenly show widespread regular electrical interference. The technologist suspects the noise may be related to connected equipment and unintended grounding paths. Which action is most appropriate?
cards.back: Recognize a possible ground loop/electrical source, check connected equipment and cables according to lab policy, and escalate safety concerns as needed
cards.rationale: Ground loop or electrical-source problems can create widespread electrical artifact. The technologist should think safety first, follow lab policy, check equipment/cables/connections, and involve appropriate support rather than bypassing safety grounding or scoring artifact as physiology.
cards.keyPoint: Ground loop or electrical-source problems can create widespread electrical artifact. The technologist should think safety first, follow lab policy, check equipment/cables/connections, and involve appropriate support rather than bypassing safety grounding or scoring artifact as physiology.

cards.front: During hookup, conductive paste from two nearby EEG electrodes touches and creates an unwanted electrical connection between the sites. What problem should the technologist suspect?
cards.back: Salt bridge between electrodes
cards.rationale: A salt bridge occurs when conductive material such as paste, gel, sweat, or moisture connects two electrodes. It can reduce the true differential signal and distort the recording. The technologist should clean/separate and reapply or correct the electrodes rather than treating it as normal physiology.
cards.keyPoint: A salt bridge occurs when conductive material such as paste, gel, sweat, or moisture connects two electrodes. It can reduce the true differential signal and distort the recording. The technologist should clean/separate and reapply or correct the electrodes rather than treating it as normal physiology.

cards.front: A patient reports taking a sedating antihistamine before the PSG. What is the best RPSGT-focused reason to document this?
cards.back: It may shorten sleep latency and suppress REM sleep.
cards.rationale: Sedating antihistamines can make a patient sleepy and may reduce REM. Medication history belongs in the clinical context and report documentation.
cards.keyPoint: Sedating antihistamines can make a patient sleepy and may reduce REM. Medication history belongs in the clinical context and report documentation.

cards.front: A patient stopped an SSRI shortly before an MSLT and now has multiple SOREMPs. What is the key interpretation concern?
cards.back: REM rebound may create a false-positive pattern.
cards.rationale: REM-suppressing medications can hide SOREMPs, and withdrawal can cause REM rebound. Medication changes must be documented and interpreted by the sleep physician.
cards.keyPoint: REM-suppressing medications can hide SOREMPs, and withdrawal can cause REM rebound. Medication changes must be documented and interpreted by the sleep physician.

cards.front: During a PSG, a patient taking chronic opioids shows repeated central apneas and rising CO2. What is the best technologist response?
cards.back: Document, monitor, and follow lab escalation protocol.
cards.rationale: Opioids may depress ventilatory drive and contribute to central apnea or hypoventilation. The technologist documents and follows safety/escalation policy, not medication management.
cards.keyPoint: Opioids may depress ventilatory drive and contribute to central apnea or hypoventilation. The technologist documents and follows safety/escalation policy, not medication management.

cards.front: Which medication class is commonly associated with REM suppression and increased PLMS in sleep-study teaching tables?
cards.back: SSRIs
cards.rationale: SSRIs are commonly taught as REM-suppressing and may be associated with increased PLMS. This can affect staging and interpretation context.
cards.keyPoint: SSRIs are commonly taught as REM-suppressing and may be associated with increased PLMS. This can affect staging and interpretation context.

cards.front: Why is alcohol use before sleep important in a PSG history?
cards.back: It may shorten sleep latency early, fragment sleep later, suppress REM, and worsen OSA.
cards.rationale: Alcohol has multiple sleep and breathing effects. It is a common exam-style distinction because it can make sleep start faster but worsen later sleep and airway stability.
cards.keyPoint: Alcohol has multiple sleep and breathing effects. It is a common exam-style distinction because it can make sleep start faster but worsen later sleep and airway stability.

cards.front: A stimulant or wake-promoting medication is taken before MSLT. What result may be falsely affected?
cards.back: Sleep latency may look longer, making the patient appear less sleepy.
cards.rationale: Alerting medications can mask sleepiness and increase sleep latency, which can confound MSLT/MWT interpretation.
cards.keyPoint: Alerting medications can mask sleepiness and increase sleep latency, which can confound MSLT/MWT interpretation.

cards.front: A patient on long-term dopamine therapy for RLS reports symptoms starting earlier in the day and spreading to the arms. What term best fits this pattern?
cards.back: Augmentation
cards.rationale: Augmentation is a worsening pattern associated with dopaminergic RLS therapy: earlier onset, stronger symptoms, spread, or need for higher dose.
cards.keyPoint: Augmentation is a worsening pattern associated with dopaminergic RLS therapy: earlier onset, stronger symptoms, spread, or need for higher dose.

cards.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
cards.front: A patient asks whether to stop a REM-suppressing antidepressant before an MSLT. What is the best technologist response?
cards.back: Follow the ordering provider/lab protocol and do not independently stop medications.
cards.rationale: Medication washout/taper decisions belong to the provider. The technologist follows protocol and documents medication use and changes.
cards.keyPoint: Medication washout/taper decisions belong to the provider. The technologist follows protocol and documents medication use and changes.

cards.front: Which patient statement should still be documented even if the patient says it is not a prescription medication?
cards.back: I took an over-the-counter sleep aid last night.
cards.rationale: OTC medications, supplements, caffeine, nicotine, alcohol, and cannabis can affect sleepiness, REM, breathing, and test interpretation.
cards.keyPoint: OTC medications, supplements, caffeine, nicotine, alcohol, and cannabis can affect sleepiness, REM, breathing, and test interpretation.

cards.front: A PSG shows increased central events in a patient using opioids. What should the RPSGT remember?
cards.back: Opioids can be associated with central sleep apnea or hypoventilation patterns.
cards.rationale: Opioids can depress ventilatory drive. The technologist recognizes and documents patterns and follows protocol; diagnosis belongs to the physician.
cards.keyPoint: Opioids can depress ventilatory drive. The technologist recognizes and documents patterns and follows protocol; diagnosis belongs to the physician.

cards.front: Which medication is commonly used as a respiratory stimulant for apnea of prematurity?
cards.back: Caffeine citrate
cards.rationale: Caffeine citrate is a key methylxanthine therapy for apnea of prematurity and is a pediatric/neonatal medication concept.
cards.keyPoint: Caffeine citrate is a key methylxanthine therapy for apnea of prematurity and is a pediatric/neonatal medication concept.

cards.front: In medication history, what does OTC usually mean?
cards.back: Over-the-counter
cards.rationale: OTC medications can still affect sleep architecture, REM, respiratory stability, and daytime testing, so they must be documented.
cards.keyPoint: OTC medications can still affect sleep architecture, REM, respiratory stability, and daytime testing, so they must be documented.

cards.front: Why do REM-suppressing medications matter when reviewing MSLT results?
cards.back: They can hide SOREMPs; stopping them can cause REM rebound.
cards.rationale: This is one of the highest-yield medication watch points for hypersomnolence testing.
cards.keyPoint: This is one of the highest-yield medication watch points for hypersomnolence testing.

cards.front: Which medication group can cause insomnia or increased alertness and should be documented when evaluating sleep complaints?
cards.back: Stimulants
cards.rationale: Stimulants and wake-promoting drugs may increase sleep latency and reduce total sleep time, and they can mask sleepiness on daytime testing.
cards.keyPoint: Stimulants and wake-promoting drugs may increase sleep latency and reduce total sleep time, and they can mask sleepiness on daytime testing.

cards.front: A patient says a medication makes them very sleepy during hook-up. What is the best first RPSGT action?
cards.back: Document the medication effect, assess safety per lab policy, and notify appropriate staff if needed.
cards.rationale: The technologist documents medication effects and follows safety policy. Medication changes and medical advice belong to the provider.
cards.keyPoint: The technologist documents medication effects and follows safety policy. Medication changes and medical advice belong to the provider.

cards.front: Before applying scalp electrodes, the technologist notices possible head lice or nits. What is the best professional response?
cards.back: Pause the hookup, protect the patient's dignity, and follow facility infection-control policy
cards.rationale: Possible head lice creates an infection-control, linen/equipment, and patient-privacy concern. The technologist should remain calm, avoid humiliating the patient, follow facility policy, and document/escalate through the proper channel.
cards.keyPoint: Possible head lice creates an infection-control, linen/equipment, and patient-privacy concern. The technologist should remain calm, avoid humiliating the patient, follow facility policy, and document/escalate through the proper channel.

cards.front: During hookup, a patient reports seeing a bed bug on their clothing or belongings. What should the technologist do first?
cards.back: Protect the patient's privacy, pause as needed, and follow the facility bed-bug/infection-control procedure
cards.rationale: A possible bed-bug exposure is handled through facility policy, environmental services/infection-control procedures, patient privacy, and appropriate documentation. The technologist should not spread contamination, shame the patient, or continue as if nothing happened.
cards.keyPoint: A possible bed-bug exposure is handled through facility policy, environmental services/infection-control procedures, patient privacy, and appropriate documentation. The technologist should not spread contamination, shame the patient, or continue as if nothing happened.

cards.front: During PSG signal setup, a learner asks why a channel has input 1 and input 2. What is the best explanation of what the differential amplifier does?
cards.back: It amplifies the voltage difference between input 1 and input 2 while rejecting signals common to both inputs
cards.rationale: A differential amplifier compares two electrode inputs, amplifies the difference, and helps reject common-mode signals that are picked up by both inputs.
cards.keyPoint: A differential amplifier compares two electrode inputs, amplifies the difference, and helps reject common-mode signals that are picked up by both inputs.
